How to read this review
Ungauged Basin Discharge

A literature review · 17 sections · 163 references

    Every quantitative claim was taken from the source paper’s own abstract or full text.

    Orientation

    How to read this review

    Prediction in ungauged basins is one problem with seven standing answers, and they differ in a single respect: what information gets moved into the basin that has no record.

    The families are not rivals so much as different bets about where the recoverable information lives — and they fail in different places, which is why the choice depends on your region rather than on a league table.

    Where things are

    • §1–§2 — the problem, and what the PUB decade settled and did not settle.
    • §3 — all seven families side by side — read it before the family sections.
    • §4–§10 — one section per family, in the order shown above.
    • §11 — the geometry layer: terrain, channel shape and the global datasets both satellite families depend on.
    • §12 — data, benchmarks and uncertainty: large-sample datasets, metrics and uncertainty, which apply to every family.
    • §13 — open gaps, including where a conceptual inundation model fits.
    • §14 — where one particular research programme sits in all of this, and what to watch out for.
    • §15–§16 — a ten-paper reading path, then the full reference list.

    Short of time? Read §3 and §13, then let §15 tell you what to read in the literature itself.

    Near the end of each of §1–§14 is a Read these first card: the four to six papers that cover most of that section, each with a Key points pop-up summarising the paper and why it comes first.

    On accuracy

    Every quantitative claim here was taken from the source paper’s own abstract or full text, opened during the writing of this review — not from memory and not from another paper’s description of it.

    §16 sets out how each source was checked. Since 17 October 2026 every one of the 163 has been read in full, and §16 records the two partial cases. Statements that are general method knowledge rather than sourced claims are marked †, and the parts of §13 that are synthesis rather than published findings say so.

    Section 01

    The problem: discharge where there is no record

    A basin is “ungauged” relative to a question, not in absolute terms.

    A catchment may have a record long enough for mean annual flow but far too short for a 1-in-100-year peak; it may have been gauged until 1995 and ungauged since. The IAHS definition keeps this relative sense: ungauged means the discharge data needed for the prediction at hand are inadequate or absent.

    This describes most rivers on Earth, and the situation is deteriorating. A 2026 commentary in npj Natural Hazards reports that roughly two-thirds of national hydrological networks are in decline, citing a 2018 World Bank assessment, and that the number of river runoff series available through the Global Runoff Data Centre has trended downward since the early-to-mid 1980s (Olsson et al. 2026). Their argument is pointed: machine-learning hydrology is being built on a shrinking observational foundation.

    The unifying idea: information transfer

    Every method in this review answers one question in a different way — what information is moved into the ungauged basin, and on what grounds? The candidates are:

    • Other catchments. Transfer calibrated parameters or flow statistics from donor gauges, chosen by distance or by similarity.
    • Catchment attributes. Map physiography, climate and soils directly onto model parameters or flow indices through a regression or a learned function.
    • Process understanding. Derive parameters from first principles or from mapped physical properties, so no donor is needed.
    • The river itself. Observe width, water-surface elevation and slope from space, and invert hydraulics for discharge.
    • A proxy for the gauge record. Calibrate on a satellite signal that merely correlates with discharge, in place of the discharge series.
    • A large sample, all at once. Train one model across hundreds or thousands of catchments so it learns the regional mapping implicitly.

    How much skill is actually lost

    In daily NSE, a model calibrated at the site scores about 0.75; without a gauge, about 0.6–0.7. The loss is largest in arid, small and sparsely gauged catchments.

    • The PUB baseline (Parajka et al. 2013; 34 studies, 3,874 catchments): median NSE 0.58 for spatial proximity and 0.66 for similarity; 0.54 arid, 0.64 cold, 0.66 humid; about 0.60 below 300 km2 against about 0.80 in larger catchments. Proximity and geostatistics win where gauges are dense, regression usually does worse, and the number of regionalised parameters makes no clear difference.
    • After 2013 (Guo et al. 2020; 33 studies): 0.75 calibrated, 0.69 by similarity, 0.66 by regression. Every method gets worse as aridity rises and better as gauge density rises.
    • Regional deep learning: an LSTM never trained on the basin reached 0.69 against 0.64 calibrated (Kratzert et al. 2019), and 0.78 against 0.58–0.63 regionalised (Arsenault et al. 2023). It needs hundreds of gauged catchments, and it falls to 0.55–0.62 when whole regions are held out (Feng et al. 2023).
    • A few measurements recover much of the loss (Seibert and Beven 2009; 11 Swedish catchments): poor below four, clearly better from eight, and levelling off near 32. Six well-chosen days gave about 0.59, against about 0.8 for full calibration. The best strategies assume the peak-flow day can be picked in advance.

    The upshot: little skill is lost where gauges are dense, and most is lost where PUB began, in arid and sparsely gauged regions. The table below shows where the wider list of open problems stands.

    Parajka et al. 2013 and Seibert and Beven 2009 read in full 17 October 2026.

    The problem restated in 2019: twenty-three unsolved problems

    The most recent statement of what hydrology has not solved is the community list of Blöschl et al. (2019): 23 questions in seven themes, voted on by 230 scientists (§02 describes how). It covers all of hydrology, not only ungauged prediction, so most of the 23 fall outside this review. The table paraphrases each question and says where the literature reviewed here stands on it.

    How to read the status column

    The status is this review’s reading of the evidence it cites, not a verdict from the 2019 paper or any other source. None of the 23 is solved outright. Progress shown, Partly addressed and Still open are used as in §02; outside this review means the question is real but this review does not cover the literature that would answer it.

    Read these first

    Start with these. Between them they cover most of what this section concludes. Key points opens a short summary of each paper and why it comes first.

    1. R6Parajka et al. 2013 HESSthe skill baseline every later result is read against

      Main points

      • A meta-analysis of 34 studies and 3,874 catchments asking whether regionalisation methods have generalisable rankings.
      • Median daily NSE: 0.54 arid, 0.64 cold, 0.66 humid; 0.58 for spatial proximity and 0.66 for similarity.
      • Humid beats arid, large beats small, and dense gauge networks favour proximity and geostatistics; regression tends to do worst.

      Why read it first

      It is the main cross-study evidence on which methods work where, and it sets the baseline any ungauged-basin result is read against.

    2. R1Seibert and Beven 2009 HESShow far a few measurements go

      Main points

      • Treats eleven Swedish catchments (6.6–950 km²) as ungauged and asks how few single discharge measurements constrain HBV usefully.
      • The ensemble is poor below four observations, clearly better from eight, and plateaus around 32.
      • Six well-chosen days reach a median efficiency of about 0.59, against about 0.54 for four to eight random days and about 0.8 for full calibration.

      Why read it first

      It puts a number on the cheapest alternative to prediction without data: a handful of gauged days. The best strategies assume the peak-flow day can be chosen in advance, which real field logistics rarely allow.

    3. R16Blöschl et al. 2019 Hydrological Sciences Journalthe open problems, as the community states them

      Main points

      • A community consultation of 230 scientists distilled about 260 candidate problems into 23 unsolved problems in seven themes.
      • Question 17 asks what proxies best replace “few accurate data by many less accurate data”; Question 19 asks for models that extrapolate to changing conditions.
      • The community preferred continuity over radical redirection; the authors note a European bias in the workshops and working group.

      Why read it first

      It is the field’s current, broadly owned agenda, and it names the surrogate-discharge problem (Q17) as open.

    4. R10Olsson et al. 2026 npj Natural Hazardswhy the gauge network’s decline raises the stakes

      Main points

      • A commentary on the paradox of AI advances built on declining in-situ networks in hydrometeorology.
      • Roughly two-thirds of national hydrological networks are in decline (citing a 2018 World Bank assessment); river-flow series available through the GRDC have trended down since the mid-1980s.
      • Warns that the decline “will gradually erode the performance and reliability of AI-based tools”, and proposes countermeasures.

      Why read it first

      It frames why prediction without gauges matters more each year, and why the most data-hungry methods face a shrinking foundation.

    Section 02

    The PUB Decade and its legacy

    The three IAHS decades at a glance

    The International Association of Hydrological Sciences has organised its science in three consecutive decades. HELPING’s plan calls them a trilogy: from hydrological predictions (PUB), to change and interdisciplinarity (Panta Rhei), to solutions (HELPING). Only the first was about ungauged basins. The rest of this section looks at PUB in detail and at what happened to its question afterwards.

    Between the decades sits the community’s own restatement of what remains unsolved, the 23 questions of 2019 (Blöschl et al. 2019). §01 sets out where each of those stands.

    The IAHS Prediction in Ungauged Basins initiative ran from 2003 to 2012, closing with the PUB Symposium in Delft on 23–25 October 2012.

    Its science and implementation plan was published at the launch: Sivapalan et al. (2003), Hydrological Sciences Journal 48(6), 857–880.

    Its review paper (Hrachowitz et al. 2013, Hydrological Sciences Journal 58(6), 1198–1255) is the single most-cited document in this literature and the right place to start reading.

    What PUB diagnosed

    The initiative identified three causes of predictive uncertainty in ungauged basins:

    1. Incomplete understanding of the processes underlying catchment response, and the feedbacks between them — producing unrealistic models with high uncertainty.
    2. Incomplete understanding of multi-scale spatio-temporal heterogeneity across landscapes and climates, since most small catchments worldwide are ungauged.
    3. Unsuitable regionalisation techniques, caused by a shortage of comparative studies and of understanding of what physically governs robust transfer.

    The intended paradigm shift

    PUB’s central strategy was to infer hydrological function (how a catchment responds) from catchment form (climate, topography, geology, soil, land use). That required moving the field away from parameter fitting toward process understanding — treating models as hypotheses to be tested rather than as given.

    The review is candid about why this mattered. Citing Kirchner (2006), it describes over-parameterised models that fit calibration data while behaving as “mathematical marionettes”, unable to reproduce behaviour under untrained conditions. Good calibration scores were never the point.

    The decade and its aftermath at a glance

    The left column is PUB itself. The second is the IAHS decades that followed it — which turned the community toward change and society rather than toward ungauged prediction. The third is where the diagnosis and the community’s own agenda were written, and the fourth is the assessment of what regionalisation actually achieved once the decade closed.

    Solid arrows mark a documented build-on or extension; dashed arrows mark a study that tests, benchmarks or limits another. The dashed link to Sivapalan marks his diagnosis of why PUB’s form-to-function ambition stalled.

    What it did not settle

    PUB did not deliver a general theory connecting catchment form to function, and it did not produce a regionalisation method that works reliably across climates. Prediction in ungauged basins is no longer a named IAHS decade — but the problem it named did not go away, and the record of what happened next is set out below.

    A note on reading order

    Hrachowitz et al. (2013) predates essentially all of the machine-learning literature. Treat it as the authoritative statement of the problem, not of the current state of solutions.

    PUB’s own problems, and where they stand now

    PUB stated its problems twice. The 2003 science plan (Sivapalan et al. 2003) posed six science questions; the 2013 closing review (Hrachowitz et al. 2013) diagnosed three causes of predictive uncertainty. The table follows each one into the literature this review covers.

    How to read the status column

    The status is this review’s reading of the evidence in the cited rows, not a verdict any source gives. None of these problems has been solved outright. Progress shown means published results now answer a large part of the question; Partly addressed means there is real progress but a central part is still open; Still open means the literature mostly documents the problem rather than answers it.

PUB science question 1 (2003) Partly addressed The gaps were diagnosed at the decade’s close (Hrachowitz et al. 2013) and explained afterwards: Sivapalan (2018) names unmappable heterogeneity as the “virtual impasse” behind physically based prediction No general form-to-function theory emerged (§02, §06)
    What is the minimum information needed to reduce predictive uncertainty? PUB science question 2 (2003) Progress shown

    • Limits of acceptability derived from signatures, separating hard from soft information (Winsemius et al. 2009; Yadav et al. 2007, §04)

    After the decade: where the problem went, 2013–2026

    The IAHS decade that succeeded PUB was Panta Rhei (2013–2022), launched in the same issue of Hydrological Sciences Journal that carried the PUB closing review — Hrachowitz et al. occupy pp. 1198–1255 and Montanari et al. pp. 1256–1275 of volume 58(6). Panta Rhei turned the community toward change and hydrology–society coupling; it closed with its own synthesis in Kreibich et al. (2025), and IAHS then moved to HELPING (Arheimer et al. 2024).

    Three further strands carry the PUB question forward: a diagnosis of why form-to-function stalled (Sivapalan), the community’s own restatement of its open problems (the UPH list), and a dedicated review of what regionalisation achieved in the post-PUB period (Guo et al.).

    What this record shows

    Three things worth carrying into an introduction.

    • The institutional attention moved; the problem did not. After 2012 no IAHS decade has been named for ungauged prediction, yet Guo et al. found publications on PUB rising through the 2010s with the contributing countries expanding sharply after 2013. The field kept working on it without a banner.
    • The community restated the problem in its own words in 2019, and two of the 23 questions are the ones this review spends most of its length on: what proxies can substitute for scarce accurate data (Question 17, which is §08), and how to build models that extrapolate beyond observed conditions (Question 19, which §09 and §10 now answer with measurements rather than suspicions).
    • The explanation for PUB’s central failure has itself been published. Sivapalan’s “virtual impasse” argument — that heterogeneity cannot be mapped everywhere and should instead be replaced by the ecosystem function it performs — is the most direct answer in the literature to why form-to-function did not arrive on schedule. It is also, read sideways, an argument for exactly the hybrid approaches of §10: let the data learn the mapping that cannot be measured.
    For a conceptual modeller

    Thyer et al. (2024) is the paper in this section closest to your own position. It argues that conceptual models are what practitioners actually use, that their weakness is internal process resolution, and that the fix is to test them against physically resolved models rather than against historical performance metrics. Read with Feng et al. (2023) in §10, it makes the case that the defensible claim for a conceptual model is fidelity, not NSE.

    Read these first

    Start with these. Between them they cover most of what this section concludes. Key points opens a short summary of each paper and why it comes first.

    1. R124Sivapalan et al. 2003 Hydrological Sciences Journalthe plan and the definition of “ungauged”

      Main points

      • The science plan of the IAHS PUB decade, 2003–2012.
      • Defines an ungauged basin by the variable needed: records inadequate in quantity or quality for that variable, at the scale and accuracy required, so every basin is ungauged for something.
      • Makes the reduction of predictive uncertainty the decade’s single measure of success, and calls for a shift from models built on calibration to models built on understanding.

      Why read it first

      It is the founding document: the definition of “ungauged” and the six science questions the whole decade was organised around.

    2. R5Hrachowitz et al. 2013 Hydrological Sciences Journalwhat the decade achieved and left open

      Main points

      • The closing review of the PUB decade, by 26 authors, organised by PUB’s six science themes.
      • Records the shift from parameter fitting toward process understanding, models as hypotheses, and comparative hydrology.
      • Diagnoses three causes of predictive uncertainty and concludes that no general form-to-function theory emerged.

      Why read it first

      It is the authoritative statement of what PUB set out to do and what it left open. Everything later in this literature responds to it.

    3. R4Blöschl et al. 2013 Cambridge University Pressthe handbook and its comparative assessments

      Main points

      • The PUB handbook, organised by flow signature (annual and seasonal runoff, floods, low flows, flow-duration curves, hydrographs) rather than by method.
      • Each chapter carries its own comparative assessment: interquartile r² 0.65–0.91 for annual runoff, NSE 0.66–0.89 for seasonal runoff, R² 0.57–0.78 for low flows.
      • For every signature, regionalisation performance falls as aridity rises.

      Why read it first

      It is the decade’s synthesis and the source of the efficiency ranges the field still quotes. Read the synthesis and recommendations chapters first.

    4. R16Blöschl et al. 2019 Hydrological Sciences Journalthe agenda that followed

      Main points

      • A community consultation of 230 scientists distilled about 260 candidate problems into 23 unsolved problems in seven themes.
      • Question 17 asks what proxies best replace “few accurate data by many less accurate data”; Question 19 asks for models that extrapolate to changing conditions.
      • The community preferred continuity over radical redirection; the authors note a European bias in the workshops and working group.

      Why read it first

      It is the field’s current, broadly owned agenda, and it names the surrogate-discharge problem (Q17) as open.

    Section 03

    The seven families side by side

    The short version

    Five columns, seven rows. If you read only one thing in this review, read this table and then §13.

    Table scrolls sideways →

    FamilyWhat it moves into the basinWhat it must haveBest reported skillWhere it breaks
    1 · Parameter regionalisation
    §04    		 A calibrated model’s parameters, from a donor catchment A regional gauge network and catchment attributes Median daily NSE 0.62–0.67 vs 0.72 at-site No donor; arid or small catchments; reliance on a single donor
    2 · Streamflow regionalisation
    §05    		 The observed flow itself, interpolated along the network Dense gauges nearby, observing the same variable Generally beats a regionalised rainfall–runoff model on common data No connected neighbours; headwaters; any change in climate or land use
    3 · Donor-free routes
    §06    		 Physical properties read from maps, or a model that already covers everywhere Global physiographic and climate layers Global parameters from 4,229 headwaters; GRUN beats 13 global models Local skill at small catchments; precipitation-product error dominates
    4 · Remote sensing of the river
    §07    		 Measured hydraulics — width, elevation, slope — inverted for discharge A river wide enough for the sensor to resolve Real SWOT: median correlation 0.73, no gauge used Magnitude bias ~50%; narrow and braided rivers; short records
    5 · Surrogate discharge
    §08    		 A proxy signal that merely correlates with discharge, used as the calibration target A satellite signal that tracks flow at the outlet, climate forcing, and a source of scale: a mean-flow estimate (C/M-ratio studies) or hydraulic geometry (width and altimetry studies) NSE 0.54–0.78; NSE and KGE both >0.6 with no discharge data at all Unitless signal; clouds blind optical sensors and ice distorts water-extent signals; no gauge at the outlet to confirm the signal tracks flow
    6 · Deep learning
    §09    		 A learned attribute-to-behaviour mapping, trained across hundreds of basins A large regional sample of gauged catchments Out-of-sample median NSE 0.69 vs 0.64 locally calibrated Small gauge networks; no internal states; a hard extrapolation ceiling
    7 · Hybrid / differentiable
    §10    		 The same learned mapping, but inside a process model A large sample and a differentiable model implementation Beats LSTM under regional holdout, and on events rarer than 5-year Still data-hungry; high build cost; few independent replications
    The one-line reading

    Families 1 and 2 need a neighbour. Families 6 and 7 need a regional sample. Families 3, 4 and 5 need neither — which is why, in a genuinely data-poor basin, the real choice is between a global product, a wide-enough river, and a satellite signal that happens to correlate with flow.

    The long version

    Read the skill column carefully. These efficiencies come from different regions, periods, catchment sizes and metrics. They are not directly comparable — they indicate what each family has been shown to achieve in its own published setting, not a ranking from a common experiment.

    Table scrolls sideways →

    FamilyQuestion it answers / gap it addressesMethodData requiredReported skill (study, year, journal)StrengthsFailure modes / gaps left
    1. Parameter regionalisation Which gauged catchment’s calibrated model should stand in for this ungauged one? Transfer whole parameter sets by proximity or similarity
    • Regional gauge network
    • Catchment attributes
    • A calibrated conceptual model
    		 Median daily NSE 0.62–0.67 vs 0.72 at-site (Parajka et al. 2005, HESS)
    • Interpretable; gives internal states
    • Mature and well documented
    • Modest computing needs
    • Needs donors
    • Single-donor, single-set transfer is fragile; averaging outputs over two or more donors helps (Arsenault & Brissette 2014)
    • Degrades in arid and sparsely gauged regions
    2. Streamflow regionalisation Can flow be estimated without transferring a model’s errors along with it? Interpolate observed discharge or its statistics along the network Dense gauge network with the same variable observed; river topology Generally beats a regionalised rainfall–runoff model across six runoff signatures in 213 Austrian catchments (Viglione et al. 2013, HESS) Avoids transferring model error
    • No rainfall–runoff relation, so no response to climate or land-use change
    • Observed flows embed dams and abstractions
    3. Donor-free What can be predicted where there is no donor gauge at all? Derive parameters from mapped physical properties, or calibrate transfer-function coefficients (MPR) Global physiographic and climate layers; optionally a large calibration sample Global distributed parameters from 4,229 headwater catchments (Beck et al. 2020, JGR-A) Works with no local gauge at all
    • Local skill at small catchments is often poor
    • Global precipitation error dominates
    • No general form-to-function theory emerged
    4. Remote sensing of the river Can the river be gauged from orbit instead of from the bank? Observe width, elevation and slope; invert hydraulics (McFLI) or assimilate into a hydraulic model Satellite altimetry / SWOT / SAR; rivers wide enough to resolve
    • Real SWOT: median correlation 0.73, median bias 50%, median NSE negative (Andreadis et al. 2025, GRL)
    • Landsat widths at 3,078 gauges, off the shelf: positive KGE at 27–39% of sites, 46–65% with richer priors (Lin et al. 2023, RSE)
    • Narrow rivers, gauge-free: median NRMSE 12%, NSE 0.56 over 27 reaches (Scherer et al. 2024, RSE)
    		 SWOT-era algorithms need no donor and no gauge (global priors only); area–discharge curves still need ground measurements
    • Magnitude biased, though timing is good; SWOT’s expected error is dominated by bias (Durand et al. 2023)
    • Width alone fails below about 40 m (Feng et al. 2019); reflectance avoids the width but needs 2,036 training gauges (Hao et al. 2024)
    • SWOT is designed for rivers over 100 m; ICESat-2 methods reach about 30 m (Chen et al. 2026)
    • Short records; braided channels fail in the SWOT algorithm tests (Durand et al. 2016)
    5. Surrogate discharge Can a satellite signal that merely correlates with discharge replace the gauge record used for calibration? Calibrate a conceptual model against a unitless satellite proxy — C/M ratio, width, altimetric level or inundation extent — with a mean-flow estimate or a hydraulic-geometry relation supplying the missing scale A satellite signal that tracks flow at the basin outlet; climate forcing; a source of scale: a mean-flow estimate, e.g. from Budyko (C/M-ratio studies), or hydraulic geometry at the outlet (width and altimetry studies)
    • Mean NSE 0.54 over 130 Murray–Darling catchments, 70% above 0.4, from remote sensing alone (Yoon et al. 2023, ERL)
    • NSE 0.54–0.78 (Yoon et al. 2022, WRR)
    • NSE and KGE both > 0.6 (Yoon et al. 2025, EMS)
    • NSE 0.63/0.62 in small Tibetan rivers (Yu et al. 2023)
    		 The C/M-ratio line needs no donor, no training sample and no gauge record: potentially the widest reach of any family, provided the signal tracks flow at the outlet
    • The signal is unitless
    • Coarse pixels relative to river width
    • Clouds blind optical sensors (Landsat, MODIS); ice distorts water-extent and reflectance signals. SAR, passive microwave and altimetry see through cloud
    • Depends on the signal tracking flow at the outlet, which an ungauged basin has no gauge to confirm; the published tests were all run at gauged sites, and some screened sites on the correlation first
    6. Deep learning (LSTM) Is there enough information in catchment attributes to skip regionalisation entirely? Train one network across hundreds of catchments on forcing + static attributes Large regional sample of gauged catchments with consistent attributes Out-of-sample median NSE 0.69 vs 0.64 locally calibrated (Kratzert et al. 2019, WRR) Best demonstrated accuracy for ungauged basins inside large gauged samples (CAMELS); differentiable models overtake it when whole regions are held out (Feng et al. 2023)
    • Requires a large training sample
    • No mechanism, no internal states
    • Only predicts what it was trained on
    • Extrapolation fails above a ceiling below its own training maximum — a theoretical limit of 73 mm d−1 against a training maximum of 183 mm d−1, and an empirical limit of 60 under extreme forcing (Baste et al. 2025). The mass-conserving hybrid in the same study has no such theoretical limit
    7. Hybrid / differentiable Can we keep the process physics and get the regionalisation power of deep learning? Make the process model differentiable; an NN learns its parameters by gradient descent on regional data Large regional sample + a differentiable model implementation
    • Regional holdout median NSE 0.56–0.62, beating LSTM (Feng et al. 2023, HESS)
    • Beats LSTM on unseen events of 5-year return period and above, by a margin that grows with rarity (Song et al. 2026, WRR)
    • Keeps mass balance and internal states
    • Better trend extrapolation than LSTM, and better on rare events
    • Predicts untrained variables such as ET, storage and baseflow
    • Now extends to channel routing, not just rainfall–runoff
    • Still needs a large training sample
    • High implementation cost
    • Young field; few independent replications
    • Numerical compensation can obscure the physical meaning of the calibrated parameters (Song et al. 2024), which tempers the interpretability claim

    The decision in one paragraph

    If a large regional training sample exists and you only need discharge, Family 6 or 7 will most likely win — and Family 7 if you also need internal states or extrapolation beyond the training climate. If the gauge network is sparse but the river is wide, Family 4 gives you an observation where nothing else does. If there is no donor, no training sample and no rating curve — the common case across much of Africa, central Asia and South America — Family 5 is the one that still functions. If you have a handful of neighbouring gauges and need an interpretable model with internal states, Family 1 remains the workhorse. Family 2 is the right choice when you need a flow statistic rather than a hydrograph, and neighbours are nested.

    Where Families 4 and 5 lead, and where they lag

    Families 4 and 5 observe the river itself, so they need no donor, no training sample and no gauge at the target. Their weakness is magnitude, not timing. §07 and §08 give the evidence in full.

    These comparisons set results from different experiments side by side, as the tables above do. They show orders of magnitude, not a ranking.

    • Lead: skill with nothing borrowed. Real SWOT gives median correlation 0.73 with no gauge (Andreadis et al. 2025), and remote sensing alone gave mean NSE 0.54 over 130 catchments (Yoon et al. 2023). Family 1 reaches similar numbers only with donors, Family 6 only with hundreds of gauged catchments.
    • Lead: the target river’s own events, including floods and droughts, without extrapolating beyond a training range.
    • Catching up: large samples and narrow rivers. Tests at 3,078 gauges (Lin et al. 2023); gauge-free estimates on rivers under 100 m (Scherer et al. 2024; Hao et al. 2024).
    • Lag: magnitude, priors, sampling, sample size. Median SWOT bias is 50%; success depends on the prior; small and flashy rivers may be under-sampled; Family 5’s largest tests are 130 catchments in one basin system (Yoon et al. 2023) and 671 Brazilian catchments, of which only 76 had usable Landsat water extent (Meyer Oliveira et al. 2023).
    • Converging. Family 4 now borrows priors from Family 3 models, Family 1’s regionalisation logic (geoBAM), Family 6 networks (Hao et al. 2024) and points toward Family 7 (Larnier et al. 2025).

    Read these first

    Start with these. Between them they cover most of what this section concludes. Key points opens a short summary of each paper and why it comes first.

    1. R6Parajka et al. 2013 HESSFamily 1 baseline across 34 studies

      Main points

      • A meta-analysis of 34 studies and 3,874 catchments asking whether regionalisation methods have generalisable rankings.
      • Median daily NSE: 0.54 arid, 0.64 cold, 0.66 humid; 0.58 for spatial proximity and 0.66 for similarity.
      • Humid beats arid, large beats small, and dense gauge networks favour proximity and geostatistics; regression tends to do worst.

      Why read it first

      It is the main cross-study evidence on which methods work where, and it sets the baseline any ungauged-basin result is read against.

    2. R34Viglione et al. 2013 HESSthe only head-to-head test between two families

      Main points

      • Predicts daily runoff for 213 Austrian catchments two ways: by a regionalised rainfall–runoff model (Family 1) and by Top-kriging (Family 2).
      • Extracts six runoff signatures from each: annual and seasonal runoff, flow-duration curves, low flows, high flows and the hydrograph.
      • Top-kriging generally beats the regionalised model on common data.

      Why read it first

      It is the cleanest head-to-head test between two families in this review, on the same catchments and the same protocol.

    3. R76Kratzert et al. 2019 WRRFamily 6’s defining result

      Main points

      • Trains LSTMs on 531 CAMELS basins with k-fold validation, so every prediction is in a basin that contributed no training data.
      • Out-of-sample median NSE 0.69, against 0.64 for SAC-SMA calibrated in each basin and 0.58 for the National Water Model.
      • Implies catchment attributes carry enough information for out-of-sample transfer, given a large regional sample.

      Why read it first

      It is the result that reframed prediction in ungauged basins. Cite this paper, not the HESS companion, for the ungauged case.

    4. R85Feng et al. 2023 HESSFamily 7 under regional holdout

      Main points

      • Tests differentiable models under regional holdout, where whole regions are excluded from training, against an LSTM.
      • Median NSE 0.56–0.62 for the differentiable models against 0.55 for the LSTM.
      • High-flow (Q98) trend R²: the LSTM falls from 0.76 to 0.27 in the holdout while the differentiable models stay near 0.77.

      Why read it first

      It is the strongest published case for keeping process structure where data-driven models are weakest: unseen regions and changing trends.

    5. R73Andreadis et al. 2025 GRLFamily 4 on real SWOT data

      Main points

      • The first large assessment of discharge from real SWOT data (March 2023 – July 2024), validated at 65 gauged reaches.
      • Median correlation 0.73 (IQR 0.51–0.89) using no gauge information.
      • Median bias 50% and median NSE negative: the dynamics are right but the magnitude often is not.

      Why read it first

      It is the reckoning for a decade of synthetic-data expectations, and the honest benchmark for any gauge-free claim.

    6. R60Yoon et al. 2024 Journal of HydrologyFamily 5’s unit problem and its fix

      Main points

      • Asks which hydrological signature can convert a unitless surrogate (SR) into discharge, and how accurate it must be.
      • Uses the Budyko mean catchment discharge, which needs only mean precipitation and PET, and tests the model’s sensitivity to it on synthetic and real data.
      • Over 384 Australian stations, analyses the 49 with SR–discharge correlation above 0.6 first; SR is noisiest at low flow.

      Why read it first

      It is the clearest statement of the unit problem in surrogate calibration and of the Budyko fix that the C/M-ratio line now relies on.

    Section 04 · Family 1

    Regionalising model parameters

    The classical approach, and still the default in engineering practice.

    Calibrate a conceptual rainfall–runoff model at gauged sites, then decide which parameter values to give the ungauged one. Three strategies dominate, defined clearly in Zhang and Chiew (2009):

    • Regression — fit relationships between calibrated parameters and catchment descriptors, then evaluate those relationships at the ungauged site.
    • Spatial proximity — take the whole parameter set from the geographically nearest gauged catchment.
    • Physical similarity — take the whole parameter set from the most attribute-similar catchment, regardless of distance.

    He, Bárdossy and Zehe (2011) group these into just two families, in their own words: “(1) distance-based and (2) regression-based.”

    Where the family boundary comes from

    The split between this family and the next is not this review’s invention. Razavi and Coulibaly (2012), reviewing two decades of regionalisation (1990–2011) in the Journal of Hydrologic Engineering, draw it explicitly: continuous streamflow regionalisation proceeds either through rainfall–runoff models, where “model parameters are used as instruments to transfer hydrological information from gauged to ungauged basins”, or through hydrologic model–independent methods, where streamflow is transferred directly by data-driven means. That is Family 1 and Family 2 respectively. Their review is also the best single account of where the field stood immediately before the machine-learning turn. It stops short of a ranking: model-independent methods had been tried in only a few cases, and the authors find “no clear indication from the literature on which regionalization approach should be preferred for a given case”, so they recommend comparing both families at each site. They also note that there was no standard method for regionalisation uncertainty, and that most methods assume stationarity. Read in full 17 October 2026.

    Family 1 at a glance

    Four ways of answering the same question, and the order they arrived in. The left column is the one that won empirically; the right column holds the papers that framed the problem or set limits on it.

    Solid arrows mark a documented build-on or extension; dashed arrows mark a study that tests, benchmarks or limits another. Where an arrow reflects this review’s reading rather than an explicit statement in the papers, the text below says so.

    The consistent result: transfer whole parameter sets, don’t regress them

    Across three independent large-sample studies on three continents, regression came last. The reason is structural rather than regional: regression fits each parameter separately, ignoring the cross-correlations between them, and calibration produces many different parameter sets that fit equally well — the equifinality problem set out in Beven’s (2005) manifesto and still the reference point for it.

    Three refinements worth knowing

    Output averaging. Run the model with several donors’ parameter sets and average the simulated hydrographs, not the parameters. Zhang and Chiew ranked it among the two biggest gains; Beck et al. (2016) confirmed it globally with ten donors per cell on 1,787 catchments.

    Regionalise the parameterisation, not the parameters (Samaniego et al. 2010, MPR). Transfer functions turn fine-scale physiographic data into parameters, which are upscaled to the grid; only 62 coefficients are calibrated instead of 28 parameters per cell. On the Upper Neckar (about 4,000 km2), both approaches fit equally well at a fixed grid. Moved to a finer grid, MPR kept mean NSE 0.80 against 0.64, and 2.5% of cells broke the water balance against 53%. Its “ungauged” test is ten internal gauges. Extended by Samaniego et al. (2017) and globally by Beck et al. (2020) (4,229 headwater catchments). 2010 paper read in full 17 October 2026.

    Calibrate the region, not each catchment (Parajka et al. 2007; 320 Austrian catchments). Each iteration kriges every parameter from neighbours and pulls the next calibration toward it. Gauged fit held (median NSE 0.71–0.73), parameters became more stable between periods (degree-day factor r2 0.30 → 0.56), and the ungauged loss fell from 0.05 to 0.02–0.03. The authors call the gain small, and it relies on about 31 gauges within 50 km. Read in full 17 October 2026.

    A fourth option the three-way framing misses

    Proximity, similarity and regression assume the parameter–attribute relation is either ignored or linear. Machine learning can learn the mapping without assuming its form.

    • Song et al. (2022), HESS 26, 505: gradient boosting for parameter regionalisation, because linear regression fails where the relation is nonlinear and lumped parameters ignore within-catchment heterogeneity.
    • Prieto et al. (2019), WRR 55, 4364: 103 flow indices compressed to four components (87% of variance), regionalised with random forests, judged by new adequacy tests. On 92 Spanish catchments with 16 held out, the regionalisation was adequate in 12 of 16 but the hydrological model in only 1 of 16 (probabilistic NSE −0.65 to 0.68). When the model is inadequate, better regionalisation does not give better flows. Fix model structure and inputs first. Read in full 17 October 2026.

    Calibrating on what you know, not only on what you measure

    The parent idea (Yadav et al. 2007, Advances in Water Resources 30(8)): regionalise signatures, not parameters. Regress streamflow indices on catchment characteristics, carry the prediction interval to the ungauged site, and keep only model runs whose indices fall inside it. On 30 catchments in England and Wales, three indices (high-pulse count, runoff ratio, FDC slope) gave reliable, sharp bands; using all 19 at once left 12 catchments with no acceptable run. Read in full 17 October 2026.

    Badly gauged rather than ungauged (Winsemius et al. 2009, WRR 45). In the Luangwa, Zambia (about 150,000 km2), discharge (1956–1973) and satellite rainfall (2002–2006) never overlap. GLUE conditions parameters on three signatures: recession, daily-flow spectral properties and a monthly water balance. The limits of acceptability are derived, not chosen, as the 95% interval of each signature’s year-to-year variability. This is the part that transfers to a satellite signal.

    • 99.94% of three million parameter sets were rejected. Only routing parameters were constrained; evaporation was insensitive to every target.
    • The posterior barely changed between two different rainfall products, the paper’s strongest result.
    • No split-sample validation was possible; the same signatures held in 68–97% of accepted sets in two later years. The method needs multiyear data and assumes stationary signatures. Read in full 17 October 2026.

    Where the transfer-function line goes next. MPR (Samaniego et al. 2017) and Beck et al. (2020) fit functions from attributes to parameters; differentiable models (§10) learn that function by gradient descent inside the model (Feng et al. 2022; Huynh et al. 2024).

    Where this family stands

    ADVANCES SO FAR

    • Settled empirically that whole parameter sets transfer better than regressed ones — three independent large-sample studies on three continents, pooled and confirmed by meta-analysis.
    • Identified what actually drives skill: educated donor selection and output averaging, not the choice of similarity measure. Confirmed again at global scale with ten-donor averaging over 1,787 catchments.
    • Shifted the object of transfer from parameters to the parameterisation itself, so one calibration serves many scales and locations, and applied that globally from 4,229 headwater catchments.
    • Replaced the assumption that the parameter–attribute relation is linear with learned mappings, and added statistical adequacy tests built for the ungauged case.
    • Produced a single-sample, 19-approach comparison that finally lets the published schemes be ranked against each other and against calibration.

    LIMITATIONS SO FAR

    • It needs donors. Sparse networks, targets unlike anything gauged, or changed land use leave the transfer nothing reliable to carry.
    • Equifinality. Many parameter sets fit a donor equally well and they do not transfer equally well, which is why single-best-set transfer is fragile.
    • Every study that measured it found all three schemes lag far behind at-site calibration.
    • Conclusions are network-density dependent: the proximity advantage found in France is tied explicitly to a dense gauge network.
    • Accuracy falls in arid and small catchments — disproportionately the catchments PUB is asked about.
    • Almost all the evidence is pseudo-ungauged cross-validation on well-instrumented catchments, not genuinely ungauged sites.

    Read these first

    Start with these. Between them they cover most of what this section concludes. Key points opens a short summary of each paper and why it comes first.

    1. R22Parajka et al. 2005 HESSthe classic controlled comparison

      Main points

      • Compares five schemes for transferring the 11 parameters of a conceptual model across 320 Austrian catchments, calibrated on runoff and snow cover.
      • Kriging of individual parameters and similarity-based whole-set transfer tie for best.
      • Median daily NSE 0.67 for both against 0.72 at-site in calibration; 0.62 and 0.66 in verification.

      Why read it first

      It is the classic controlled comparison, and its efficiency numbers are still quoted as the reference gap between regionalised and at-site models.

    2. R23Oudin et al. 2008 WRRwhy proximity wins where gauges are dense

      Main points

      • Compares regression, spatial proximity and physical similarity with two lumped models on 913 French catchments.
      • Spatial proximity is best where the gauge network is dense; regression is barely better than one median parameter set for the whole country.
      • All three lag far behind full model calibration.

      Why read it first

      It settles the regression-versus-transfer question on a large sample, and ties the proximity result to network density, which is the caveat most often dropped.

    3. R24Zhang and Chiew 2009 WRRwhere the effort pays: donor choice and averaging

      Main points

      • Tests which design choice matters on 210 unimpacted south-east Australian catchments with two daily models.
      • The largest gains come from educated donor selection and averaging the outputs of several donors, not from the similarity measure.
      • Proximity slightly beats physical similarity; MODIS leaf-area index adds only a marginal improvement.

      Why read it first

      It shows where the effort pays in Family 1, and it is the Australian large-sample study, directly relevant to a UNSW context.

    4. R26Arsenault and Brissette 2014 WRRwhy a single donor is fragile

      Main points

      • Tests regression, proximity and similarity on 268 Quebec catchments (1.6 million km²), with ten equally good calibrations per catchment and 1,000 bootstrap draws.
      • Parameter-set selection matters, but “equifinality does not contribute significantly to the overall uncertainty”.
      • Output averaging beats parameter averaging; a single donor is about 20 percentage points worse in success rate than two; even the best method never exceeds 75% success.

      Why read it first

      It is the standard citation for why single-donor transfer is fragile, and its own conclusion is more specific than the equifinality story it is usually cited for.

    5. R29Pool et al. 2021 WRRthe rankings tested at scale

      Main points

      • Compares 19 published regionalisation approaches head to head on 671 US catchments with HBV, by leave-one-out.
      • The approaches pick donors from geography, attributes, signatures or combinations, and transfer whole parameter sets.
      • Catchments benefit from a well-chosen approach, but which approach is well chosen depends on the catchment.

      Why read it first

      It is the largest single-sample comparison of the field’s approaches, benchmarked against calibration, so it tests Family 1’s rankings at scale.

    Section 05 · Family 2

    Regionalising the streamflow itself

    Instead of transferring model parameters, transfer the flow.

    These methods interpolate observed discharge or its statistics directly across the river network, and never calibrate a rainfall–runoff model at the target site.

    de Lavenne et al. (2016) state the trade-off cleanly. Transferring parameters also transfers everything wrong with the model — its simplifying assumptions, its parameter identification problems, its rainfall-input errors. Regionalising observations avoids that. The cost is that observed runoff also carries human influence — dams, abstractions, irrigation — which is hard to separate out, and that the method is useless where rainfall is the real unknown.

    Family 2 at a glance

    This family splits by what gets interpolated: the flow field itself, a single signature, or the whole hydrograph. The right-hand column holds the one study that tests it against Family 1 on common ground.

    Solid arrows mark a documented build-on or extension; dashed arrows mark a study that tests, benchmarks or limits another. Where an arrow reflects this review’s reading rather than an explicit statement in the papers, the text below says so.

    The main techniques

    Table scrolls sideways →

    Technique and yearKey reference / journalResearch question / gap addressedMethodData requiredFindingsLimitations
    Top-kriging 2006Skøien, Merz and Blöschl, HESS 10, 277–287 Ordinary kriging ignores that river catchments are nested and share area — can geostatistics be made to respect stream-network topology?
    • Best linear unbiased estimator applied on the stream network
    • Kriging weights from catchment area and nested topology, not Euclidean distance
    • Returns a variance, so uncertainty comes with the estimate
    • Can use short gauge records by accounting for each gauge’s uncertainty
    		 Gauge network with spatial coverage; river topology
    • Built on about 7,000 Austrian catchments, of which roughly 600 are gauged, records 5–110 years
    • The variable is the specific 100-year flood, area-normalised to 100 km2 with exponent −0.33 and log-transformed
    • More plausible and more accurate than ordinary kriging for the 100-year flood in two Austrian regions
    • Uncertainty lowest on the main stem, growing toward headwaters — CV about 0.2 on the Mur main stem, above 1 in some headwaters
    • Later studies: beat regression for flood and low-flow quantiles
    • Needs the same variable observed nearby †
    • Uncertainty grows sharply toward headwaters
    • No rainfall–runoff relation, so no response to climate or land-use change †
    • The validation is thinner than the claim.     ‡ These rows cite chapters of the Blöschl et al. (2013) handbook. Chapters 7 and 9 were read in full on 17 October 2026 from the UNSW library copy, and their rows now carry each chapter’s comparative-assessment numbers.

    † Limitations marked with a dagger are general properties of the technique, not statements quoted from the cited source.

    Top-kriging is the standout

    Skøien, Merz and Blöschl (2006) introduced topological kriging, a best linear unbiased estimator adapted to stream networks that accounts for both catchment area and the nested structure of the network. Tested on the 100-year flood in two Austrian regions, it gave more plausible and more accurate estimates than ordinary kriging, and — usefully — returns uncertainty that is lowest on the main stem and grows toward the headwaters.

    Subsequent comparisons, as summarised by de Lavenne et al. (2016), found it competitive or better than the alternatives:

    • Archfield et al. (2013) found Top-kriging substantially outperformed regression on catchment descriptors and canonical kriging for flood quantiles in 61 catchments in the southeastern United States.
    • Laaha et al. (2014) found it generally better than regression for low-flow quantiles across 300 Austrian catchments, and at least as good at locations without upstream observations.
    • de Lavenne et al. (2016) found Top-kriging and geomorphology-based inverse modelling gave similar performance for equal calibration effort across the Loire basin. They also showed the Ghosh distance, which accounts for catchment nesting, works well for weighting and screening donors — particularly for Strahler orders above five, where donors are strongly nested.

    The head-to-head test against Family 1

    Most of this review compares families through separate studies in separate places. One paper puts Families 1 and 2 on the same catchments, the same data and the same metrics — and it is the third part of the PUB comparative assessment, the companion to the Parajka et al. paper cited throughout §04.

    Viglione, Parajka, Rogger, Salinas, Laaha, Sivapalan and Blöschl (2013), HESS 17(6), 2263, predict daily runoff for 213 Austrian catchments two ways — by a regionalised rainfall–runoff model (Family 1) and by Top-kriging (Family 2) — then extract six runoff signatures from each: annual runoff, seasonal runoff, flow duration curves, low flows, high flows and the hydrograph. Performance is scored in cross-validation by bias, error spread and the proportion of unexplained spatial variance.

    Their result is unambiguous and is the single cleanest piece of evidence in this review for choosing between the two families:

    • Top-kriging generally outperformed the regionalised rainfall–runoff model — across the signatures, on a common dataset.
    • Predictive performance increases with catchment area for both methods and all six signatures.
    • Dependence on climate characteristics is weaker than dependence on area.

    Read against Parajka et al. (2013) Part 1, which found dense networks favour proximity and geostatistics, this is the same conclusion arrived at by a different route. The caveat is the same one that applies to all of Family 2: Austria has an unusually dense gauge network, and Top-kriging needs it.

    A strand this review otherwise treats only through the handbook: regional flood frequency

    §05’s table covers flood estimation through the Rosbjerg et al. handbook chapter, which scopes the problem but predates the machine-learning literature on it. Regional flood frequency analysis (RFFA) has since become one of the most active applications of statistical learning to ungauged sites — estimating a flood quantile at an unmonitored location from regional data, without any rainfall–runoff model at all.

    Desai and Ouarda (2020), Journal of Hydrology 594, 125861, apply random forest regression to regional hydrological frequency analysis at ungauged sites, replacing the linear regression on catchment descriptors that RFFA has traditionally used. The case study is 151 hydrometric stations in southern Quebec. Applied within neighbourhoods delineated by canonical correlation analysis (CCA-RFR, 30 trees), random forests gave the lowest errors of any model tested: relative RMSE 29–35% across the 10-, 50- and 100-year quantiles, where every other model was at about 34% or above. Two cautions come with that. Applied to all stations without the neighbourhoods, random forests were the worst model (relative RMSE 81–96%). And CCA-RFR had the lowest Nash criterion of all (0.51–0.58, against 0.64–0.84 for the others), which the authors put down to small basins and the smaller samples inside neighbourhoods — so which model is “best” depends on the metric. Read in full 17 October 2026, from the accepted manuscript.

    The structural point is the one Razavi and Coulibaly made in 2012 and that §04 borrows: regionalising a flow statistic directly is a model-independent route, and it inherits the strengths and weaknesses of this family rather than of Family 1. If your target is a design flood rather than a hydrograph, this is where to look.

    Two sources this section should not be without

    The low-flow canon (Smakhtin 2001, J. Hydrology 240, 147–186; over 1,700 citations): low-flow mechanisms, estimation from records (FDCs, frequency analysis, baseflow separation, recessions) and estimation in ungauged catchments. For a dryland reach, the key part is transmission losses between a reach and a downstream gauge: evaporation, riparian ET, recharge and bed losses through alluvium, which “can be substantial not only during low flows but also during the early stages of flood events”. They break the assumption that flow at one reach equals flow at a distant gauge, and their regional importance “is largely unknown”. Read in full 17 October 2026.

    The source of QPPQ (Mohamoud 2008, HSJ 53(4), 706): regional FDCs by step-wise regression on 29 Mid-Atlantic catchments, tested on three held-out sites. Over 21 years, daily R2 was 0.80–0.86 (monthly 0.88–0.98), about equal to the drainage-area ratio. Skill falls with donor distance; with no nearby gauge the method “may not accurately predict streamflow”. Read in full 17 October 2026.

    The PUB handbook names inundation as a constraint (2013). The chapter summary calls for using “the enormous amounts of spatial information becoming available as proxy data, such as snow, remotely sensed soil moisture and inundation patterns”, compared against simulated patterns rather than becoming “grist to optimisation schemes aimed at curve fitting”. Worth quoting in an inundation-modelling introduction.

    The geomorphological method as software. transfR (R, CRAN 1.1.18, July 2026; INRAE) inverts a donor’s streamflow to net rainfall (Boudhraâ et al. 2018), interpolates it to the ungauged catchment and convolves it with that catchment’s geomorphological unit hydrograph; several donors add robustness. It also runs as the SIMFEN web service (Dallery et al., HSJ 67(16)), Brittany only, with up to five donors within 50 km. It reports no skill scores of its own. Read in full 17 October 2026.

    Where this family stands

    ADVANCES SO FAR

    • Adapted geostatistics to the stream network rather than to Euclidean space, accounting for nesting and shared area, and returning an uncertainty with every estimate.
    • Beat regression for both flood and low-flow quantiles, and on a common 213-catchment dataset generally beat a regionalised rainfall–runoff model across all six runoff signatures.
    • Added a physically motivated alternative that matches it for equal calibration effort, plus a nesting-aware distance for screening donors.
    • Reached operational form: an R package and an end-user web service, which is rarer in this literature than it should be.
    • The signature strands — low flow, flow duration curves, flood frequency — have their own mature canon and are now absorbing statistical learning.

    LIMITATIONS SO FAR

    • Needs the same variable observed nearby: a reasonably dense network and hydrologically connected neighbours. It cannot reach a basin with neither.
    • Uncertainty grows sharply toward the headwaters, and predictive skill rises with catchment area — so it is weakest exactly where catchments are smallest.
    • It never models the rainfall–runoff relation, so it says nothing about how a catchment would respond under a different climate or land use.
    • Observed flows carry dams, abstractions and irrigation, which are hard to separate from the natural signal.
    • Representing runoff in the frequency domain discards timing; the hydrograph is the hardest signature to predict.

    Read these first

    Start with these. Between them they cover most of what this section concludes. Key points opens a short summary of each paper and why it comes first.

    1. R32Skøien et al. 2006 HESSTop-kriging, the founding method

      Main points

      • Introduces Top-kriging: a best linear unbiased estimator whose weights come from catchment area and nested river topology, not Euclidean distance.
      • Built on about 7,000 Austrian catchments (about 600 gauged); more plausible than ordinary kriging for the specific 100-year flood in two regions.
      • Returns an uncertainty that is lowest on the main stem and grows toward the headwaters.

      Why read it first

      It is the founding Family 2 method. Note that its validation is thin: leave-one-out on eight gauges per sub-region, judged from bar plots.

    2. R11Castellarin et al. 2013 PUB handbook, ch. 7regionalising a signature: flow-duration curves

      Main points

      • Treats the flow-duration curve as a compact signature of runoff variability, used for water supply, hydropower and environmental flows.
      • Comparative assessment of 10 cross-validated studies (8–1,080 catchments each): NSE of FDC quantiles has an interquartile range of 0.60–0.90.
      • In humid regions, one, two or five years of observed runoff gave better long-term FDCs than the regionalisation methods.

      Why read it first

      It is the reference chapter for regionalising a signature rather than a model, and it shows when a short record beats any transfer method.

    3. R34Viglione et al. 2013 HESSthe test against Family 1

      Main points

      • Predicts daily runoff for 213 Austrian catchments two ways: by a regionalised rainfall–runoff model (Family 1) and by Top-kriging (Family 2).
      • Extracts six runoff signatures from each: annual and seasonal runoff, flow-duration curves, low flows, high flows and the hydrograph.
      • Top-kriging generally beats the regionalised model on common data.

      Why read it first

      It is the cleanest head-to-head test between two families in this review, on the same catchments and the same protocol.

    4. R35de Lavenne et al. 2016 WRRhydrograph transfer with a physical basis

      Main points

      • Transfers measured hydrographs by deconvolving the donor’s width-function unit hydrograph and reconvolving with the target’s.
      • Matches Top-kriging for equal calibration effort across the Loire basin.
      • The nesting-aware Ghosh distance screens and weights donors well, especially at Strahler orders above five.

      Why read it first

      It is the physically motivated alternative to Top-kriging, and the method behind the transfR software, so it is the practical entry to hydrograph transfer.

    Section 06 · Family 3

    Donor-free routes

    A priori parameters, classification, global models

    If no donor is available, the information has to come from somewhere else: from physical reasoning about what the landscape implies, or from a model built to run everywhere at once.

    Family 3 at a glance

    The donor-free routes divide into deriving parameters without calibration, sorting catchments into classes, and building products that cover everything. The right-hand column holds the two papers that bound how well any of it can work. Both limits apply to every family, not only this one; §12 returns to signature uncertainty.

    Solid arrows mark a documented build-on or extension; dashed arrows mark a study that tests, benchmarks or limits another. Where an arrow reflects this review’s reading rather than an explicit statement in the papers, the text below says so.

    A priori and physically constrained parameters

    The idea is to estimate parameters from mapped physical properties — soil depth and texture, geology, topography, vegetation — rather than by calibration, so the model can be applied anywhere the maps exist. This was PUB’s declared ambition: infer function from form (Hrachowitz et al. 2013).

    In practice it has worked best as a constraint rather than a replacement. Physically derived parameter ranges with explicit uncertainty bounds narrow the feasible parameter space; calibration or regional information then does the rest. Hughes and colleagues’ long-running work on the Pitman model in southern Africa is the clearest sustained example, and the Hrachowitz review treats it as the model case of a practical tool refined under scientific scrutiny.

    The most scalable version is Multiscale Parameter Regionalisation (Samaniego, Kumar and Attinger 2010), which calibrates the coefficients of transfer functions from physiographic data to parameters, rather than the parameters themselves. In its first test, streamflow at the outlet could not separate it from the standard approach; soil-moisture patterns and the water balance across grid sizes could. One calibration then serves multiple resolutions and locations (Samaniego et al. 2017), and Beck et al. (2020) applied the idea globally using observed streamflow from 4,229 headwater catchments.

    Catchment classification

    Classification is the scientific companion to regionalisation: if catchments can be sorted into functional classes, transfer within a class should be defensible. Sawicz et al. (2011) analysed 280 catchments in the eastern USA in a six-dimensional signature space and found nine homogeneous classes via Bayesian clustering, then interpreted those classes against climatic and landscape attributes. Kuentz et al. (2017) extended the approach across Europe.

    A caution for anyone building on signatures: Westerberg et al. (2016) quantified the uncertainty in hydrological signatures themselves for gauged and ungauged catchments. Signature uncertainty is not negligible, and a classification built on noisy signatures inherits that noise.

    The large-domain routes, compared

    This family had no evidence table in earlier drafts, which flattered it. Below are the six studies that carry its weight — three on how to get parameters without donors, two on the global products that result, and one on the forcing error that limits all of them.

    Large-domain and global models

    Global models put a number everywhere. Two developments since 2019 matter: GRUN reconstructed global runoff from observations and beat 13 global models, and World-Wide HYPE scaled catchment modelling to the whole landmass. They are now a standard baseline and can be a calibration target: Skoulikaris and Piliouras (2023) rectified 30 years of large-scale model discharge against sparse observations, tuned a regional lumped model on it and transferred it by similarity (R2 0.654–0.949, KGE 0.759–0.790, NSE 0.649–0.745 where observed).

    A cousin of Family 5

    A modelled series stands in for the missing gauge record, as a satellite signal does in §08.

    The weakness is local skill. Coarse resolution, generic parameters and precipitation error make the number at a small catchment often poor. Beck et al. (2017) tested 22 precipitation products against 76,086 gauges and through HBV in 9,053 catchments and found marked differences: the choice of precipitation product often matters more than the choice of model.

    Where this family stands

    ADVANCES SO FAR

    • Established that physically derived parameters work best as a constraint that narrows the feasible space, not as a replacement for calibration.
    • Made one calibration serve many resolutions by regionalising transfer functions rather than parameters.
    • Gave the field a vocabulary for similarity through classification in signature space, extended from the eastern USA across Europe.
    • Produced global products that are now genuine baselines rather than placeholders: an observation-trained runoff reconstruction that beats an ensemble of 13 global models, and catchment-modelling technique applied to more than 130,000 catchments.
    • Showed that large-scale model output can be repurposed as a stand-in for the missing gauge record — the same move the surrogate family makes with satellites.

    LIMITATIONS SO FAR

    • No general form-to-function theory emerged. This is PUB's central unmet ambition, and this family is where it was meant to arrive.
    • Local skill at small catchments is often poor. Even the most refined global catchment model averages ~1,000 km2 per unit.
    • Forcing error dominates. Global precipitation products differ markedly in accuracy, and that error propagates into every donor-free prediction — often more than the choice of model structure does.
    • Signature uncertainty is not negligible, so any classification built on signatures inherits that noise.
    • The most accurate route in this family still needs some observations to rectify against, so it is not fully donor-free.

    Read these first

    Start with these. Between them they cover most of what this section concludes. Key points opens a short summary of each paper and why it comes first.

    1. R43Samaniego et al. 2017 HESSregionalising the parameterisation (MPR)

      Main points

      • Shows that most land-surface and hydrological models do not keep consistent parameter fields across spatial resolutions.
      • Multiscale Parameter Regionalisation calibrates the coefficients of transfer functions from physiographic data to parameters, not the parameters themselves.
      • One calibration then serves many resolutions and locations.

      Why read it first

      It is the clearest statement of the transfer-function line, which runs from Family 3 into Family 7’s learned regionalisation.

    2. R41Beck et al. 2017 HESSthe precipitation limit on every donor-free method

      Main points

      • Evaluates 22 global precipitation datasets: uncorrected ones against 76,086 gauges, gauge-corrected ones through HBV calibration in 9,053 catchments.
      • Finds “marked differences in spatio-temporal patterns and accuracy” among them; MSWEP-ng correlated best among uncorrected products.
      • The best gauge-corrected product’s “good performance…is unlikely to translate to sparsely or ungauged regions”.

      Why read it first

      Every donor-free prediction inherits its rainfall input’s error; this paper shows that the product choice is a first-order control on skill.

    3. R45Beck et al. 2020 JGR: Atmospheresparameters for the whole land surface

      Main points

      • Optimises transfer equations linking model parameters to climate and landscape, at 0.05° and fully distributed, using 4,229 headwater catchments.
      • Applies the equations globally to produce parameter maps for the whole land surface, including ungauged regions.
      • Evaluated with KGE in tenfold cross-validation with a gridded HBV.

      Why read it first

      It is the most direct route to parameters anywhere on Earth grounded in observed streamflow, and the global baseline donor-free methods are compared with.

    4. R46Arheimer et al. 2020 HESSa global catchment model, and its honest skill

      Main points

      • Applies catchment-modelling technique (HYPE) to more than 130,000 catchments covering the land surface, from 20 open databases and stepwise parameter estimation.
      • Even the first version performs better than traditional gridded global models of river flow.
      • But the median monthly KGE is 0.4, which the authors say most catchment modellers “would probably judge as poor”, with severe problems in dry regions.

      Why read it first

      It shows what a global catchment model can and cannot do: better than the alternatives is not the same claim as good.

    Section 07 · Family 4

    Remote sensing of the river from space

    This family changes the question.

    Instead of predicting discharge from rainfall, it measures the river’s observable hydraulics — width, water-surface elevation, slope — and inverts for discharge. The basin stays ungauged on the ground; the river is gauged from orbit.

    Family 4 at a glance

    The left columns are the methods; the right-hand column is the reckoning. The roots (1997–2015) worked from field measurements and real imagery; the SWOT-era algorithms after them were built and tested on synthetic data until 2025.

    Solid arrows mark a documented build-on or extension; dashed arrows mark a study that tests, benchmarks or limits another. Where an arrow reflects this review’s reading rather than an explicit statement in the papers, the text below says so.

    How the field is organised

    Gleason and Durand (2020) is the orienting review, and its framing is unusually useful: it classifies work by gauging context — gauged, semi-gauged, regionally gauged, politically ungauged, and totally ungauged — rather than by sensor. “Politically ungauged” names basins where gauges exist but data are not shared, which is a large share of the real-world problem.

    The method categories they identify:

    • Calibration or assimilation into hydrologic models — use satellite signals to constrain a rainfall–runoff model.
    • Calibration or assimilation into hydraulic models — including flood-inundation mapping and 4D-variational data assimilation.
    • Geomorphic inverse problems — chiefly mass-conserved flow law inversion (McFLI), solving Manning’s equation or hydraulic geometry relations from observed width, height and slope alone.

    What the accuracy actually looks like

    The honest reading

    Satellite discharge gets the shape of the hydrograph roughly right and the magnitude often wrong. Gleason and Durand’s pragmatic case: where nothing is known, a factor-of-two error can still be an improvement.

    What SWOT is (Biancamaria et al. 2015, Surveys in Geophysics 37(2), 307–337, the standard reference). A Ka-band interferometer imaging two 50 km swaths either side of a 20 km nadir gap, on a 20.86-day repeat. Native pixels are metres across but only metric-to-decametric in height; the 10 cm (1σ) figure holds when averaged over 1 km2.

    • SWOT will not measure water depth. It measures elevation, slope and a water mask, so the geometry problem of §11 remains.
    • It is designed for rivers wider than 100 m (goal 50 m). At 100 m it sees more than 60% of 50,000 km2 sub-basins; only at 50 m does that reach 10,000 km2. Small and medium catchments are outside the mission by design, which is why a Sentinel-1 approach on narrow rivers is not made redundant.
    • It is not a gauge replacement: “in most circumstances, in situ gages will be, by far, more precise than any remote sensing discharge estimates”.
    • Error sources: layover at water margins (where extent methods work), rain above about 3 mm/h, and calm water. Sampling alone puts 8.1% mean error on monthly means (10.0% at the equator), and about 3.55% of land is never seen. Pre-launch expectation for AMHG: 26–41% relative RMSE, excluding river types it cannot handle.

    Read in full 17 October 2026.

    SWOT launched in December 2022, and Andreadis et al. (2025), the first large real-data assessment, broadly confirms those expectations.

    Why this matters for inundation modelling

    The observations that constrain discharge here (SAR extent, altimetric water level) are also what an inundation model predicts, so extent becomes a calibration target in basins with no rating curve.

    What Family 4 does that the other families cannot

    Family 4 is the only family that measures the target river itself, with no donor, no training sample and no gauge. That gives it four advantages over Families 1–3 and 6–7, and one large weakness.

    Comparisons with other families set results from different experiments side by side (§03). They show orders of magnitude, not a ranking.

    1. It needs nothing borrowed. SWOT discharge is expected to get mean flow within 30% with no gauge (Alaska example) and flow dynamics within 15% for nearly all reaches (Durand et al. 2023). Real SWOT data give median correlation 0.73 with no gauge information (Andreadis et al. 2025). Family 1 needs donor gauges nearby; Family 6 needs hundreds of gauged catchments to train on.
    2. It sees the target’s own events. SWOT will give “the event flow hydrographs for all of the world’s ungaged basins” (Durand et al. 2023). An observation does not extrapolate beyond a training range, which is where a stand-alone LSTM has a measured ceiling (Baste et al. 2025, §09); and it does not assume a donor relation still holds after land-use or climate change. That last point is untested (§13).
    3. It recovers the channel, not only the flow. Assimilating SWOT levels into a river-network model infers “inflow hydrographs, effective bathymetry, and spatially distributed friction”, with discharge NRMSE 0.05–0.18, 18–71% better than the prior (Larnier et al. 2025). That prior comes from a hydrological model calibrated on the same gauges, so this shows what the satellite adds, not a gauge-free result. No regionalisation or deep-learning method produces channel geometry.
    4. It now has large samples and reaches narrow rivers. At 3,078 gauges, off-the-shelf inversion gave positive KGE at 27% (BAM) and 39% (geoBAM) of sites, 46–65% with richer priors (Lin et al. 2023). Width alone fails below about 40 m (Feng et al. 2019), but gauge-free Manning with altimetry and PlanetScope reached median NRMSE 12% and NSE 0.56 on 27 reaches, many under 100 m (Scherer et al. 2024), and a reflectance model gave positive KGE in 68.6% of ungauged rivers, with no loss on braided ones (Hao et al. 2024).

    The weakness is magnitude. Real SWOT has median bias 50% and median NSE below zero (Andreadis et al. 2025), and the expected error is “dominated by bias” (Durand et al. 2023). Accuracy also depends on the prior (Lin et al. 2023), and hydrographs of “smaller and flashier rivers” may not be resolved. Where a large gauged sample exists, Family 6 still gives better discharge.

      • Reflectance of six Landsat bands with no water mask (Hao et al. 2024).
    • How it becomes discharge. Two routes:
      • A width power law: fitted to a gauge (Smith and Pavelsky; Riggs, at 2,168 gauges), or tied along the river by AMHG and solved with priors (Gleason and Smith; BAM in Feng; geoBAM; Lin).
      • A learned mapping from reflectance to the change from mean flow (Hao).
    • Where the scale comes from. Width alone does not fix the size of the flow, so it comes from outside the image:
      • A gauge (Smith and Pavelsky; Riggs).
      • A global model or reanalysis mean flow (Feng, Lin, Hao), which sets the bias.
      • Geomorphic priors by river type, including bankfull depth and bed shape r (Brinkerhoff).
    • Main limitations.
      • Width changes little with flow in entrenched or low-b channels, which are most of the gauged sites (Lin).
      • Below about 40 m width fails (Feng); reflectance avoids that but needs a large gauged training set (Hao).
      • Clouds cut optical sampling: under 10% of target dates on the Lena; 10–25% of Landsat and Sentinel-2 images cloud-free in the Arctic.
