    • How the observation is made. Water level, slope and, in two papers, surface velocity:
      • SWOT or airborne SWOT-like swaths (Durand et al. 2023; Andreadis et al. 2025; Tuozzolo et al. 2019), or simulated SWOT-like data (Durand et al. 2016; Hagemann et al. 2017).
      • Nadir altimetry at virtual stations (Paris et al. 2016, 2026; Bjerklie et al. 2018, with Landsat width).
      • Surface velocity: MODIS-derived (Moramarco et al. 2019) or satellite video (Masafu et al. 2023).
      • Field data standing in for satellite variables (Bjerklie et al. 2003).
    • How it becomes discharge. Three routes:
      • \(Q = \tfrac{1}{n}\,A^{5/3}\,W^{-2/3}\,S^{1/2}\) with the unseen baseline area \(A_0\) and roughness \(n\) inverted along a mass-conserving reach (SWOT algorithms), or with bed level and roughness from width–level pairs and channel form (Bjerklie 2018).
      • A rating curve \(Q = a\,(H - z)^{b}\) per altimetry station, fitted to model discharge (Paris 2016, 2026).
      • Velocity times area: an entropy velocity profile (Moramarco) or surface velocity scaled by a coefficient over known topography (Masafu).
    • Where the scale comes from. Mostly from outside the satellite data:
      • A prior on mean annual flow from a water-balance model (SWOT algorithms; Tuozzolo); real SWOT bias tracks the prior’s bias (62% prior, 50% median bias; Andreadis).
      • Model discharge for altimetry ratings: MGB-IPH (Paris 2016) or a gauge-corrected global reanalysis (Paris 2026).
      • Measured velocity sets the magnitude directly, but only with a section: fitted by entropy theory (Moramarco) or surveyed (Masafu).
    • Main limitations.
      • Timing is good, magnitude often is not: median NSE below 0 on real SWOT data.
      • SWOT sees rivers wider than 100 m; nadir altimetry only where a track crosses; satellite velocity only for large rivers or cloud-free video.
      • Ratings inherit the error of the model discharge they are fitted to.
      • Most SWOT tests are simulated; SWOT does not measure depth.

    • How the observation is made. The channel itself is rebuilt, in three ways:
      • By fitting a curve to paired water level and width or area: SWOT-like height–width (Schaperow et al. 2019), altimetry level with Landsat width (Wu et al. 2023), altimetry level with PlanetScope area (Scherer et al. 2024), or ICESat-2 bank photons as \(y = k\,x^{r} + z\) (Chen et al. 2026).
      • From ICESat-2 cross-sections inside a hydraulic model (Coppo Frias et al. 2023; Musaeus et al. 2024).
      • By assimilation: a hydraulic model adjusts bed and friction until it reproduces SWOT levels (Oubanas et al. 2018, simulated; Larnier et al. 2025, real).
    • How it becomes discharge. Manning on the rebuilt section, a hydraulic model, or no discharge at all:
      • Manning–Strickler with roughness from mass conservation across sections (Scherer) or from meander length and slope (Chen).
      • Steady or diffusive-wave hydraulic models on ICESat-2 sections (Coppo Frias; Musaeus), or Saint-Venant with bed, friction and inflow inverted (Oubanas; Larnier).
      • Bathymetry only, offered as a prior for discharge algorithms (Schaperow; Wu).
    • Where the scale comes from. From geometry in two papers; from gauges or models in four:
      • Observed bed shape and bed level set the flow area, so no mean-flow prior is needed (Scherer; Chen).
      • Coppo Frias and Musaeus calibrate or build the sections with gauged or modelled discharge; Larnier’s inflow prior comes from a model calibrated on the validation gauges.
    • Main limitations.
      • The never-seen part of the bed is assumed: a width-to-depth rule (Scherer), a hydraulic-geometry curve (Schaperow; Wu) or the extension of the bank curve (Chen).
      • Accuracy falls with low channel exposure: Wu’s bed is overestimated below 40% exposure, and errors of 3–11 m are reported as 1.25–6.18% of absolute elevation.
      • Flow area is the largest error source (Chen); bed level and roughness trade off (Oubanas).
      • Needs an altimetry or ICESat-2 track at the reach; small samples (one to 27 reaches).

    All 33 Family 4 papers, ranked for this research programme

    The order is this review’s judgement for a programme that uses Sentinel-1 water extent and takes its scale from channel geometry, not a ranking by the sources. Key points opens each paper’s research question, what the satellite observes and how that becomes discharge, method, advance, findings and limitations, in plain language.

    Must know: the papers this work builds on or answers to

    1. 1Chen et al. 2026 RSERebuilds the riverbed as a power-law curve from satellite laser points on the banks, the same idea as a parabolic bed.

      Research question

      Can the hidden underwater part of a river channel be rebuilt from satellites well enough to compute discharge with Manning’s equation, with no gauge?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      River width from Sentinel-2 (optical) and Sentinel-1 (radar) images, averaged over 2 km. Bank elevations and water-surface slope from ICESat-2 laser photons. The bank points are fitted with a bed curve y = k·x^r + z (r sets the shape, z the bed level); width then gives water depth and flow area on that curve, and Manning’s equation gives discharge. Roughness comes from a published formula using the river’s meander length and slope.

      How they did it

      Twelve reaches, 30 to 500 m wide, on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau, 2019–2024. Every ICESat-2 track within 2 km of each gauge is projected onto one cross-section; r and z are searched within set ranges and the best fit is kept. Braided or abrupt channels get piecewise fits. Results are compared with a width rating curve that is calibrated on the gauge.

      What it advanced

      Gets bed shape and bed level from the satellite itself instead of assuming them, and turns width into discharge in m³/s with no gauge.

      Findings

      Daily discharge: mean R² 0.87, NSE 0.84 and KGE 0.86, better than the gauge-calibrated width rating at 10 of 12 reaches. The fitted bed level was within 0.00–1.20 m of the surveyed bed, cross-sections within 3–15%, and roughness within 10% of gauge-derived values at most reaches. The fitted shape r ranged from 1.0 to 9.8, so a plain parabola (r = 2) rarely fitted. Flow area was the largest source of error.

      Limitations

      All twelve reaches are at stable gauged sites on one plateau. The search ranges for r and z were set by trial, braided reaches needed hand-chosen piecewise fits, and at one site the tracks were more than 2 km away. ICESat-2 passes rarely, so slope is a long-term average. Frozen months give no width.

      Why it matters here

      Rebuilds the riverbed as a power-law curve from satellite laser points on the banks, the same idea as a parabolic bed.

    2. 2Scherer et al. 2024 RSEGauge-free discharge for narrow rivers from imagery, altimetry and Manning, with an honest uncertainty band.

      Research question

      Can reach discharge be estimated for narrow, ungauged rivers from satellites alone, with realistic uncertainty?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      Water area from 3 m PlanetScope images, classified with the Segment Anything Model, and water level from 20 years of radar altimetry (DAHITI). A hypsometric curve links level and area, which maps the part of the bed that is ever exposed; the part never seen comes from an empirical width-to-depth rule. Slope comes from ICESat-2 (IRIS). Manning–Strickler is applied across 30 vertical strips of each cross-section.

      How they did it

      Several cross-sections close together in each reach; the roughness parameters are tuned so that all cross-sections give the same discharge (mass conservation). All input uncertainties are carried through to the result.

      What it advanced

      Builds the channel from observations and closes the problem by mass conservation instead of a gauge or a model prior; reaches rivers narrower than 100 m.

      Findings

      27 reaches worldwide: median NRMSE 12%, NSE 0.56 and R² 0.77. The 90% uncertainty band covered 91% of gauge values.

      Limitations

      Needs an altimetry track across the reach and cloud-free images from low to high flow. The reach must have no large tributaries, obstructions or braiding; backwater caused an overestimate on the Kelantan. Some cases needed expert bounds on roughness. Only 27 sites.

      Why it matters here

      Gauge-free discharge for narrow rivers from imagery, altimetry and Manning, with an honest uncertainty band.

    3. 3Gleason and Smith 2014 PNASThe first discharge from satellite images alone (AMHG): the gauge-free idea every later Family 4 method answers to.

      Research question

      Can absolute discharge come from satellite images alone, with nothing measured on the ground?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      Repeated river widths from Landsat TM images at many cross-sections. Along a river, the coefficient and exponent of each cross-section’s width–discharge power law (W = a·Q^b) fall on one line (at-many-stations hydraulic geometry, AMHG). That link removes half the unknowns, so the remaining ones can be fitted from the widths.

      How they did it

      A genetic algorithm finds width–discharge curves for every cross-section that obey the AMHG line and give the same discharge along a mass-conserving reach, then averages them. AMHG itself was checked with 88 gauging stations and three hydraulic models.

      What it advanced

      Showed that a river’s own width pattern carries its discharge scale, against the long-held view that these power laws are unpredictable from site to site.

      Findings

      Discharge errors of 20–30% (RMSE 23% Mississippi, 30% Athabasca, 20% Yangtze), and the ups and downs were tracked well.

      Limitations

      The width curves fit far worse than depth or velocity (r² 0.13–0.97). The semi-arid, braided-at-times Rio Grande failed outright (RMSE 1,083%). Large single-channel rivers only; big overbank floods are underestimated.

      Why it matters here

      The first discharge from satellite images alone (AMHG): the gauge-free idea every later Family 4 method answers to.

    4. 4Smith and Pavelsky 2008 WRRWater area divided by reach length (effective width) rated against discharge: the closest Family 4 relative of an area-based method.

      Research question

      Can daily but coarse satellite images give a usable discharge rating, and does it become transferable along a river if the reach is long enough?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      Water area on 250 m MODIS near-infrared images, mapped with a threshold reset for every image (halfway between 20 stable water pixels and 20 stable land pixels), divided by reach length to give an effective width. A power-law rating, width = a·Q^b, is fitted against a gauge 700 km downstream.

      How they did it

      65 cloud-free images over a 316 km braided reach of the Lena, 2001–2005; rating fitted on 2001 and tested on 2002–2005; the reach split into sub-reaches from 0.25 to 256 km.

      What it advanced

      The first continuous map of a hydraulic-geometry exponent from space, and evidence that a rating transfers along a river once the reach is long enough.

      Findings

      Width predicts discharge 8 days later (r² up to 0.81); mean error 11% in the calibration year and 27% (median 20%) afterwards. Beyond 60–90 km reaches the exponent settles at b = 0.48 within ±10%.

      Limitations

      Needs a gauge to fit the rating. One braided Arctic river; fewer than 10% of target dates were cloud-free.

      Why it matters here

      Water area divided by reach length (effective width) rated against discharge: the closest Family 4 relative of an area-based method.

    5. 5Andreadis et al. 2025 GRLThe first large test of real SWOT discharge: the honest benchmark for any gauge-free claim.

      Research question

      Do a decade of expectations built on simulated data hold up with real SWOT observations?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      Real SWOT water-surface elevation, width and slope averaged over about 10 km reaches, kept only when the mission’s quality flags and outlier filters pass. The SWOT algorithms turn them into discharge with Manning-type flow laws whose unknown parameters are set by a prior on mean annual flow; no gauge is used.

      How they did it

      First 15 months of the mission (March 2023 to July 2024), checked against 65 gauged reaches with the cleanest data.

      What it advanced

      Moved satellite discharge from simulation to real data at scale, and showed where the error comes from.

      Findings

      Median correlation 0.73 (middle half 0.51–0.89) with no gauge information, but median bias 50% and median NSE below zero. About 11,274 ungauged places already have usable measurements. The bias follows the bias of the mean-flow prior (62% here).

      Limitations

      Short record and only the best-quality data; rivers must be wide enough for SWOT (designed for over 100 m).

      Why it matters here

      The first large test of real SWOT discharge: the honest benchmark for any gauge-free claim.

    6. 6Larnier et al. 2025 WRRRebuilds bathymetry and roughness along a whole river network from SWOT, ICESat-2 and Sentinel-1, the channel-recovery idea at network scale.

      Research question

      Inferring inflows, bed and friction from satellite water levels alone is underdetermined. Can a hydrological model close the problem across a whole river network?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      SWOT water levels along the network (cleaned by a wavelet filter), ICESat-2 elevations and Sentinel-1 water masks (for widths) build the first channel geometry. A 1D Saint-Venant network model with friction K = α·h^β produces discharge, and variational data assimilation adjusts inflows (12 points), bed elevation (2,572 points) and friction (24 patches) to match the observed levels.

      How they did it

      Maroni basin, French Guiana, 2023. The prior inflows come from the MGB hydrological model, which the paper says was manually calibrated on in-situ discharge at five gauges (2016–2023); the same five gauges are used to check the result.

      What it advanced

      Recovers the channel and the flow together over a whole network, not one reach at a time.

      Findings

      With SWOT data alone assimilated, discharge NRMSE 0.05–0.18 at the five gauges, 18–71% better than the prior; 68% of the water-level fit within ±0.25 m.

      Limitations

      One basin. Not gauge-free: the prior inflows come from a model calibrated on the validation gauges, so the improvement is over a gauge-informed start. Uses SWOT’s short calibration phase.

      Why it matters here

      Rebuilds bathymetry and roughness along a whole river network from SWOT, ICESat-2 and Sentinel-1, the channel-recovery idea at network scale.

    7. 7Legleiter and Kinzel 2026 WRRTests how well simple channel shapes, including Dingman’s single exponent behind a power-law bed, match 46,971 surveyed cross-sections.

      Research question

      How well do simple mathematical shapes reproduce real river cross-sections, and can they fill in the part a sensor cannot see?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      No satellite data: 46,971 surveyed cross-sections at US gauging stations (National Cross-Section Database). Four shape models are fitted to each: Dingman’s single-exponent shape (r = 1 triangle, r = 2 parabola), two asymmetric shapes from the literature, and a new one built from stacked probability curves (SPARCS).

      How they did it

      Each model is fitted to every section; accuracy is compared by five metrics, and sections are cut at a depth limit to mimic a sensor that sees only the shallow part.

      What it advanced

      The first large test of channel-shape approximations against real sections, with parameters that read as mean depth, asymmetry, bar convexity and bed flatness.

      Findings

      The new model and one asymmetric model matched depth with median R² 0.77 and cross-section area within 1%. The symmetric Dingman shape had a lower median R² and a wider spread. When only the part shallower than half the maximum depth was seen, median R² fell from 0.70 to 0.46.

      Limitations

      The sections come from gauging stations, so straight, uniform channels dominate; no model can produce mid-channel bars or several threads.

      Why it matters here

      Tests how well simple channel shapes, including Dingman’s single exponent behind a power-law bed, match 46,971 surveyed cross-sections.

    8. 8Wu et al. 2023 J. HydrologyFits a power-law bed to satellite water level and width: the same shape idea, fitted from data, with an error metric to read carefully.

      Research question

      Can a river’s bed elevation be estimated from satellite water level and width alone, without any bathymetric survey?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      Water level at altimetry virtual stations and river width from Landsat. A power-law cross-section (shape r) gives a nonlinear relation between level and width; fitting it gives the bed elevation and r.

      How they did it

      Five reaches of the upper Yangtze; widths averaged over 1–10 km; sensitivity of the result to level and width errors tested.

      What it advanced

      Gets bed elevation and shape from satellite data alone, with no prior bathymetry.

      Findings

      Fitted shapes r = 4.1–7.7 (flatter bed, steeper banks as r rises). Bed elevation was off by 3–11 m, which the paper reports as 1.25–6.18% because it divides by the absolute elevation above sea level. Errors fell sharply as more of the channel was exposed.

      Limitations

      Overestimates the bed when less than 40% of the channel is exposed, and is very sensitive to level errors. The percentage error hides metre-scale bed errors.

      Why it matters here

      Fits a power-law bed to satellite water level and width: the same shape idea, fitted from data, with an error metric to read carefully.

    9. 9Coppo Frias et al. 2023 HESSBuilds hydraulic models from ICESat-2 cross-sections on the same reaches Chen et al. 2026 used, but with gauged discharge.

      Research question

      Can ICESat-2’s detailed elevation profiles replace surveyed cross-sections in a river hydraulic model?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      ICESat-2 photons (0.7 m along track) give the exposed cross-section; the inland-water product gives water levels. A steady-state hydraulic model with a Dingman-type section is calibrated for depth, roughness and bed shape against those levels, with gauged discharge as its input.

      How they did it

      Yellow River from Jimai to Mentang, 2018–2021; calibration and validation periods split by gauge data availability; the calibrated parameters also tested in a full hydrodynamic model.

      What it advanced

      First use of ICESat-2 cross-sections for river hydraulic modelling, reaching rivers narrower than 100 m.

      Findings

      Water-level RMSE 0.41 m (0.44 m in validation, 0.59 m in the full model); discharge RMSE 107 m³/s at Jimai and 122 m³/s at Mentang.

      Limitations

      Not gauge-free: gauged discharge drives the calibration. ICESat-2 passes rarely.

      Why it matters here

      Builds hydraulic models from ICESat-2 cross-sections on the same reaches Chen et al. 2026 used, but with gauged discharge.

    Important context

    1. 10Brinkerhoff et al. 2020 WRRUses bed shape (Dingman’s r: 1 triangle, 2 parabola, infinity a box) as a prior chosen by river type.

      Research question

      Flow-law inversion depends on prior guesses that satellites cannot measure. Do priors chosen by river type beat one set of priors for every river on Earth?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      Landsat river widths (RivWidthCloud) in the Mackenzie basin, and simulated SWOT-like width and height. geoBAM rewrites the at-many-stations power law in terms of bankfull width, bankfull depth, bed shape r, roughness and slope, and draws their priors from more than 370,000 field measurements grouped by river type.

      How they did it

      Rivers are assigned a type by unsupervised clustering or by an expert scheme; Bayesian sampling then estimates discharge from the widths.

      What it advanced

      Showed that better geomorphic priors, not a new algorithm, are what reduce the error.

      Findings

      Median NSE rose from −0.05 to 0.26 (Mackenzie, 108 gauged rivers) and from 0.16 to 0.46 (19 SWOT-like rivers).

      Limitations

      A river given the wrong type gets worse; median NSE on real widths is still only 0.26.

      Why it matters here

      Uses bed shape (Dingman’s r: 1 triangle, 2 parabola, infinity a box) as a prior chosen by river type.

    2. 11Lin et al. 2023 RSEThe largest real-data test of width-only inversion: how often it works at 3,078 gauges.

      Research question

      Do flow-law algorithms that work at a few rivers still work when run unchanged at thousands of rivers?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      Widths from 357,389 Landsat scenes (1984–2019) measured with RivWidthCloud, skipping cloud, snow and shadow. BAM and geoBAM turn width into discharge through at-many-stations hydraulic geometry, with the discharge prior from the global GRADES model (not fitted to gauges).

      How they did it

      Run “off the shelf” at 3,078 gauged reaches as if ungauged, then again with richer priors on seasonality and monthly flow; the factors behind success are analysed.

      What it advanced

      Shifted the question from the best accuracy at a few places to how often a method works anywhere.

      Findings

      Positive KGE at 27% (BAM) and 39% (geoBAM) of sites, 46–65% with richer priors. Works best where the width exponent b is high and the climate is humid.

      Limitations

      Low-b channels (almost two-thirds of the sites), dry climates and very wide rivers do worst, and the prior controls the bias.

      Why it matters here

      The largest real-data test of width-only inversion: how often it works at 3,078 gauges.

    3. 12Durand et al. 2023 WRRHow SWOT discharge is built and how accurate it should be: the reference for the global product.

      Research question

      How will SWOT discharge be computed, and how accurate will it be, including in ungauged basins?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      SWOT radar pixels are mapped onto river nodes; width is inundated area divided by reach length, and slope comes from node elevations along the river. A modified Manning equation, Q = (1/n)·(A₀ + δA)^(5/3)·W^(−2/3)·S^(1/2), needs two unknowns per reach (the unseen baseline area A₀ and roughness n), estimated by several inversion algorithms.

      How they did it

      Sets out the processing chain and the first full uncertainty budget, split into random and systematic error. The “unconstrained” branch uses only model priors; a “gage-constrained” branch adds gauges where they exist.

      What it advanced

      Gives the field an explicit error budget and shows that the problem is bias, not noise.

      Findings

      Expected error under 30% for two-thirds of reaches, mostly bias; changes over time within 15% for nearly all reaches; mean flow within 30% without gauges (Alaska example).

      Limitations

      Written before launch; rivers over 100 m wide; about 10-day sampling may miss the peaks of smaller, flashier rivers.

      Why it matters here

      How SWOT discharge is built and how accurate it should be: the reference for the global product.

    4. 13Bjerklie et al. 2003 J. HydrologyRegression formulas for discharge from what a satellite can see, including a width rating that assumes a parabolic channel.

      Research question

      Which combinations of width, slope, depth and velocity, all potentially visible from space, could estimate discharge without a gauge?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      No satellite data: more than 1,000 field discharge measurements (from over 200,000 to under 1 m³/s) are used to fit general formulas, for example Q = 7.22·W^1.02·Y^1.74·S^0.35 (width W, mean depth Y, slope S). It also derives a width rating for a parabolic channel from Manning’s equation.

      How they did it

      Multiple regression on reach-averaged field data, tested on held-out measurements and with simulated measurement error.

      What it advanced

      Showed that a constant slope per river can replace a measured one, and that resistance need not be measured because it varies with channel geometry.

      Findings

      Average relative error below 20% for the main formulas (10% for the width–velocity one).

      Limitations

      Built from field data, not satellites; still needs depth or velocity, which satellites cannot measure directly, and over-predicts in small rivers (under 10 m³/s).

      Why it matters here

      Regression formulas for discharge from what a satellite can see, including a width rating that assumes a parabolic channel.

    5. 14Feng et al. 2019 WRRShows where width-based methods stop: below about 40 m they fail.

      Research question

      Can CubeSat images, alone or fused with Landsat and Sentinel-2, give width-based discharge for medium and small rivers?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      Widths from Landsat 8 and Sentinel-2 (water where MNDWI exceeds EVI or NDVI and EVI is below 0.1) and from Planet CubeSats (NDWI with an Otsu threshold refined by breakpoint analysis), measured along 30 m-wide cross-section buffers. BAM turns width into discharge; in the ungauged case the prior comes from reanalysis runoff.

      How they did it

      11 Arctic rivers 16 to over 1,000 m wide; compared with rating curves fitted to gauges.

      What it advanced

      Fusion of several satellites gave 2–6 times more days with an estimate, without loss of accuracy.

      Findings

      Ungauged nRMSE 34–71% for large rivers and 61–69% for medium ones; BAM can beat a satellite rating curve given the same widths.

      Limitations

      Rivers under 40 m fail: too narrow for Landsat and Sentinel-2, and the CubeSats’ four bands cannot resolve the water well enough.

      Why it matters here

      Shows where width-based methods stop: below about 40 m they fail.

    6. 15Hao et al. 2024 WRRReflectance instead of width for narrow rivers, relevant where SAR area discriminates poorly at low flow.

      Research question

      Width is hard to measure on narrow rivers. Can the colour (reflectance) of the river surface carry the discharge signal instead?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      No water mask: the model reads time series of Landsat top-of-atmosphere reflectance (red, green, blue, near-infrared and two shortwave-infrared bands) on cloud-free days. A Transformer predicts the percentage change from mean flow, and the series is scaled to the long-term mean from the GRADES global model.

      How they did it

      Trained on 2,036 gauges (GRDC and Caravan), tested on rivers held out as ungauged.

      What it advanced

      Avoids the mixed pixels at the water edge that spoil width on narrow rivers.

      Findings

      Positive KGE in 68.6% of ungauged rivers, against 28.4% for BAM and 33.1% for geoBAM, though two-thirds were under 100 m wide; no loss on braided rivers.

      Limitations

      Needs a large gauged training set, and the magnitude comes from a global model, so bias follows that model.

      Why it matters here

      Reflectance instead of width for narrow rivers, relevant where SAR area discriminates poorly at low flow.

    7. 16Oubanas et al. 2018 WRRInverts bed, roughness and discharge together with a full hydraulic model, using simple trapezoidal sections as the first guess.

      Research question

      Can discharge be estimated when the bathymetry and roughness are also unknown, as in a truly ungauged river?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      Simulated SWOT water level and width every 200 m along the river. A full 1.5D Saint-Venant model (SIC2) is fitted to them by variational assimilation (4D-Var), adjusting inflow, bed level and Strickler roughness together; the first guesses come from Manning with trapezoidal sections built from the SWOT data.

      How they did it

      One year on 133 km of the Po and six months on 153 km of the Sacramento, with synthetic data.

      What it advanced

      Showed that discharge, bed and roughness can be recovered at the same time.

      Findings

      Relative RMSE 12.1% (Po) and 11.2% (Sacramento) at overpass times.

      Limitations

      Synthetic data; bed level and roughness trade off against each other, so the recovered values are not reliable outside the run.

      Why it matters here

      Inverts bed, roughness and discharge together with a full hydraulic model, using simple trapezoidal sections as the first guess.

    8. 17Schaperow et al. 2019 WRRRecovers the unseen bed from height–width curves, the step any gauge-free Manning method needs.

      Research question

      Can SWOT-like water height and width reveal the submerged channel shape well enough to estimate bed elevation and low-flow area?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      Simulated SWOT-like height and width built from 5 m bathymetry of the Upper Mississippi. Four curve-fitting methods describe the height–width relation; the two nonlinear ones follow hydraulic geometry and extrapolate the bed.

      How they did it

      Tested on thirty 10 km reaches at different channel exposures, then on about 4,000 HydroSWOT sites; an NLSB-based prior for low-flow area is proposed for SWOT discharge algorithms.

      What it advanced

      A bathymetry prior that works on any non-braided reach, not only at selected sites.

      Findings

      Depth within a median 1.1% and low-flow area within 13% when as little as 40% of the channel is exposed.

      Limitations

      Simulated observations; braided reaches excluded; gives bathymetry, not discharge.

      Why it matters here

      Recovers the unseen bed from height–width curves, the step any gauge-free Manning method needs.

    9. 18Musaeus et al. 2024 WRRCompletes ICESat-2 cross-sections below the water line with the diffusive-wave equation, another way to fill the unseen bed.

      Research question

      Can complete river cross-sections be built from ICESat-2 without field surveys or inverse hydraulic modelling?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      ICESat-2 terrain profiles where tracks cross the river, plus water level and slope from simultaneous beams. The submerged part is computed from the diffusive-wave equation with the best available discharge (gauges and a regional rainfall–runoff model).

      How they did it

      A stretch of the Mekong; a 1D hydrodynamic model runs on the new sections, with Manning numbers tuned by sub-reach.

      What it advanced

      Turns ICESat-2 crossings into full cross-sections for an operational hydrodynamic model.

      Findings

      Water-level RMSE 0.676 m against ICESat-2, and KGE 0.880 against gauged water levels.

      Limitations

      Needs discharge from gauges or a model; fails where flow is supercritical or accelerating.

      Why it matters here

      Completes ICESat-2 cross-sections below the water line with the diffusive-wave equation, another way to fill the unseen bed.

    10. 19Bjerklie et al. 2018 J. HydrologyThe Manning roughness route Chen et al. 2026 rely on, tested on the Yukon with and without calibration.

      Research question

      Can discharge, depth and velocity be estimated from satellite width, level and slope with general hydraulic relations?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      Water area from Landsat (DSWE) divided by reach length gives width; Jason-2 gives level and slope. Manning’s equation and a velocity-profile equation give discharge, with the bed level from paired width and level and roughness from channel morphology.

      How they did it

      Two reaches of the Yukon, Alaska (35 and 38 km), with and without calibration on three gauged discharges.

      What it advanced

      Gives a way to set roughness and the zero-flow level from what satellites see.

      Findings

      Uncalibrated mean discharge within about 20% (13% to −21%); within about 5% after calibration on three measurements.

      Limitations

      Uncalibrated estimates are biased at low and high flow; the change of roughness with depth is the key unknown.

      Why it matters here

      The Manning roughness route Chen et al. 2026 rely on, tested on the Yukon with and without calibration.

    11. 20Paris et al. 2026 Nature CommunicationsGlobal mean river depth from altimetry, the depth term a geometry method otherwise takes from a regression.

      Research question

      Can satellite altimetry and a global flow reanalysis give rating curves, discharge and mean depth for rivers worldwide?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      Water levels from nadir altimetry missions at more than 26,000 locations (Hydroweb-Next). A rating curve at each station is fitted by Bayesian sampling to a 30-year global discharge reanalysis that includes gauge-based bias correction; the fitted bed level gives mean depth.

      How they did it

      Extreme climate years filtered out before fitting; results checked against public discharge databases.

      What it advanced

      A near-global set of rating curves and mean depths with uncertainty.

      Findings

      Median KGE 0.41 between rated and modelled discharge across about 32,000 virtual stations.

      Limitations

      The reference discharge is a model reanalysis of uneven quality, so a good fit does not guarantee accurate discharge.

      Why it matters here

      Global mean river depth from altimetry, the depth term a geometry method otherwise takes from a regression.

    12. 21Cerbelaud et al. 2026 NatureSWOT shows that rivers with similar discharge have very different bank shapes: evidence against one assumed shape.

      Research question

      What do SWOT’s first year of width and elevation reveal about river channel shapes and river storage worldwide?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      SWOT width and water-surface elevation at 126,674 reaches, October 2023 to September 2024. Hypsometric curves fitted by an errors-in-variables method give the active cross-section and its change in area, hence storage change.

      How they did it

      Storage variability compared with a global model simulation, basin by basin.

      What it advanced

      The first near-global observation of active channel shape.

      Findings

      Shapes range from concave to convex, and rivers with comparable discharge have markedly different shapes. Global annual storage variability is 313.1 ± 129.5 km³, about 28% below the lowest modelled estimate.

      Limitations

      One water year; frozen Arctic rivers and SWOT’s revisit interval limit the record; wide rivers only.

      Why it matters here

      SWOT shows that rivers with similar discharge have very different bank shapes: evidence against one assumed shape.

    13. 22Riggs et al. 2023 ERLThe largest gauged test of width ratings: what width can do when a gauge is available.

      Research question

      Can satellite river widths fill gaps and extend gauge records worldwide?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      River width from Landsat and Sentinel-2 at many candidate cross-sections near each gauge; a rating curve chooses the measurement location and rating function that best fit the gauge.

      How they did it

      2,168 gauges; also reviews the availability of 45,837 public gauge records.

      What it advanced

      Turns satellite width into near real-time discharge where a gauge has gone quiet.

      Findings

      More than 275,000 daily estimates; median bias 1.4%, median KGE 0.46. 37% of public records are discontinuous and 77% have no real-time data.

      Limitations

      Each curve needs that gauge’s own record: it extends gauges, it does not replace them.

      Why it matters here

      The largest gauged test of width ratings: what width can do when a gauge is available.

    Useful background

    1. 23Smith et al. 1997 Hydrological ProcessesThe root of the area–discharge idea, and the first warning that such curves are site-specific.

      Research question

      What can satellites measure about rivers: flooded area, water level, or discharge itself?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      Water area from visible, infrared and radar images, and water level from radar altimetry. Area becomes discharge through a curve fitted to ground discharge measurements at each site.

      How they did it

      A review of sensors and of area–discharge and stage studies up to 1997.

      What it advanced

      Set out the area–discharge method and the radar advantage under vegetation.

      Findings

      Radar altimeters “show great promise” for level on large rivers; radar sees water under plants and forest canopy where optical sensors cannot.

      Limitations

      Area–discharge curves “will vary significantly between rivers and therefore must be constructed for each site”, except perhaps braided rivers; clouds and trees block optical sensors.

      Why it matters here

      The root of the area–discharge idea, and the first warning that such curves are site-specific.

    2. 24Gleason and Wang 2015 GRLExplains when AMHG exists, and therefore when width-only inversion can work.

      Research question

      Why does at-many-stations hydraulic geometry exist at all?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      No new satellite data: it works on width–discharge curves at many cross-sections of 50 rivers.

      How they did it

      Mathematical analysis of where the cross-section curves intersect.

      What it advanced

      Showed that AMHG arises when the curves of all cross-sections cross near the same width and discharge, and gave an index of how often they do (p_int).

      Findings

      Rivers where fewer than about 15% of curve crossings fall in the observed range have weak AMHG (r² below 0.80).

      Limitations

      Supports leaving out rivers with very low or very high (braided) width exponents and flashy dry-land channels.

      Why it matters here

      Explains when AMHG exists, and therefore when width-only inversion can work.

    3. 25Durand et al. 2016 WRRThe benchmark that defined what SWOT algorithms were expected to do, and showed that bias dominates.

      Research question

      Before SWOT: can discharge be recovered from water level, width and slope alone, and which algorithm works?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      Simulated SWOT-like level, width and slope from hydraulic models of 19 rivers, with added errors of 5 cm, 5 m and 0.1 cm/km. Five algorithms (AMHG, GaMo, MetroMan, MFG, MFCR) estimate the unknown baseline area and roughness, most with a prior on mean annual flow from a water-balance model.

      How they did it

      All algorithms run on the same data and reaches; an ensemble median is also scored.

      What it advanced

      The first common test of the competing algorithms.

      Findings

      At least one algorithm reached under 35% relative RMSE in 14 of 16 non-braided rivers.

      Limitations

      Synthetic data with small errors; bias often dominated; braided rivers failed.

      Why it matters here

      The benchmark that defined what SWOT algorithms were expected to do, and showed that bias dominates.

    4. 26Hagemann et al. 2017 WRRThe Bayesian method (BAM) behind most width-only results in this family.

      Research question

      The SWOT inverse problem has more unknowns than equations. How can discharge be estimated defensibly anyway?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      Width, slope and height along a river. Manning’s equation, Q = (1/n)·A^(5/3)·W^(−2/3)·S^(1/2) with A = A₀ + δA, and/or AMHG; priors on A₀ from 10,081 US cross-sections (hydroSWOT), on n from published values, and on mean flow from a water-balance model.

      How they did it

      Bayesian sampling on the 19 simulated rivers of Durand et al. 2016, plus real widths from earlier AMHG work.

      What it advanced

      Turned the underdetermined problem into a probabilistic one with stated priors.

      Findings

      Median NSE 0.79–0.89 for the Manning versions on simulated data; AMHG-only was biased by more than 200% on some rivers, and a poor mean-flow prior biased results by orders of magnitude.

      Limitations

      Depends on priors from other rivers; tested on simulated, not real, observations.

      Why it matters here

      The Bayesian method (BAM) behind most width-only results in this family.

    5. 27Biancamaria et al. 2015 Surveys in GeophysicsWhat SWOT can and cannot see: no depth, and rivers over 100 m.

      Research question

      What will the SWOT mission measure over rivers, and how well?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      A Ka-band radar interferometer imaging two 50 km swaths on a 20.86-day repeat, giving water level, slope and a water mask.

      How they did it

      Mission design and capability review.

      What it advanced

      The standard reference for SWOT’s design.

      Findings

      Water level to about 10 cm when averaged over 1 km²; designed for rivers wider than 100 m (goal 50 m).

      Limitations

      SWOT does not measure depth, and “in most circumstances, in situ gages will be, by far, more precise than any remote sensing discharge estimates”.

      Why it matters here

      What SWOT can and cannot see: no depth, and rivers over 100 m.

    6. 28Gleason and Durand 2020 Remote SensingThe field’s own map: how methods are grouped and what “ungauged” really means.

      Research question

      The field was fragmented. What does “ungauged” mean when data exist but are not shared, and how should methods be grouped?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      A review: groups methods into assimilation into hydrological models, assimilation into hydraulic models, and geomorphic inversion (McFLI).

      How they did it

      Structured review, mostly of post-2010 work, organised by gauging context rather than by sensor.

      What it advanced

      Defined McFLI and named “politically ungauged” basins.

      Findings

      Using width, height and slope together beats width alone; timing is captured well, magnitude often not; the prior matters more than the algorithm.

      Limitations

      Does not tabulate accuracies, because studies are not comparable.

      Why it matters here

      The field’s own map: how methods are grouped and what “ungauged” really means.

    7. 29Paris et al. 2016 WRRAltimetry rating curves whose cease-to-flow level tracks the river bed.

      Research question

      Can satellite altimetry and a basin model give rating curves, with uncertainty, across a poorly gauged basin?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      ENVISAT and Jason-2 water levels at about 920 virtual stations. A rating curve Q = a·(H − z)^b at each is fitted by Bayesian sampling to discharge from the MGB-IPH model; slope is added near confluences to handle backwater.

      How they did it

      Amazon basin, more than 100 tributaries; 80% of data to fit, 20% to validate.

      What it advanced

      Rating curves with uncertainty, a bed level from the cease-to-flow parameter, and a backwater correction.

      Findings

      NSE 0.68 against validation data and 0.71 against gauges; bed level within 10% of ADCP sections.

      Limitations

      Only as good as the model discharge; needs a ground-track crossing.

      Why it matters here

      Altimetry rating curves whose cease-to-flow level tracks the river bed.

    8. 30Moramarco et al. 2019 WRRBathymetry from surface velocity and water level, a geometry route that needs no hydraulic model.

      Research question

      Can bathymetry and discharge be estimated from surface velocity and water level when the river bed is unknown?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      Water level from ENVISAT and surface velocity from MODIS at one site; ground data at three Italian sites. Entropy theory describes the velocity across the section; roughness, slope, bed elevation and an entropy parameter are found by matching the observed maximum surface velocity.

      How they did it

      Genetic algorithm with 1,000 random starts for uncertainty; 18 ground discharge measurements as benchmark.

      What it advanced

      Bathymetry and discharge together without a hydraulic model.

      Findings

      Ground data: area and discharge errors about 10% at the median. Satellite data: area within 9%, but discharge errors above 30%.

      Limitations

      Satellite velocity works only on large rivers; one satellite site.

      Why it matters here

      Bathymetry from surface velocity and water level, a geometry route that needs no hydraulic model.

    9. 31Masafu et al. 2023 GRLSurface velocity from satellite video: a different observable, tested on an Australian river.

      Research question

      Can satellite video measure river surface velocity well enough to give discharge?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      28 seconds of 5 Hz commercial satellite video at 1.2 m over the Darling River during a 1-in-5-year flood. Particle image velocimetry gives surface velocity; times a depth-averaging coefficient and high-resolution channel topography, it gives discharge.

      How they did it

      Platform motion stabilised and its residual error assessed; velocities checked against a calibrated 2D model.

      What it advanced

      Discharge from a satellite without a rating curve, during a flood.

      Findings

      Discharge within 0.3–15% of gauge measurements.

      Limitations

      Cloud-free video only; the coefficient α and the channel topography, which does not come from the satellite, drive the error; one flood.

      Why it matters here

      Surface velocity from satellite video: a different observable, tested on an Australian river.

    10. 32Tuozzolo et al. 2019 GRLThe first real test of SWOT-style discharge, and the first warning that the prior sets the bias.

      Research question

      Do SWOT discharge algorithms work on real swath-altimetry data, before SWOT existed?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      AirSWOT, an airborne Ka-band radar like SWOT, measured water level, width and slope on six days over 40 km of the Willamette. Three algorithms (MetroMan, BAM and a variational method) turned them into discharge, each with a prior on mean annual discharge.

      How they did it

      Compared with in-situ gauges; sensitivity to the prior tested.

      What it advanced

      Moved SWOT algorithms from simulation to real observations.

      Findings

      NRMSE 10–31%.

      Limitations

      Sensitive to the prior mean annual discharge; clouds removed width data; six days only.

      Why it matters here

      The first real test of SWOT-style discharge, and the first warning that the prior sets the bias.

    11. 33Frasson et al. 2019 GRLGlobal width, slope and sinuosity, and how far one width–discharge law can be trusted.

      Research question

      How do river width, slope, sinuosity, meander wavelength and discharge relate across the globe?

      What is observed, and how it becomes discharge

      No discharge method: Landsat river centrelines and SRTM elevation give width, slope, meander wavelength and sinuosity for rivers wider than 90 m between 60°N and 56°S, compared with modelled discharge.

      How they did it

      Global mapping and analysis of the relations.

      What it advanced

      Spatially continuous maps that feed the priors of satellite discharge algorithms.

      Findings

      One width–discharge power law predicts width to −35% to +81% across rivers from 100 to 50,000 m³/s; narrower rivers show a wider range of slope and sinuosity.

      Limitations

      Relations weaken in places; rivers under 90 m are not mapped.

      Why it matters here

      Global width, slope and sinuosity, and how far one width–discharge law can be trusted.

    Where this family stands

    ADVANCES SO FAR

    • Defined the problem class — mass-conserved flow law inversion — and reorganised a fragmented literature by gauging context, including the politically ungauged basins where gauges exist but data are not shared.
    • Established feasibility on synthetic data: at least one algorithm reached under 35% relative RMSE in 14 of 16 non-braided rivers.
    • Gave the underconstrained inversion a statistically defensible treatment through Bayesian priors drawn from ADCP measurements.
    • Showed discharge, bathymetry and roughness can be inverted simultaneously — the actual ungauged condition — at 11–12% relative RMSE.
    • Moved from synthetic to real: SWOT data give median correlation 0.73 using no gauge information, across roughly 11,274 ungauged locations already measurable.
    • Reconstructed the submerged geometry that Manning-based retrieval assumes, from satellite morphology alone, at mean R2 0.87.
    • Large-sample evaluation: 3,078 gauges, positive KGE at 27–39% of sites off the shelf and 46–65% with richer priors (Lin et al. 2023).
    • Narrow rivers without a gauge: median NRMSE 12% and NSE 0.56 on reaches many under 100 m (Scherer et al. 2024); positive KGE in 68.6% of ungauged rivers from reflectance (Hao et al. 2024).
    • Network-scale assimilation of SWOT levels that also infers bathymetry and friction, 18–71% better than the prior (Larnier et al. 2025), starting from the inflows of a gauge-calibrated hydrological model.

    LIMITATIONS SO FAR

    • Timing is good; magnitude is not. Median bias on real SWOT data is 50%, and bias dominated total error even in the synthetic benchmarks.
    • Width-based methods need wide rivers: they fail below about 40 m (Feng et al. 2019) and in braided channels. Altimetry with high-resolution imagery (Scherer et al. 2024) or reflectance (Hao et al. 2024, no loss on braided rivers) narrows this.
    • The real-data record is short — SWOT contributes about three years so far.
    • Accuracy depends more on the prior information supplied than on which algorithm is chosen, and those priors come from other rivers.
    • Results are not comparable across studies; the field's own review deliberately declines to tabulate accuracies.

    Read these first

    Start with these. Between them they cover most of what this section concludes. Key points opens a short summary of each paper and why it comes first.

    1. R66Gleason and Smith 2014 PNASdischarge from images alone (AMHG)

      Main points

      • Finds that at-a-station hydraulic-geometry coefficients and exponents fall on one line along a river (AMHG), which halves the unknowns.
      • Estimates discharge from repeat satellite widths alone: RMSE 20–30% on the Mississippi, Athabasca and Yangtze.
      • The semi-arid Rio Grande failed outright (RMSE 1,083%), and the width fit is far weaker than the depth and velocity fits.

      Why read it first

      It is the paper that made gauge-free discharge from images credible, and the basis of BAM and the SWOT algorithms that followed.

    2. R69Durand et al. 2016 WRRwhat the SWOT algorithms were expected to do

      Main points

      • Compares five discharge algorithms on synthetic SWOT-like height, width and slope for 19 rivers, before SWOT launched.
      • At least one algorithm reached under 35% relative RMSE in 14 of the 16 non-braided rivers, despite out-of-bank flows and backwater.
      • Bias often dominated the error, and braided rivers failed.

      Why read it first

      It is the benchmark that defined what SWOT-era algorithms can do, and the expectations that real SWOT data were later checked against.

    3. R72Gleason and Durand 2020 Remote Sensingthe field’s framing and vocabulary

      Main points

      • Reviews remote sensing of discharge, organised by gauging context rather than by sensor, and defines the McFLI class.
      • Multi-input inversion (width, height and slope) beats width alone; dynamics are captured well but biases are often large.
      • Accuracy depends more on prior information than on the algorithm chosen.

      Why read it first

      It orients you in a fragmented subfield and gives the vocabulary (McFLI, gauging context) the rest of Family 4 uses.

    4. R73Andreadis et al. 2025 GRLwhat real SWOT data deliver

      Main points

      • The first large assessment of discharge from real SWOT data (March 2023 – July 2024), validated at 65 gauged reaches.
      • Median correlation 0.73 (IQR 0.51–0.89) using no gauge information.
      • Median bias 50% and median NSE negative: the dynamics are right but the magnitude often is not.

      Why read it first

      It is the reckoning for a decade of synthetic-data expectations, and the honest benchmark for any gauge-free claim.

    Section 08 · Family 5

    Surrogate discharge

    Calibrating on a proxy

    This family is easy to confuse with §07, and the difference matters.

    Family 4 inverts hydraulics to recover discharge: width, elevation and slope go into Manning’s equation and m³/s comes out. Family 5 does something weaker and, in ungauged basins, often more useful.

    It takes a satellite signal that merely correlates with discharge — one that may carry no physical units at all — and uses it as the calibration target for a conceptual rainfall–runoff model. The model still produces the discharge. The satellite signal replaces the gauge record, not the gauge reading.

    Family 5 at a glance

    The spine of this family is the left column — a single lineage running from one unitless microwave ratio to global SAR. The right-hand column is the move that made the proxy quantitative.

    Solid arrows mark a documented build-on or extension; dashed arrows mark a study that tests, benchmarks or limits another. Where an arrow reflects this review’s reading rather than an explicit statement in the papers, the text below says so.

    The founding move

    Sun et al. (2011) named the idea: satellite river variables as surrogates for discharge measurements. The change is in the calibration objective:

    • Couple the rainfall–runoff model to power-law hydraulic geometry at the outlet.
    • The model then outputs width or water level, not discharge.
    • Calibrate model and geometry parameters together against the satellite measurement.

    The step before was Smith and Pavelsky (2008), who still needed a gauge 700 km downstream to rate MODIS width on the Lena (§07); Sun and colleagues removed it. They showed it with river width on the Mekong at Pakse and with TOPEX/Poseidon level on the Upper Mississippi, getting fairly reasonable streamflow with no streamflow data at all. The same group then applied the method to a basin that really is ungauged, the Irrawaddy in Myanmar (Sun et al. 2015), and later work took it to smaller rivers with high-resolution images (Sun et al. 2018; Huang et al. 2022).

    The signal that became the standard

    Brakenridge et al. (2007) introduced the passive-microwave C/M ratio: a Calibration pixel over dry land against a Measurement pixel over the river. It responds to the water area in the pixel, is unitless, daily and cloud-proof, and correlates with in-situ flow (Yoon et al. 2022). Most later work in this family, including the UNSW lineage below, calibrates on it.

    A naming warning: check the orientation before you cite it

    The same quantity appears as “C/M ratio” (Yoon et al. 2022), “MC ratio, Measurement-calibration ratio” (Yoon et al. 2025), both at once (Yoon et al. 2024) and “CM” (Filippucci et al. 2025). One orientation rises with discharge and the other falls, so define it by the pixels, not the initials.

    The unit problem, and the fix

    The recurring obstacle in this family is stated most clearly by Yoon et al. (2024): the surrogate signal has no defined unit. A C/M or reflectance ratio tracks the shape of the hydrograph but says nothing about magnitude, so calibrating on it alone leaves the model’s water balance unconstrained.

    The UNSW answer is to supply the missing scale from climate rather than from a gauge. Mean catchment discharge is estimated from the Budyko relationship — which needs only long-term average precipitation and potential evapotranspiration — and that single number converts the unitless series into a quantified one. It is an elegant move: the two things an ungauged basin does have are a satellite signal and a climatology.

    A second route: geometry. Two calibration studies take the scale from the channel instead of from climate. Liu et al. (2015) turned modelled flow into water level and water area with a Manning channel model whose shape parameters were calibrated alongside the hydrological ones, with no rating curve; using both signals gave daily NSE 0.758, against 0.469 with water area alone and 0.717 with level alone. Hulsman et al. (2020) found that altimetric levels led to overestimated flows until cross-section and slope from terrain data were used with Manning (NSE 0.60). Ahmad and Kim (2019) showed why geometry matters for a water-area signal: the Sentinel-1 area–flow relation was accurate where the channel had gentle side slopes and was not regulated, and weaker for small streams.

    A classification note

    Chen et al. (2026) — the ICESat-2 / Sentinel-1/2 HGIDR algorithm, reporting mean R2 0.87, NSE 0.84 and KGE 0.86 across twelve Qinghai-Tibet Plateau reaches — belongs in §07, not here. It estimates the Manning coefficient from satellite-observed morphology and inverts the Manning equation, which is hydraulic inversion rather than surrogate calibration. It is in §07’s evidence table.

    Beyond river signals: calibrating on other satellite variables

    A parallel strand constrains other parts of the water balance (evapotranspiration, storage, land-surface temperature or their spatial patterns). Not every paper replaces the gauge; some add to it.

    • Huang et al. (2020), WRR: remotely sensed ET and storage across seven calibration schemes in 30 Yalong River catchments, China, written for ungauged prediction.
    • Dembélé et al. (2020), WRR: calibrates on spatial patterns only, so product bias stays out of the parameters. Not gauge-free: added to 11 gauges in the Volta (415,600 km²), it cost 7% in streamflow and gained 105% for soil moisture and 26% for evaporation. Streamflow “is a necessary variable, but alone it is not sufficient”. Read in full 17 October 2026.
    • Hulsman et al. (2020), HESS: multi-mission altimetry plus GRACE storage to select parameters in a data-scarce basin.
    • Skoulikaris and Piliouras (2023) use model discharge, not a satellite signal, in place of the gauge (§06), but the move is this family’s.

    My reading, not a stated result: the two halves fail in opposite directions. River signals track shape without magnitude; ET and storage pin volume without timing. That is the case for combining them.

    What Family 5 does that the other families cannot

    Family 5 is the only family that calibrates a process model where no discharge record exists anywhere nearby, using a signal from the target river itself. That gives it four advantages, and its own set of limits.

    Comparisons with other families set results from different experiments side by side (§03). They show orders of magnitude, not a ranking.

    1. Calibration without any gauge. SRM “only uses remotely sensed data” and reached mean NSE 0.54 over 130 Murray–Darling catchments, with 70% above 0.4 (Yoon et al. 2023); the Bayesian version gave NSE 0.54–0.78 at reference stations (Yoon et al. 2022). Family 1 reaches a median of 0.54 in arid catchments only with donor gauges (Parajka et al. 2013), and Family 6 needs hundreds of gauged catchments.
    2. Extremes at the target. SRM “effectively predicts high-flow and low-flow events related to flood and drought” (Yoon et al. 2023). The signal is observed, not learned from other basins, so it does not meet the training-range ceiling of a stand-alone LSTM (Baste et al. 2025).
    3. A full model, not just a number. Because the satellite signal calibrates a conceptual model, the result is a continuous daily series with internal states, where Family 4 gives discharge only on overpass days and may miss “smaller and flashier rivers” (Durand et al. 2023).
    4. Scale without a gauge. The missing unit comes from climate through a Budyko mean flow (Yoon et al. 2024) rather than from a rating curve, and satellite gauging reaches now cover about 10,000 gauged and 370,000 ungauged reaches, with model-based ones “often similar to gauge-based” (Hou et al. 2020).

    The limits. The signal has no unit, and Budyko is compromised in arid regions (§08 above). It works only where the proxy tracks flow at the site. And the evidence is thin beside Families 1 and 6: 130 catchments in one basin system is the largest test with good skill, and when Landsat water extent was tried on 671 Brazilian catchments, only 76 had a usable signal and 30% of those beat the benchmark (Meyer Oliveira et al. 2023).

    Summary of this table
    • How the surrogate is derived. All five turn water area into a width:
      • Sun et al. 2010, 2015 and 2018 trace the water by eye or by hand on JERS-1 radar or sub-metre optical images, then divide the area by the reach length (effective width).
      • Huang et al. 2020 and 2022 map water with MNDWI or NDWI and an Otsu threshold, then measure width at a cross-section (RivWidth or hand-drawn cross-sections).
    • How it becomes discharge. No study fits width to a gauge; the formula’s parameters are calibrated together with the hydrological model:
      • Sun papers: model flow turned into width, \(W = a\,Q^{b}\).
      • Huang et al. 2022: width turned into flow, \(Q = a\,W^{b}\) (from Manning, \(b\) left free).
      • Huang et al. 2020: width combined with water level, \(Q = c\,W\,(H + z)^{5/3}\).
    • Used to calibrate a hydrological model? Yes, all five:
      • HYMOD (Sun 2010, 2015).
      • A hydrological model coupled to hydraulic geometry under GLUE (Sun 2018).
      • CREST-RS (Huang 2020, 2022).
    • Main limitations.
      • Few images (four to sixteen per site), one cross-section per basin, one to four rivers per study.
      • Width changes little with flow, so most model parameters stay loose (4 of 5 in Sun 2010) and low flow is underestimated (Sun 2015).
      • Optical images are cut by cloud, so widths come mostly from the dry season (Huang 2020, 2022).
      • Huang 2020’s SWOT-like test still uses gauged water levels.

    Summary of this table
    • How the surrogate is derived. Three routes, plus one paper that does not say:
      • Threshold map of water pixels on Sentinel-1 radar: Ahmad and Kim 2019; Han et al. 2026.
      • Water fraction in coarse cells, no threshold: GFDS passive microwave (Revilla-Romero et al. 2015, 2016) or MODIS band 7 (van Dijk et al. 2016; Hou et al. 2020).
      • Ready-made Landsat water map, Global Surface Water: Meyer Oliveira et al. 2023.
      • Not stated: Liu et al. 2015.
    • How it becomes discharge. No common method:
      • Rating fitted to a gauge: Ahmad and Kim (\(Q = a\,N^{b}\)); one variant of Revilla-Romero 2015; van Dijk’s reaches, chosen by correlation with gauged flow.
      • Cumulative distribution matching against gauged or global-model flow: Hou.
      • Scaling calibrated with the model, the scale from climate: Han.
      • Manning from model flow to water area, the other way round: Liu.
      • Rescaling into the range of simulated flow, for assimilation: Revilla-Romero 2016.
      • No conversion, only ranks or correlation: Meyer Oliveira; the raw-signal variant of Revilla-Romero 2015.
    • Used to calibrate a hydrological model? Four of eight:
      • Calibrate a model: LISFLOOD (Revilla-Romero 2015), SWAT (Liu 2015), HBV (Meyer Oliveira 2023), GR4J inside SRM (Han 2026).
      • Assimilate instead, updating LISFLOOD’s states: Revilla-Romero 2016.
      • No model, a direct extent–discharge relation: van Dijk 2016, Ahmad and Kim 2019, Hou 2020 (Hou can train it on global-model flow where there is no gauge).
    • Main limitations.
      • The signal has no unit, so the size of the flow must come from elsewhere: a gauge, a global model or climate.
      • Coarse pixels miss narrow rivers: only 76 of 671 Brazilian catchments usable; R below 0.7 for 86% of van Dijk’s rivers.
      • Weakened by forest canopy (Revilla-Romero 2016), dams and levees (Ahmad and Kim; Han), low-flow and steep reaches (Han), and cloud on optical images.
      • Still need gauged flow: Ahmad and Kim, van Dijk, and one variant of Revilla-Romero 2015.

    Beside each satellite dataset: free can be downloaded at no cost today; paid commercial images that must be bought.

    In the conversion column: no gauge needed gauge in some variants gauge needed (whether gauged discharge is still needed to get discharge).
