    Summary of this table
    • How the surrogate is derived. Three kinds of signal:
      • Ratios that compare the river with a reference: passive-microwave C/M, a dry-land pixel over a river pixel (Brakenridge et al. 2007; Yoon et al. 2022); SMOS L-band SR, each day against the record’s own extremes (Yoon et al. 2023, 2024, 2025); Landsat near-infrared multiple pixel ratio (Yu et al. 2023); multispectral CM and CMW indices (Filippucci et al. 2025).
      • Water level straight from radar altimetry: Sun et al. 2011; Hulsman et al. 2020.
      • No river signal, only evaporation and GRACE storage: Huang et al. 2020.
    • How it becomes discharge. Four routes:
      • Linear rating \(Q = a\cdot SR + b\) calibrated with the model, the scale from a Budyko mean flow (Yoon 2023, 2024, 2025) or a prior on flow magnitude (Yoon 2022).
      • Rating curve or cumulative distribution matching against gauged flow: Brakenridge; Filippucci.
      • Model flow turned into water level: \(H = c\,Q^{f} + H_{0}\) (Sun 2011), or Manning with terrain cross-sections (Hulsman).
      • No conversion: rank correlation with a water-balance filter (Yu); calibration on evaporation (Huang 2020).
    • Used to calibrate a hydrological model? Eight of ten:
      • Calibrate a model: Yoon 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025; Yu 2023; Sun 2011; Hulsman 2020; Huang 2020.
      • No model, the ratio turned into discharge directly by a gauge rating or distribution matching: Brakenridge 2007; Filippucci 2025.
    • Main limitations.
      • Ratio signals have no unit, so the size of the flow comes from Budyko, a prior or a gauge.
      • Microwave pixels are about 25 km.
      • Small or single-region tests: three catchments; Australia only; one basin.
      • Altimetry sees only large rivers, where a track crosses.
      • Optical ratios fail on frozen, cloudy and narrow rivers.
      • Still need a gauge: Brakenridge; Huang 2020; the calibrated variant of Filippucci.

    All 25 Family 5 papers, ranked for this research programme

    The order is this review’s judgement for a programme that uses Sentinel-1 water extent and takes its scale from geometry, not a ranking by the sources. Key points opens each paper’s research question, what it uses in place of measured discharge, method, advance, findings and limitations, in plain language.

    Must know: the papers this work builds on or answers to

    1. 1Han et al. 2026 IEEE JSTARSThe method this work grows from: river water seen in radar images, used in place of a flow gauge.

      Research question

      Can radar satellite images show how river flow rises and falls over time, even in small and complex rivers that older, coarser satellites could not see?

      What stands in for discharge

      The number of water pixels in a fixed stretch of river on Sentinel-1 radar images (10 m pixels), so in effect the area of water. The paper calls this series SR and stresses it has no unit and is not a discharge. Sentinel-1 gives an image only every several days, so SR exists only on image dates. It becomes flow inside a rainfall–runoff model (GR4J), whose settings and the SR scaling are tuned together; the model supplies the days between images.

      How they did it

      They pick out water in each radar image with an automatic brightness threshold, keep only pixels that are connected, river-shaped and stable over time, and count them. They then check carefully how much of the match with real flow is genuine and how much is just both series changing slowly over time.

      What it advanced

      Earlier surrogate work used microwave pixels about 25–45 km wide. Radar at 10 m brings small rivers into reach, and the paper tests ordinary rises and falls in flow, not only floods.

      Findings

      Over 19 rivers in 13 countries, the water count matched gauged flow with a typical correlation of 0.71 (1 is perfect). But for the change from one image to the next (divided by the days between them) it fell to 0.28, and the authors say the higher number overstates the link. Used to calibrate a model, it reached NSE 0.47 and 0.53 in two basins (NSE: 1 is perfect, 0 is no better than always guessing the average flow).

      Limitations

      Works worse where rivers are held in by levees, where water is stored and released, where flow stays low for long periods, and on steep rivers. There is no single flow size above which it works. In one basin the model could not be calibrated at all. Images come only every several days (using both ascending and descending passes adds more), so daily flow between images comes from the model, not the satellite.

      Why it matters here

      The method this work grows from: river water seen in radar images, used in place of a flow gauge.

    2. 2Liu et al. 2015 WRRUses water level and water area together through a Manning channel model: the closest match to a width-and-extent approach.

      Research question

      Can satellite water level and water area replace measured flow when calibrating a model, and can the same set-up also estimate water depth?

      What stands in for discharge

      Water level from the ENVISAT altimeter (114 readings) and water area from Landsat (53) at four reaches of the Red River. A channel model (XSECT, a trapezoid with Manning's equation) turns the model's flow into level and area; its shape and roughness are tuned with the hydrological model, so no rating curve is needed.

      How they did it

      SWAT and XSECT are tuned together by a genetic algorithm to match the satellite level and area, then checked against 10 USGS gauges.

      What it advanced

      Puts a physical channel between flow and the satellite signals, so the scale comes from geometry rather than from a fitted rating curve; it also estimates water depth.

      Findings

      Daily NSE 0.758 with both signals, 0.469 with water area alone, 0.717 with level alone, and 0.845 when tuned on gauged flow. Modelled water depth matched gauge readings with an average R² of 0.831.

      Limitations

      One basin with rivers about 100 m wide and good weather-station data. Results drop quickly with fewer or noisier satellite readings: with 5 m of level error, NSE fell to −0.805.

      Why it matters here

      Uses water level and water area together through a Manning channel model: the closest match to a width-and-extent approach.

    3. 3Yoon et al. 2024 Journal of HydrologyNames the core difficulty, that the satellite signal has no unit, and fixes it using climate.

      Research question

      The satellite signal rises and falls with the river but has no unit. How do we turn it into cubic metres per second, and how accurate does that conversion need to be?

      What stands in for discharge

      A reflectance ratio from SMOS L-band microwave over the river cell: how much its reflectance has risen since the driest day, compared with how far it still is below the wettest day. Called SR, with no unit. It becomes flow by matching the long-term average flow from the Budyko formula, which needs only average rainfall and evaporation demand.

      How they did it

      They test, first on made-up data and then on real Australian catchments, how much the final flow depends on getting the average flow right; the first real tests use 49 catchments where the signal tracks flow well (correlation above 0.6).

      What it advanced

      Gives the signal a scale without any gauge, which is what turns a signal that merely correlates into a discharge model.

      Findings

      The result is only as good as two things: the satellite signal and the average-flow estimate. The Budyko estimate worked well enough in these catchments.

      Limitations

      Only Australia. Depends on the Budyko formula being right for the catchment. The signal is noisiest at low flow, so that is where the conversion is least trustworthy.

      Why it matters here

      Names the core difficulty, that the satellite signal has no unit, and fixes it using climate.

    4. 4Yoon et al. 2025 EMSThe method packaged as free software (SRM): the tool you are most likely to compare against.

      Research question

      The method existed only in papers. Can it be turned into a tool anyone can download and run?

      What stands in for discharge

      The same SMOS L-band reflectance ratio (SR) as above. A straight-line rating curve (flow = a × SR + b) turns it into flow, with a and b fitted during calibration using the Budyko average flow.

      How they did it

      An R package that downloads the satellite data, builds SR, and calibrates a hydrological model, using a new way of scoring the model that needs SR and the average flow but no measured discharge.

      What it advanced

      No measured discharge is needed at any step, and it can be run anywhere SMOS data exist.

      Findings

      In three Australian catchments over 2012–2021, NSE 0.62–0.79 and KGE 0.66–0.84 (both: 1 is perfect).

      Limitations

      Only three test catchments. SMOS pixels are about 25 km across, too coarse for narrow rivers. It underestimates big floods. The Budyko average flow is unreliable in dry and semi-dry regions. The signal is also affected by land cover and wet soil.

      Why it matters here

      The method packaged as free software (SRM): the tool you are most likely to compare against.

    5. 5Yoon et al. 2023 ERLThe biggest test of the family so far, in Australia: the benchmark for an Australian study.

      Research question

      Can we model flow in a river with no gauge using only satellite data, with no measured flow at all?

      What stands in for discharge

      The SMOS L-band reflectance ratio (SR), compared with the older passive-microwave ratio from the Global Flood Detection System. Scaled to flow with the Budyko average flow. Gauges are used only to check the answer.

      How they did it

      Run this on 130 catchments of the Murray–Darling Basin and compare with the gauged flows afterwards.

      What it advanced

      The largest test with good results: 130 catchments, with no measured flow used in calibration.

      Findings

      Average NSE 0.54, with 70% of catchments above 0.4. It caught floods and droughts.

      Limitations

      All in one river system. Best in the southern, mountainous catchments. A bad signal gives a bad model, and finding out whether the signal is good needs a gauge.

      Why it matters here

      The biggest test of the family so far, in Australia: the benchmark for an Australian study.

    6. 6Meyer Oliveira et al. 2023 WRRThe largest test of Landsat water extent for calibration, and a sobering one.

      Research question

      Can Landsat water extent calibrate a simple model across many catchments, and is it held back more by infrequent images or by coarse pixels?

      What stands in for discharge

      Water extent (stream width) from Landsat. The HBV model is tuned so its flow rises and falls in the same order as the water extent (Spearman rank correlation).

      How they did it

      First a test with made-up, perfect width data at daily, monthly and dry-season-only resolution; then real Landsat data for 671 Brazilian catchments (CAMELS-BR).

      What it advanced

      Tests extent-based calibration at a scale no earlier paper here did, and separates the effect of timing from the effect of pixel size.

      Findings

      With perfect data, monthly sampling still helped (median relative performance 0.17, against 0.35 for daily; above 0 means better than the benchmark). With real data, only 76 of 671 catchments had water extent large and variable enough; 30% of those beat the benchmark, and results improved with river width.

      Limitations

      Coarse Landsat pixels: the median correlation between water extent and flow was only 0.52. One country.

      Why it matters here

      The largest test of Landsat water extent for calibration, and a sobering one.

    7. 7Hulsman et al. 2020 HESSShows that adding river shape from terrain data is what makes a satellite water-level signal work: the closest support for using geometry for scale.

      Research question

      Can satellite measurements of river water level, together with satellite measurements of total water storage, replace a flow gauge for tuning a model?

      What stands in for discharge

      River water level from several radar altimetry satellites at 18 points along the river. It is compared with the model by turning modelled flow into water level, either through a simple power-law rating curve or through Manning's equation with the river's cross-section and slope taken from global terrain data. GRACE water storage is used first, but as a check on storage, not as a stand-in for flow.

      How they did it

      A distributed model of the semi-dry Luangwa basin in Zambia, 2002–2016. GRACE first removes model settings that get seasonal storage wrong; the water levels then remove more, in three different ways.

      What it advanced

      The only study here that uses both a river signal and a storage signal, and it shows that knowing the river's shape is the key step.

      Findings

      Tuned on a real gauge, NSE 0.78. GRACE alone: −1.4. Water levels used directly, or through power-law curves: flows too high. With cross-section, slope and Manning: NSE 0.60. Better cross-sections and more water-level points helped further.

      Limitations

      One basin, and rivers large enough for altimetry. Detailed cross-sections existed only at the outlet.

      Why it matters here

      Shows that adding river shape from terrain data is what makes a satellite water-level signal work: the closest support for using geometry for scale.

    8. 8Revilla-Romero et al. 2015 RSEUses the area of water seen from space to tune a model, and admits the missing-unit problem.

      Research question

      Many rivers have no gauge, or the data are not shared. Can the area of water seen by satellite take the place of flow when tuning a model?

      What stands in for discharge

      The Global Flood Detection System signal: a passive-microwave ratio between a pixel over the river and a dry reference pixel, which rises as the water area grows. It has no unit. Used raw, or turned into flow with gauge data to compare.

      How they did it

      Tune part of the LISFLOOD model at 30 sites three ways (with real flow, with satellite-based flow, and with the raw satellite signal) and compare.

      What it advanced

      Makes the area of water itself the thing the model is tuned to.

      Findings

      The model improved (higher correlation with real flow) at 21 of 30 stations, and the authors see promise for places with no gauge, or where a gauge has closed.

      Limitations

      Only 30 sites, picked because their signal looked good. The authors themselves note that the signal having no unit is a limitation.

      Why it matters here

      Uses the area of water seen from space to tune a model, and admits the missing-unit problem.

    Important context

    1. 9Ahmad and Kim 2019 International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and GeoinformationSentinel-1 water area against flow at many stations: the closest radar precedent, and evidence that channel shape matters.

      Research question

      Can water area measured by Sentinel-1 radar estimate flow in streams of many sizes?

      What stands in for discharge

      The water area inside a hand-drawn polygon along each reach on Sentinel-1 images, found with one backscatter threshold after matching the images' histograms. A power law fitted to gauged flow turns area into discharge, so a gauge is still needed.

      How they did it

      15 stations in the Han River basin, Korea (mean flow 2–305 m³/s); the threshold is chosen to give the strongest area–flow correlation.

      What it advanced

      Shows radar water area tracks flow in small and medium streams, not only big rivers.

      Findings

      A clear relation at 13 of 15 stations, with correlation R 0.68–0.98 (mean 0.89): above 0.90 for medium and large streams, about 0.80 for small ones. It worked best where the channel has gentle side slopes.

      Limitations

      Needs a gauge for the rating; failed at two stations controlled by dams; pixels of about 20 m limit small streams.

      Why it matters here

      Sentinel-1 water area against flow at many stations: the closest radar precedent, and evidence that channel shape matters.

    2. 10Huang et al. 2022 RSEWidth-only calibration in narrow mountain rivers, with good results.

      Research question

      Can daily flow be estimated in ungauged mountain headwaters using only satellite data, including river width from high-resolution images?

      What stands in for discharge

      River width at a cross-section from high-resolution images (IKONOS, QuickBird, RapidEye, GeoEye-1, WorldView-2) and Landsat. The CREST-RS model is tuned to match these widths; no measured flow is used.

      How they did it

      Run on four Tibetan Plateau headwaters (Lhasa, Salween, Mekong, Yangtze) with rivers about 100 m wide; the model includes snow and glacier melt.

      What it advanced

      Shows width calibration works in narrow rivers, down to about 50 m, where altimetry cannot reach.

      Findings

      NSE up to 0.8, and above 0.5 overall.

      Limitations

      Optical images are blocked by cloud; results depend on the accuracy, number and spread of the width observations.

      Why it matters here

      Width-only calibration in narrow mountain rivers, with good results.

    3. 11van Dijk et al. 2016 WRRTests water-area gauging worldwide, and shows which rivers it works on.

      Research question

      Can we turn satellite pictures of flooded area into river flow automatically, for thousands of rivers at once?

      What stands in for discharge

      The flooded area seen in MODIS optical images and in passive microwave, in grid cells chosen automatically along each river. It is related to flow by a statistical fit against monthly gauge records.

      How they did it

      Compare the satellite water area with monthly flow at more than 8,000 gauges, and let a computer choose which cells make good “satellite gauging reaches”.

      What it advanced

      Satellite gauging that builds itself, at global scale.

      Findings

      MODIS usually beat microwave. It works best on big, natural lowland rivers (correlation above 0.9), and better the more the monthly flow varies.

      Limitations

      86% of rivers gave a weak match (correlation below 0.7), often small or dammed rivers, leaving 1,263 usable reaches. Poor in dry regions, where floods are rare and short. Monthly values only, and coarse pixels.

      Why it matters here

      Tests water-area gauging worldwide, and shows which rivers it works on.

    4. 12Hou et al. 2020 RSEShows that a computer model can replace the gauge when building a satellite gauging point, and which river shapes suit water-area methods.

      Research question

      Where there is no gauge, can modelled flow be used instead, so satellite gauging points can be set up anywhere?

      What stands in for discharge

      The fraction of each 0.05° grid cell covered by water, from MODIS short-wave infrared, a band where water and dry land contrast strongly. It is matched to flow from a gauge or, where there is none, from a global hydrological model.

      How they did it

      Build both kinds of satellite gauging point at about 10,000 gauged and 370,000 ungauged river reaches, and study which ones succeed.

      What it advanced

      Takes the gauge out of the process of linking water area to flow.

      Findings

      Model-based points were often as good as gauge-based ones, and sometimes better than the model itself. They work best on wide rivers whose flooded area changes a lot, with broad floodplains or many channels.

      Limitations

      Gets the timing of high and low flows right, but not necessarily the amount of water. Coarse pixels favour wide rivers. Only as good as the model's flow.

      Why it matters here

      Shows that a computer model can replace the gauge when building a satellite gauging point, and which river shapes suit water-area methods.

    5. 13Yoon et al. 2022 WRRA careful statistical way to tune a model to a satellite signal, with error bars.

      Research question

      The microwave C/M ratio follows river flow, but imperfectly. How should a model be tuned to such a signal?

      What stands in for discharge

      The C/M ratio from the Global Flood Detection System: brightness of a dry land pixel divided by brightness of a pixel over the river. Turned into a surrogate flow series, using some prior knowledge of how big the flows are.

      How they did it

      A Bayesian method (it gives a range of likely answers, not a single one) that tunes the model to the surrogate flow instead of measured flow.

      What it advanced

      Puts the idea on a proper statistical footing, with uncertainty.

      Findings

      NSE 0.54–0.78 at three Australian reference catchments with little human influence.

      Limitations

      Only three, untouched catchments. It still needs rough prior knowledge of how big the flows are: the missing-unit problem again.

      Why it matters here

      A careful statistical way to tune a model to a satellite signal, with error bars.

    6. 14Sun et al. 2010 HESSThe paper that started the family, and a warning about what a width signal can tell you.

      Research question

      Tuning a model normally needs measured flow, which ungauged rivers lack. Can river width measured from space be used instead?

      What stands in for discharge

      River width at the basin outlet, measured on 16 JERS-1 radar images of the Mekong at Pakse. Width and flow are linked by a power law, width = a × flow^b, and a and b are tuned together with the model.

      How they did it

      Tune the five-setting HYMOD model so that the width it implies matches the satellite width.

      What it advanced

      The founding example of tuning a model with no flow data at all.

      Findings

      The two width–flow settings were pinned down well, but four of the model's five settings were hardly constrained at all.

      Limitations

      One cross-section, one basin. Assumes settings that get width right also get flow right, which the authors themselves doubt. Nothing constrains the model between satellite passes.

      Why it matters here

      The paper that started the family, and a warning about what a width signal can tell you.

    7. 15Brakenridge et al. 2007 WRRWhere the C/M microwave signal comes from, with the missing-unit problem present from day one.

      Research question

      Can a satellite measure river flow, and whether the river is frozen, from orbit?

      What stands in for discharge

      The C/M ratio of passive-microwave brightness (AMSR-E, pixels about 25 km wide): a dry land pixel divided by a pixel over the river. Water gives off less microwave radiation than land, so the ratio rises as the water area in the river pixel grows.

      How they did it

      Compare the ratio with gauged flow on several rivers.

      What it advanced

      A daily signal that sees through cloud and follows the river's state.

      Findings

      Careful calibration between images, and good contrast between water and land, matter more than small pixels.

      Limitations

      Not gauge-free: it needs at least some measured flow to turn the ratio into a discharge.

      Why it matters here

      Where the C/M microwave signal comes from, with the missing-unit problem present from day one.

    Useful background

    1. 16Sun et al. 2015 Environmental ResearchThe width method applied to a basin that is truly ungauged.

      Research question

      Does width-based calibration work in a real ungauged basin, where the only data are public weather data and satellite images?

      What stands in for discharge

      River width at Pyay on the Irrawaddy from six JERS-1 radar images, as effective width (water area divided by reach length). A power law, width = a × flow^b, links it to the model's flow; a and b are tuned with the model.

      How they did it

      Tune HYMOD with GLUE, keeping 997 of 50,000 random parameter sets, and check against the only public flow data: the 10-year average monthly flow.

      What it advanced

      The authors' first application of the method to an ungauged basin, with practical rules for real use.

      Findings

      Simulated monthly flow matched the 10-year average with NSE 0.957 (given as 95.7%), and the width–flow parameters were well constrained.

      Limitations

      Low flow underestimated; only six images; needs at least one image in every wet and dry season; not for rectangular channels, where width barely changes with flow.

      Why it matters here

      The width method applied to a basin that is truly ungauged.

    2. 17Sun et al. 2018 RSEWidth calibration on a smaller regional river, with satellite weather data too.

      Research question

      Can a model of a regional river be calibrated on river width from a few high-resolution images, with no ground data at all?

      What stands in for discharge

      River width from four commercial high-resolution images (two QuickBird, one IKONOS, one WorldView-1), linked to flow by at-a-station hydraulic geometry (a power law).

      How they did it

      Force the model with satellite weather data, tune it with GLUE to match the widths, and test how errors from riverside trees affect the result.

      What it advanced

      Takes width calibration from very large rivers to a regional one, with no in-situ data used for modelling.

      Findings

      NSE 0.643 in calibration and 0.558 in validation (given as 64.3% and 55.8%). Width errors from trees mattered less than expected, because the width–flow parameters adjusted to absorb them.

      Limitations

      Only four images and one basin; extra hydrological-signature information was needed to narrow the uncertainty.

      Why it matters here

      Width calibration on a smaller regional river, with satellite weather data too.

    3. 18Yu et al. 2023 Journal of HydrologyBrings the method to small mountain rivers.

      Research question

      The ratio method worked on rivers 200–300 m wide. Can it work on small mountain rivers?

      What stands in for discharge

      A multiple pixel ratio from Landsat near-infrared: reflectance of a reference area compared with the flooded river channel. Because it is matched by rank (does it go up when flow goes up?), a water-balance check is added to get the amount right.

      How they did it

      Six ways of tuning a model, tested on two Tibetan Plateau basins with channels 91 and 132 m wide.

      What it advanced

      Extends the method to much smaller rivers.

      Findings

      NSE 0.63 and 0.62 when tested on years not used for tuning.

      Limitations

      Two basins only; braided channels. Ranking ignores the amount of water, which the water-balance check must put back.

      Why it matters here

      Brings the method to small mountain rivers.

    4. 19Filippucci et al. 2025 RSEJoins many satellites into one long record, and shows how far it gets without any gauge.

      Research question

      Satellites stop working and are replaced, so records are short. Can several be joined into one long record?

      What stands in for discharge

      A CM ratio of reflectance indices (a land calibration pixel against a river measurement pixel) from 10 multispectral products on 8 satellites, merged into one series. Turned into flow with a gauge, or by an uncalibrated version for ungauged sites.

      How they did it

      Choose the best index at each of 54 sites worldwide and line the satellites up statistically so their records join smoothly over two decades.

      What it advanced

      Twenty-year records, and a version that needs no gauge.

      Findings

      With a gauge: average rank correlation 0.78, KGE 0.41. Without: 0.55 and 0.29.

      Limitations

      Struggles on frozen rivers, in cloudy places, and where the river is narrow compared with the pixel.

      Why it matters here

      Joins many satellites into one long record, and shows how far it gets without any gauge.

    5. 20Sun et al. 2011 Hydrological ProcessesThe general recipe the family follows, tested with gauge data made to look like satellite data.

      Research question

      Can any river feature seen from space, its width or its water level, be used to tune a model?

      What stands in for discharge

      River width or water-surface level, linked to flow by power laws (hydraulic geometry), so the model's output is width or level instead of flow.

      How they did it

      Use measured width and level at Pakse on the Mekong, thinned out to one reading a month or one every six months, as a satellite would give.

      What it advanced

      The general framework that later papers use.

      Findings

      NSE 0.84–0.95 on test years. Adding satellite-like errors kept the error below 20% of average daily flow, and how often the satellite passes mattered more than errors in the width–flow law.

      Limitations

      No real satellite data: these are gauge records thinned out. One very large river. Least certain at low flow.

      Why it matters here

      The general recipe the family follows, tested with gauge data made to look like satellite data.

    6. 21Sun et al. 2011 Hydrological ProcessesThe same idea using water level measured by satellite.

      Research question

      Can satellite measurements of river water level replace flow records for tuning a model?

      What stands in for discharge

      River water level from the TOPEX/Poseidon radar altimeter at the outlet (117 readings, Upper Mississippi at Clinton). A hydraulic model turns the model's flow into water level for comparison.

      How they did it

      Tune the model to match the satellite water levels, and compare with tuning on real flow.

      What it advanced

      Shows the idea works with water level, not only width.

      Findings

      NSE 0.65 with no flow data, against 0.79 when tuned on real flow. Throwing out noisy readings left only 10, and NSE fell to 0.24.

      Limitations

      Altimeters then saw only big rivers. Rainfall still came from gauges. The 1999–2000 dry season was underestimated either way.

      Why it matters here

      The same idea using water level measured by satellite.

    7. 22Huang et al. 2020 WRRWater level plus width in narrow rivers: a trial run for SWOT data.

      Research question

      Can satellite water level, or water level plus width as SWOT will provide, tune a model in a narrow river with no flow data?

      What stands in for discharge

      Water level from the Jason-2 altimeter, alone or with river width from Landsat, turned into flow by two empirical formulas.

      How they did it

      Tune the CREST-RS model on two Tibetan rivers, the Upper Brahmaputra and the Lhasa, in five scenarios.

      What it advanced

      Moves from unitless ratios to water level, and tries the SWOT combination before SWOT launched.

      Findings

      Daily flow estimated in narrow rivers without any measured flow.

      Limitations

      Two rivers only. The “SWOT-like” test used gauged water levels as a stand-in, so it is partly simulated.

      Why it matters here

      Water level plus width in narrow rivers: a trial run for SWOT data.

    8. 23Revilla-Romero et al. 2016 Journal of HydrologyUses water extent to update a model day by day, not to calibrate it.

      Research question

      Does feeding daily satellite water extent into a large-scale model improve its flows across whole continents?

      What stands in for discharge

      The GFDS passive-microwave signal of surface-water extent, daily at 0.1°. It is not turned into flow directly: it updates the model's state through data assimilation.

      How they did it

      An ensemble Kalman filter updates LISFLOOD across Africa and South America for one year; results are checked at 101 gauges.

      What it advanced

      By the authors' account, the first continent-scale assimilation of surface-water extent into a hydrological model.

      Findings

      NSE improved at 61 of 101 stations, in both the timing and the volume of flood peaks.

      Limitations

      Worst in lowland jungle, where closed forest interferes with the signal; flow got worse at some stations.

      Why it matters here

      Uses water extent to update a model day by day, not to calibrate it.

    The other half of the family: evaporation, storage and patterns

    1. 24Dembélé et al. 2020 WRRSatellite maps help a model, but alongside gauges, not instead of them.

      Research question

      Satellite products have errors in their values. Can their spatial patterns alone, which are more reliable, make a model better?

      What stands in for discharge

      Nothing stands in for discharge here: measured flow at 11 gauges is still used. Satellite maps of evaporation, soil moisture and water storage are added, comparing only their patterns, not their values.

      How they did it

      Tune the mHM model for the Volta basin in West Africa using the gauges plus a score for how well the model reproduces the satellite patterns.

      What it advanced

      Uses what satellite maps do best, the pattern, so their errors do not leak into the model.

      Findings

      River flow got 7% worse, but soil moisture got 105% better and evaporation 26% better. The authors: flow “is a necessary variable, but alone it is not sufficient”.

      Limitations

      Not a no-gauge method: the satellite data are added to gauges, not used instead of them.

      Why it matters here

      Satellite maps help a model, but alongside gauges, not instead of them.

    2. 25Huang et al. 2020 WRRTunes a model to satellite evaporation, needing only one gauge.

      Research question

      Can satellite maps of evaporation and water storage replace flow data when tuning a model for ungauged catchments?

      What stands in for discharge

      Nothing measures the river itself: the model is tuned to satellite evaporation (PML), with GRACE storage in some versions. The evaporation data are first bias-corrected using a water balance fitted at a single gauge.

      How they did it

      Seven satellite-based tuning schemes on 30 catchments of the Yalong River, China, compared with tuning on real flow and with borrowing settings from the nearest gauged catchment.

      What it advanced

      Tuning that is almost flow-free: one gauge for the whole region.

      Findings

      Corrected evaporation worked much better than raw. Running the model on a grid beat treating each catchment as one unit, and beat borrowing from neighbours, especially in headwater and large catchments. Adding GRACE helped very little.

      Limitations

      One basin. Still needs one gauge to correct the evaporation data.

      Why it matters here

      Tunes a model to satellite evaporation, needing only one gauge.

    Where this family stands

    ADVANCES SO FAR

    • Changed the calibration objective from discharge to an observable hydraulic variable, so a model needs no discharge record.
    • Settled on a unitless, daily, all-weather signal, the C/M ratio.
    • Bayesian calibration with quantified uncertainty: NSE 0.54–0.78 at Australian reference stations.
    • Tested at scale from remote sensing alone: mean NSE 0.54 over 130 Murray–Darling catchments, 70% above 0.4, including flood and drought events (Yoon et al. 2023).
    • Reached small mountain rivers (NSE 0.63 and 0.62) with rank correlation and a water-balance filter.
    • Width alone, with no gauge data at all: NSE 0.643 and 0.558 on a Tibetan regional river (Sun et al. 2018), up to 0.8 in headwaters about 100 m wide (Huang et al. 2022).
    • Water level and water area together, through a Manning channel model: daily NSE 0.758, against 0.469 with area alone and 0.845 with gauged flow (Liu et al. 2015).
    • Took the unit from climate, not a gauge: a Budyko mean flow from long-term precipitation and PET.
    • Became software (NSE and KGE above 0.6) and spread to ten multispectral products, SAR in 19 rivers in 13 countries, and altimetry on narrow rivers.
    • Opened a parallel route via ET, storage and spatial patterns.

    LIMITATIONS SO FAR

    • The signal has no unit; the Budyko fix inherits Budyko’s error at the site.
    • Coarse pixels: the L-band product behind the packaged model is about 25 km.
    • Fails on frozen rivers, cloudy regions and rivers narrow relative to the pixel.
    • Depends on the proxy–discharge correlation holding at the site; the most careful study screens for it first.
    • Few large tests beside Families 1 and 6: 130 catchments in one basin system (Yoon et al. 2023); of 671 Brazilian catchments only 76 had Landsat water extent large and variable enough, and 30% of those beat the benchmark (Meyer Oliveira et al. 2023); several key papers use three catchments.
    • The two halves are barely combined: only Hulsman et al. (2020) uses both, in one basin.

    Read these first

    Start with these. Between them they cover most of what this section concludes. Key points opens a short summary of each paper and why it comes first.

    1. R48Brakenridge et al. 2007 WRRthe C/M-ratio signal

      Main points

      • Uses passive microwave to measure river state: the C/M ratio of a dry-land calibration pixel to a river measurement pixel.
      • Water surface area grows as flow widens, so any temporally calibrated observation sensitive to water area tracks discharge, daily and in all weather.
      • Works “in conjunction with even limited ground-based discharge information”, so the unit problem is present from the start.

      Why read it first

      It is where the C/M-ratio signal, the most used Family 5 proxy, comes from, together with its main limitation.

    2. R49Sun et al. 2010 HESSthe founding move: calibrate on width

      Main points

      • Calibrates a rainfall–runoff model on satellite river width at the basin outlet instead of discharge, linked through at-a-station hydraulic geometry (Mekong at Pakse).
      • The two geometry parameters come back strongly constrained, while four of HYMOD’s five parameters stay spread across their priors.
      • Names four conditions for using it in an ungauged basin, including an alluvial, self-formed outlet reach.

      Why read it first

      It is the founding move of surrogate calibration, and it shows what a width signal identifies and what it does not.

    3. R52Revilla-Romero et al. 2015 Remote Sensing of Environmentwater extent as the calibration target

      Main points

      • Calibrates LISFLOOD on surface water extent from the Global Flood Detection System (passive microwave) at 30 pre-screened gauging sites.
      • Raw extent improves skill (correlation) at 21 of the 30 stations, mainly for high flows.
      • Its own highlights: the data “provide promising opportunities for calibration in fully ungauged regions”, but “the dimensionless character of the GFDS data poses some limitations”.

      Why read it first

      It is the main test of water extent as a calibration target, the signal an inundation model also predicts.

    4. R60Yoon et al. 2024 Journal of Hydrologythe unit problem and the Budyko fix

      Main points

      • Asks which hydrological signature can convert a unitless surrogate (SR) into discharge, and how accurate it must be.
      • Uses the Budyko mean catchment discharge, which needs only mean precipitation and PET, and tests the model’s sensitivity to it on synthetic and real data.
      • Over 384 Australian stations, analyses the 49 with SR–discharge correlation above 0.6 first; SR is noisiest at low flow.

      Why read it first

      It is the clearest statement of the unit problem in surrogate calibration and of the Budyko fix that the C/M-ratio line now relies on.

    5. R63Han et al. 2026 IEEE JSTARSSAR extent for small rivers, and its honest diagnostics

      Main points

      • Turns Sentinel-1 SAR water extent into a surrogate discharge with adaptive thresholding and connectivity and geometry filters, for 19 rivers in 13 countries.
      • Median level correlation is about 0.7, but only 0.28–0.36 for elapsed-time-normalised changes: “level correlation alone overstates the strength of short-term co-variation”.
      • Drives an SRM to median NSE 0.47 and 0.53 in two basins; weaker in levee-confined, storage-influenced, low-flow and steep reaches.

      Why read it first

      It is the parent method of the §14 programme, and it already reports NSE and runs the persistence diagnostic, so it sets the bar.

    Section 09 · Family 6

    The deep learning turn

    This is where the field changed.

    The mechanism is simple to state: train one model across hundreds of catchments at once, feeding it both meteorological time series and static catchment attributes. The network learns the attribute-to-behaviour mapping internally, so regionalisation stops being a separate post-processing step and becomes part of the model.

    Family 6 at a glance

    One dominant lineage on the left, the people testing and contesting it in the second column, and on the right the responses to its central weakness: it needs more data than the places that need it have.

    Solid arrows mark a documented build-on or extension; dashed arrows mark a study that tests, benchmarks or limits another. Where an arrow reflects this review’s reading rather than an explicit statement in the papers, the text below says so.

    Where this began

    The strand starts with Kratzert, Klotz, Brenner, Schulz and Herrnegger (2018), HESS 22, 6005 — now past 2,000 citations. They proposed the LSTM for rainfall–runoff modelling on the argument that its ability to learn long-term dependencies suits catchment storage effects, snow in particular, and tested it on 241 CAMELS catchments against SAC-SMA coupled with Snow-17.

    That paper is about gauged modelling. The ungauged claim arrives the following year, in the two companion papers below.

    The two 2019 papers, and why they are often confused

    Two companion papers appeared in 2019 and are routinely cited interchangeably. They test different things.

    • Kratzert et al. (2019, HESS) is the gauged regional study. It introduces the Entity-Aware LSTM, which uses static attributes to learn catchment similarity. Across 531 CAMELS basins, mean NSE was 0.63 with MSE loss and 0.67 with a basin-averaged NSE loss; an LSTM without static attributes reached only 0.23 and 0.39. Attributes were worth roughly 0.30–0.44 mean NSE.
    • Kratzert et al. (2019, WRR) is the ungauged study, and the one to cite for PUB.

    The result that reframed the problem

    Table scrolls sideways →

    Study and yearJournalResearch question / gap addressedMethodData requiredFindingLimitation
    Kratzert et al. 2019WRR 55(12), 11344–11354 Can a network trained across many basins predict in a basin it has never seen — and beat a model calibrated at that basin? Classical regionalisation had never been benchmarked against a single regional ML model
    • LSTMs trained on 531 CAMELS basins
    • k-fold validation, so every prediction is in a basin that contributed no training data

    Why it works. Kratzert et al. put the interpretation precisely: the result shows there is typically enough information in available catchment attributes about similarities and differences in rainfall–runoff behaviour to produce out-of-sample simulations more accurate than calibrated conventional models. The information PUB was looking for was there all along; the conventional transfer methods were not extracting it.

    Another architecture: the catchment network as a graph

    An LSTM treats each catchment as an independent sequence and learns similarity only through static attributes. A graph neural network instead represents the basins themselves as nodes in a graph, learns the spatiotemporal dependencies between them, and predicts across all nodes at once.

    Sun, Jiang, Mudunuru and Chen (2021), WRR 57(12), adapt and benchmark several GNN architectures — ChebNet, Graph Convolutional Network and GraphWaveNet — for end-to-end graph learning on CAMELS. The design detail that matters for this review is their two settings:

    • Fixed graph topology (transductive learning) — the gauged case.
    • Variable graph topology (inductive learning) — which, in their words, is the setting applicable to prediction in ungauged basins.

    They report GNNs to be generally robust and computationally efficient. The reason to know about this strand is not that it has displaced the LSTM — it has not — but that it encodes a different assumption: that the relevant similarity between catchments is relational and spatial, rather than a vector of attributes. For a river network, that is a natural assumption, and it is closer to how Family 2 thinks.

    Deep learning on Family 4’s signal. Hao et al. (2024), WRR, trained a Transformer on time-series Landsat reflectance at 2,036 gauges. In rivers held out as ungauged it gave positive KGE in 68.6%, against 28.4% for BAM and 33.1% for geoBAM, although two-thirds were under 100 m wide. The price is this family’s usual one, a large gauged training sample (§07).

    Transfer learning: borrowing a trained network instead of a donor catchment

    The answer to the data paradox: instead of a donor catchment, transfer a network pre-trained on a data-rich region and fine-tune it on whatever the target has.

    • Ougahi and Rowan (2026): LSTMs pre-trained on 441 basins (Scotland, Switzerland, British Columbia), fine-tuned on 36 data-poor basins paired by K-means. Lagged streamflow plus ERA-5 helped most in snow- and glacier-fed basins.
    • Willard et al. (2025) survey predictions in unmonitored sites. Most transfer learning is few-shot (some target data, as above). The truly ungauged case is zero-shot, where model choice still rests on expert judgement, and in one cited test (Le et al. 2022) models moved as-is lost to local models trained on minimal data. Comparisons between method classes are “few and inadequate”. Read in full 17 October 2026.

    A coupling that is not differentiable: the LSTM as post-processor

    The physical model runs, then an LSTM corrects its output. For the US National Water Model, post-processing helped a lot, but an LSTM on forcing alone matched it and beat it in ungauged basins (Frame et al. 2021). Shokri et al. (2026) tested the same question on 218 CAMELS-AUS catchments (LSTM post-processing AWRA-L against a precipitation-and-PET LSTM), including a spatially out-of-sample test, the most relevant Australian benchmark here.

    Where this family stands

    ADVANCES SO FAR

    • Demonstrated that catchment attributes carry enough information for out-of-sample transfer: median NSE 0.69 in basins the model never saw, against 0.64 for models calibrated at those very basins.
    • Survived the obvious objection. Given exactly the same regional data as the process models, the LSTM still beat them in 93–97% of catchments, at median NSE 0.78.
    • Scaled to global extreme floods: reliability at five-day lead time matching or beating a leading system's nowcasts, now running operationally in more than 80 countries.
    • Made regionalisation part of the model rather than a post-processing step — the structural change this family represents.
    • Produced routes around its own data requirement: transfer learning from data-rich regions, and architectures such as graph neural networks whose inductive setting is explicitly the ungauged case.

    LIMITATIONS SO FAR

    • It needs a large regional training sample. The results come from CAMELS-scale datasets; in a region with twenty gauges the advantage is simply not established.
    • No mechanism and no internal states. It returns discharge, not an explanation, and cannot produce a variable it was never shown — inundation extent, depth and velocity are not in its output.
    • Extrapolation is now a measured failure, not a suspicion. A stand-alone LSTM could not predict above a hard ceiling that sat below the maximum present in its own training data.
    • Post-processing an operational physical model with an LSTM gives no benefit in ungauged basins over training on forcing alone — the physical model's output carried nothing the network could not get from the weather.
    • The evidence base is concentrated on North America and Europe, and on minimally impacted catchments by design.

    Read these first

    Start with these. Between them they cover most of what this section concludes. Key points opens a short summary of each paper and why it comes first.

    1. R76Kratzert et al. 2019 WRRthe result that reframed the problem

      Main points

      • Trains LSTMs on 531 CAMELS basins with k-fold validation, so every prediction is in a basin that contributed no training data.
      • Out-of-sample median NSE 0.69, against 0.64 for SAC-SMA calibrated in each basin and 0.58 for the National Water Model.
      • Implies catchment attributes carry enough information for out-of-sample transfer, given a large regional sample.

      Why read it first

      It is the result that reframed prediction in ungauged basins. Cite this paper, not the HESS companion, for the ungauged case.

    2. R84Arsenault et al. 2023 HESSthe fair comparison, and its caveat

      Main points

      • Gives an LSTM exactly the same regional data as 18 hydrological-model and regionalisation configurations, on 148 north-east North American catchments.
      • The LSTM wins in 93–97% of catchments: median NSE 0.78 against 0.58–0.63, and it beats models calibrated on the target itself in up to 78% of cases.
      • The authors note their catchment filter (over 500 km², at least 30 years) “probably favours the LSTM models in all cases”.

      Why read it first

      It closes the unequal-information loophole and sets the current benchmarking standard, with a caveat its abstract leaves out.

    3. R78Nearing et al. 2020 WRRthe case for learning from data

      Main points

      • Argues that deep learning reveals far more information in large hydrological datasets than hydrologists have turned into theory or models.
      • Says the community holds “deeply subjective and non-evidence-based preferences” for models built on a particular notion of process understanding.
      • Calls for a quantitative understanding of where and why process knowledge adds value.

      Why read it first

      It is the strongest form of the case against process models, and anyone defending one should answer it.

    4. R91Baste et al. 2025 HESSthe measured extrapolation ceiling

      Main points

      • Drives a stand-alone LSTM trained on 196 Swiss catchments with synthetic design storms of increasing intensity, against a hybrid conceptual–LSTM model.
      • The LSTM cannot exceed a theoretical limit of 73 mm d⁻¹, below the 183 mm d⁻¹ maximum in its own training data, and shows a concave response.
      • The mass-conserving hybrid has no such theoretical limit.

      Why read it first

      It turns the extrapolation worry about deep learning into a measured ceiling, which matters for floods beyond the record.

    Section 10 · Family 7

    Hybrid and differentiable models

    The most active frontier, and the one most relevant to anyone who has built a conceptual model and does not want to abandon it.

    The idea: keep the process equations, but make the whole model differentiable so a neural network can learn its parameters — or parts of its internal structure — by gradient descent on regional data. The payoff is that you get the LSTM’s regionalisation ability and the process model’s internal states, mass balance, and extrapolation behaviour.

    The proof that this is not a consolation prize came in Feng, Liu, Lawson and Shen (2022), WRR 58(10), which built δ models on an HBV backbone with embedded neural networks and reached median NSE 0.732 across 671 US basins on Daymet forcing against 0.748 for a state-of-the-art LSTM with the same setup — and 0.715 against 0.722 on a second forcing set. Essentially the LSTM’s accuracy, while also outputting soil and groundwater storage, snowpack, evapotranspiration and baseflow, none of which the network was trained on. Simulated ET and baseflow fraction agreed decently with independent estimates.

    Read this one first

    The orienting reference for this family sits in the strongest venue of anything cited here: Shen, Appling, Gentine, Bandai, Gupta, Tartakovsky, Baity-Jesi, Fenicia and co-authors (2023), Nature Reviews Earth & Environment — Differentiable modelling to unify machine learning and physical models for geosciences. It is the field’s own statement of what differentiable modelling is for. Its abstract states the case plainly: process-based modelling offers interpretability and physical consistency but struggles to use large datasets efficiently, while deep networks predict well yet cannot answer specific scientific questions — and differentiable modelling is offered as the path that dissolves that barrier.

    Family 7 at a glance

    The newest family, and the only one assembled almost entirely since 2022. Read it left to right as scope widening: from one basin, to regions, to the channel network, to events no model has seen.

    Solid arrows mark a documented build-on or extension; dashed arrows mark a study that tests, benchmarks or limits another. Where an arrow reflects this review’s reading rather than an explicit statement in the papers, the text below says so.

    The argument that matters most for a process modeller

    Feng et al. (2023) tested something the pure-ML literature mostly does not: whether the model still works when the physics has to do the extrapolating. Their trend results are the striking part. For high-flow (Q98) trends, the LSTM’s R2 fell from 0.76 in the gauged setting to 0.27 in the ungauged regional holdout, while the differentiable models stayed near 0.77. For annual mean flow trends, R2 was 0.64 (LSTM) against 0.88 (differentiable with dynamic parameters).

    The δ models also reproduced evapotranspiration seasonality against MODIS with median correlation around 0.84, despite never being trained on ET. A pure LSTM trained on discharge cannot do this at all.

    That is the structural argument for hybrid models in ungauged basins: the process structure constrains behaviour where data do not, and it produces internal variables — storage, ET, flow depth — that a discharge-trained network never learns.

    Where this is heading

    The 2024–2026 literature has moved from proof-of-concept to operational scale, and two papers mark the shift.

    Song, Bindas, Shen, Ji, Knoben, Lonzarich, Clark and co-authors (2025), WRR, built high-resolution (~37 km²) differentiable versions of the US National Water Model — naming calibration and parameter regionalisation under big data as the NWM’s key challenges. One version routes implicitly, unit-hydrograph style, and predicts at basin outlets; the other uses explicit Muskingum–Cunge routing to produce a discretised product covering rivers across the conterminous United States.

    Huynh, Garambois, Renard, Colléoni, Monnier and Roux (2025), HESS 29, 3589, extend their own 2024 work into a spatially distributed hybrid framework, hybridising a differentiable hydrological model with neural networks on top of differentiable kinematic-wave routing, aimed explicitly at high-resolution regionalised flood modelling.

    The direction of travel is consistent across both: regionalisation is being absorbed into the model as a differentiable mapping, and the models are becoming continental. This is also where Family 1’s transfer-function line ends up: MPR (§04, §06) fits attribute-to-parameter functions by calibration, and these models learn them end to end. For an inundation modeller the second paper is the more interesting of the two, because its target is distributed flood behaviour rather than outlet discharge.

    The satellite side is arriving at the same machinery. Larnier et al. (2025), WRR, assimilate SWOT water levels into a 1D Saint-Venant network model fed by a hydrological model, in the poorly gauged Maroni basin, and reach discharge NRMSE of 0.05–0.18 at five gauges, starting from inflows of a hydrological model calibrated on those gauges. They close by calling for “fully differentiable hydrological-hydraulic models” with learnable parts, which is this family’s approach applied to Family 4’s observations (§07).

    Where this family stands

    ADVANCES SO FAR

    • Showed a differentiable process model can approach LSTM accuracy — median NSE 0.732 against 0.748 on 671 basins — while also returning soil and groundwater storage, snowpack, evapotranspiration and baseflow, none of which it was trained on.
    • Beat the LSTM where it matters for this review: under regional holdout, the genuinely ungauged case.
    • Held high-flow trend R2 near 0.77 under that holdout while the LSTM collapsed from 0.76 to 0.27, and reproduced MODIS evapotranspiration seasonality at correlation ~0.84 without ever being trained on ET.
    • Kept the model inspectable: states and fluxes stay explicit, and learned state dynamics can be read as processes.
    • Extended gradients to places they could not previously reach — through implicit numerical schemes, and through channel routing, which is the part an inundation model depends on.
    • Learned regionalisation inside a distributed model, at median NSE 0.6–0.71 and about 30% better than a lumped calibrated baseline, now extended to a distributed hybrid flood framework.
    • Answered the extrapolation charge directly: beat the LSTM on unseen events of five-year return period and above, with the margin widening as events grew rarer.

    LIMITATIONS SO FAR

    • Still needs a large regional training sample — it solves the mechanism problem, not the data problem.
    • High implementation cost. It requires a differentiable implementation of the process model, which most operational codes are not.
    • A young field with few independent replications; much of the evidence comes from a small number of groups.
    • Evidence is concentrated on CONUS and CAMELS, plus one French flash-flood region.
    • Low-flow trends stayed weak for every model tested, hybrid and neural alike.
    • In the routing work, channel geometry proved unidentifiable from downstream hydrographs; only roughness could be recovered, and only with moderate precision.

    Read these first

    Start with these. Between them they cover most of what this section concludes. Key points opens a short summary of each paper and why it comes first.

    1. R86Shen et al. 2023 Nature Reviews Earth & Environmentwhat differentiable modelling is for

      Main points

      • The field’s own statement of what differentiable modelling is for.
      • Process models offer interpretability and physical consistency but struggle with large datasets; deep networks predict well but cannot answer specific scientific questions.
      • Differentiable modelling computes gradients through process equations, so neural networks can learn unknown relationships inside a physical structure.

      Why read it first

      It is the orienting perspective for Family 7, in the strongest venue cited in this review.

    2. R83Feng et al. 2022 WRRprocess structure at LSTM accuracy

      Main points

      • Builds differentiable models (δHBV) on an HBV backbone with embedded neural networks that learn the parameterisation.
      • Median NSE 0.732 across 671 US basins against 0.748 for a state-of-the-art LSTM with the same setup (0.715 against 0.722 on a second forcing set).
      • Also outputs soil and groundwater storage, snowpack, evapotranspiration and baseflow, none of which it was trained on.

      Why read it first

      It is the proof that a process model can approach LSTM accuracy while keeping its states, the premise of Family 7.

    3. R85Feng et al. 2023 HESSholding up in unseen regions

      Main points

      • Tests differentiable models under regional holdout, where whole regions are excluded from training, against an LSTM.
      • Median NSE 0.56–0.62 for the differentiable models against 0.55 for the LSTM.
      • High-flow (Q98) trend R²: the LSTM falls from 0.76 to 0.27 in the holdout while the differentiable models stay near 0.77.

      Why read it first

      It is the strongest published case for keeping process structure where data-driven models are weakest: unseen regions and changing trends.

    4. R94Song et al. 2026 WRRbeating the LSTM on rare extremes

      Main points

      • Tests differentiable δHBV versions against an LSTM on unseen extreme events in CAMELS, stratified by return period.
      • δHBV1.1p beats the LSTM for events of 5-year return period and above, with the margin growing with rarity: 0.06 higher median NSE and lower peak error in 80% of the rare events.
      • States the mechanism: mass balance and first-order fluxes let the model output values outside the range of its training data.

      Why read it first

      Together with Baste et al. 2025, it turns the idea that process structure buys extrapolation from an argument into a measured result.

    Section 11 · Shared by Families 4 and 5

    The geometry layer: terrain and channel shape

    Terrain, channel shape and the global datasets that supply them. This is not an eighth family: nothing here estimates a discharge. It is the prior that turns an observed water surface into a flow quantity; without it, Families 4 and 5 have a signal and no units.

    Family 4 needs width, height and slope at once; Family 5 observes one proxy with no way to express it in m³/s. Both need geometry never measured at the site: height of ground above the channel, bed shape below the water, bankfull width and depth. That geometry is now a set of global, a priori layers.

    • Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND) normalises each cell’s elevation to the drainage it flows to (Rennó et al. 2008; Nobre et al. 2011). One HAND contour predicts inundation extent without flood observations (Nobre et al. 2016).
    • Synthetic rating curves: stepping the level through HAND gives reach geometry and a stage–discharge curve (Zheng et al. 2018b), but only after a bottom shift from a calibrated HEC-RAS model and per-site Manning’s n, on two US rivers with 10 m terrain. It is the closest precedent for turning HAND geometry into flow.
    • The bed below the water, which no elevation product sees: power-law sections give analytical hydraulic geometry from one shape exponent (Dingman 2007), building on Leopold & Maddock 1953 and tested by Dingman & Afshari 2018.
    • Global layers: bankfull width and depth (Andreadis et al. 2013), water occurrence (Pekel et al. 2016), river width (Allen & Pavelsky 2018), bare-earth elevation (Hawker et al. 2022) and a non-convergent river network (Wortmann et al. 2025). Being global and fixed in advance makes gauge-free methods possible, and also limits their accuracy.

    The geometry layer at a glance

    Five layers of prior information, and the order they arrived in. None of them produces a discharge on its own — each one supplies a piece of the geometry that turns an observed water surface into a flow quantity. The left column is the terrain lineage; the right-hand column is the hydraulic route this layer is an alternative to.

    Solid arrows mark a documented build-on or extension; dashed arrows mark a study that tests, benchmarks or limits another. Where an arrow reflects this review’s reading rather than an explicit statement in the papers, the text says so.

    Why this sits outside the seven families

    • The families are sorted by what reaches the ungauged basin: a donor, a regional relation, a physical prior, a satellite view of the river, a proxy, a trained network. Geometry is static and global, and on its own it produces no discharge. Add one water observation and it gives an area, a depth and a volume.
    • It removes the bottleneck of two families. Family 5 has plenty of signal but no units; Family 4 has a flow law with terms it cannot observe. Both gaps are geometric.
    • It is what a conceptual inundation model is built from (HAND, reach network, bankfull geometry, routing), used in reverse: inundation from discharge rather than discharge from inundation (§13).

Averaged over 20 cross-sections the at-a-station exponents are b = 0.26, f = 0.40, m = 0.34; in the downstream direction at mean annual discharge they are about 0.5, 0.4 and 0.1.     How accurate is the prior, really?

    Every gauge-free geometry method inherits these errors. In short: the horizontal layers are good, the vertical ones are not.

    • Width is checked against satellites. Global bankfull width was 8–62% off on nine major rivers, at correlation 0.88 (Andreadis et al. 2013). Standard parameterisations capture only 30–40% of global width variance; machine learning raised that to R2 0.81 (Lin et al. 2020).
    • Depth is not measured from space (SWOT does not measure it; Biancamaria et al. 2015). Every global bankfull depth is itself an inference; its confidence bounds are all that is known.
    • DEM source matters more than grid size. Resolution from 3 to 20 m had no significant effect on flood-extent quality, while better elevation data (lidar 3DEP rather than NHDPlus HR) improved about 80% of catchments (Aristizabal et al. 2024). Lidar is not needed everywhere, and a resolution test should come back flat.
    • When HAND mapping is wrong, the error splits between a wrong discharge and a wrong synthetic rating curve, and some configurations reliably misstate depth (Garousi-Nejad et al. 2019; Li et al. 2023).

    Where this layer stands

    ADVANCES SO FAR

    • Channel geometry without survey: reach-averaged HAND geometry gives a synthetic rating curve where no cross-section was measured.
    • Inundation extent becomes predictable: one HAND contour maps flood extent with no flood observations.
    • A shape parameter turns area into depth: a power-law section specifies the bed by one exponent.
    • Global a priori layers for every term: bankfull width and depth, water occurrence, bare-earth elevation, a non-convergent river network.
    • Better elevation data improved flood extent in about 80% of catchments; resolution between 3 and 20 m changed only compute time.

    LIMITATIONS SO FAR

    • Nothing here estimates discharge; every layer needs a water observation from Family 4 or 5.
    • Large errors in global channel layers: bankfull width 8–62% off on nine major rivers; reach schemes capture 30–40% of width variance; depth is worse and not measured from space.
    • HAND fails where the synthetic curve misstates depth, where network conditioning changes the result, and on flat terrain.
    • No bathymetry: in-bank volume is assumed from a shape parameter and a database bankfull depth.
    • Validation is mostly Northern-Hemisphere and large-river (US catchments for HAND; the largest rivers for bankfull databases).

    Read these first

    Start with these. Between them they cover most of what this section concludes. Key points opens a short summary of each paper and why it comes first.

    1. R97Leopold and Maddock 1953 USGS Professional Paper 252the origin of hydraulic geometry

      Main points

      • Shows that width, depth, velocity and suspended load vary with discharge as power functions at a cross-section and downstream.
      • Averaged over 20 cross-sections, the at-a-station exponents are b = 0.26, f = 0.40 and m = 0.34; because Q = wdv, they sum to 1 identically.
      • Warns that averaging the exponents “does not imply any expectation that the values should be closely similar” between rivers.

      Why read it first

      It is the origin of hydraulic geometry, the relation every width-based and geometry-based discharge method still rests on.

    2. R104Nobre et al. 2016 Hydrological Processesinundation extent from terrain alone (HAND)

      Main points

      • Uses the Height Above the Nearest Drainage (HAND) terrain model to map potential inundation extent from a single contour.
      • The method is static and calibration-free, and does not depend on flood observations; validated against a flood event in southern Brazil.
      • It gives potential extent for a given stage: the stage itself must come from elsewhere.

      Why read it first

      It is the primary source for the HAND contour as an inundation predictor, which a conceptual inundation model builds on.

    3. R110Zheng et al. 2018b JAWRAa rating curve from HAND, and its hidden calibration

      Main points

      • Steps the water level up through the HAND grid, reads reach-averaged channel geometry, and builds a synthetic rating curve with Manning’s equation.
      • Reach-averaged width matched HEC-RAS to 3.2%; the rating curve sat 0.02 m from HEC-RAS at the fitted n = 0.043.
      • Not gauge-free: a bottom shift is read off a calibrated HEC-RAS model, and roughness needs per-site tuning (best-fit n up to 0.15).

      Why read it first

      It is the closest published precedent for turning HAND geometry into a flow quantity, and it shows where the shortcuts hide.

    4. R103Andreadis et al. 2013 WRRthe global bankfull prior and its uncertainty

      Main points

      • Builds a near-global bankfull width and depth database by applying hydraulic-geometry equations across HydroSHEDS, with 95% confidence intervals.
      • Width checked against Landsat on nine major rivers: errors 8–62%, correlation 0.88. Depth checked on two US rivers: mean error 24%.
      • Width and depth are essentially functions of drainage area, so regression uncertainty propagates straight into them.

      Why read it first

      It is the standard source of a bankfull prior for ungauged reaches, and it ships its own uncertainty band.

    5. R108Dingman and Afshari 2018 Journal of Hydrologybed shape, verified in the field

      Main points

      • Field-verifies the analytical at-a-station hydraulic-geometry relations of Dingman (2007) on 109 surveyed cross-sections at 34 New Zealand reaches (bankfull width 8–234 m).
      • Fits between the quasi-analytical and empirical coefficients and exponents are highly significant.
      • But the shape exponent is fitted to a measured section, and the velocity–depth exponent is “generally considerably different from conventional uniform-flow equations such as Manning/Chezy”.

      Why read it first

      It is the verification behind using a bed-shape exponent with a bankfull width and depth, and it marks exactly what still needs a survey.

    Section 12 · Shared by all seven families

    Data, benchmarks and uncertainty

    Data, benchmarking and uncertainty

    Three issues cut across every family above, and reviewers will expect a PUB paper to engage with them.

    Large-sample datasets — and their quality problem

    Table scrolls sideways →

    • Newman et al.: 671 minimally disturbed basins from the USGS HCDN-2009 reference gauges; daily forcing for 1980–2010 from Daymet (1 km), plus Maurer and NLDAS (12 km), as basin means, HRUs and elevation bands; USGS daily streamflow

    The practical conclusion: use original national data where it exists, use Caravan where it does not, and say which you used and why. For an Australian study the original is CAMELS-AUS, and it is the right default — it carries rating-curve uncertainty for three-quarters of its catchments and ships several atmospheric datasets, so forcing and observation uncertainty can both be examined rather than assumed away. Newer national editions (CAMELS-DE, CAMELS-CH, CAMELS-FR, CAMELS-DK, CAMELS-IND and others released 2023–2026) keep widening the coverage.

    Benchmarking and metrics

    • NSE under-predicts peaks; report its parts (Gupta et al. 2009). NSE peaks when variability ratio α = r < 1. On 49 Austrian basins, NSE calibration kept α near one in 18% of basins, KGE calibration in all. Give r, α and β with any score. Read in full 17 October 2026.
    • NSE and KGE are not comparable (Knoben et al. 2019). The mean-flow benchmark is NSE = 0 but KGE ≈ −0.41. Always say “better than what”.
    • The bar to beat: simple models on 1,100+ British catchments reach median NSE 0.72–0.78 (Lane et al. 2019), and every method must get the same data (Arsenault et al. 2023).

    Uncertainty and equifinality

    • The benchmark itself is uncertain (Westerberg et al. 2016; 43 UK catchments). Signatures carry ±10–15% (mean flow) to ±30–40% (high and low flows), and a long record does not cancel it because rating error is systematic. Ignoring it dropped regionalisation reliability to 18% from 83–93%: gauging error gets read as catchment behaviour. Read in full 17 October 2026.
    • Donor choice matters; equifinality does not (Arsenault and Brissette 2014; 268 Quebec catchments: “equifinality does not contribute significantly”). Average model outputs from four to seven donors, use few descriptors (four was optimal), and expect at most 75% success. No basin attribute predicts which method works. Corrected 17 October 2026 from the full text.

    Incommensurability: the concept this review was missing

    A model prediction and a measurement are often different quantities under the same name, because of scale, support and heterogeneity (Beven 2005). An inundation-derived signal and gauged discharge are such a pair. Judge models against an effective observation error that need not be zero-mean or Gaussian; if no model fits inside it, that itself points to structural, conceptual or data error. Read in full 17 October 2026.

    Read these first

    Start with these. Between them they cover most of what this section concludes. Key points opens a short summary of each paper and why it comes first.

    1. R126Addor et al. 2017 HESSthe dataset behind Families 6 and 7

      Main points

      • The CAMELS dataset: catchment attributes for 671 minimally disturbed US basins, with the hydrometeorology of Newman et al. (2015).
      • Attributes in six classes: topography, climate indices, hydrological signatures, land cover, soil and geology, with competing sources used to expose attribute uncertainty.
      • The benchmark model is worst in the arid High Plains and desert Southwest, and the data are small headwater basins with no discharge uncertainty.

      Why read it first

      It is the dataset most Family 6 and 7 results are trained and tested on, so its limits are their limits.

    2. R118Knoben et al. 2019 HESSthe metric trap: NSE versus KGE

      Main points

      • Shows that the mean-flow benchmark gives NSE = 0 but KGE = 1 − √2 ≈ −0.41.
      • So NSE and KGE values cannot be compared directly, and a negative KGE above −0.41 still improves on the mean flow.
      • Recommends purpose-dependent evaluation with explicit benchmarks, such as a KGE skill score.

      Why read it first

      Read it before writing any efficiency score into a results section: it prevents the most common misreading of KGE.

    3. R40Westerberg et al. 2016 WRRhow uncertain the signatures themselves are

      Main points

      • Quantifies signature uncertainty that comes from discharge-data uncertainty, by Monte Carlo sampling of feasible rating curves, for 43 UK catchments.
      • The highest uncertainties, a median relative ±30–40%, are in signatures of high- and low-flow magnitude and dynamics.
      • Propagates these uncertainties into signature regionalisation alongside the regionalisation uncertainty itself.

      Why read it first

      Signatures are the currency of classification and signature-based calibration, so their own uncertainty propagates into everything built on them.

    4. R123Clerc-Schwarzenbach et al. 2024 HESSthe cost of standardised forcing

      Main points

      • Compares Caravan’s re-derived ERA5-Land forcing with the original CAMELS-US, -BR and -GB data for the same 1,252 catchments.
      • Mean annual precipitation differs by −53% to +101%, and Caravan’s PET is unrealistically high in many catchments.
      • Caravan forcing degraded calibration performance in most catchments, mainly because of precipitation; the authors recommend the original data wherever possible.

      Why read it first

      Read it before using Caravan forcing for anything: standardisation has a measurable cost.

    Section 13

    Open gaps and where the field is heading

    Research gaps since PUB: which were resolved, and by what

    The gaps the literature named during and after the PUB decade, in one ledger: the ones published work has since closed, the ones it has narrowed, and the ones still open.

    How to read the status column

    The status is this review’s reading of the cited evidence, not a verdict from the sources. Resolved means the gap as it was posed now has a published answer, valid where the conditions of those studies hold. Partly resolved means real progress with a central part still missing. Open means the literature documents the gap but does not yet answer it. The open gaps are discussed in the cards that follow.
