    Of the 22 gaps, 9 are resolved, 7 partly resolved and 6 open. The resolved ones cluster mostly in Families 1, 2 and 6, where large gauged samples made controlled comparisons possible. The open ones cluster where gauges are absent: arid regions, regions with no gauges at all, and the depth below the water surface. That is also where the §14 programme sits.

    Gaps the literature names explicitly

    A 2025 systematic review of AI methods for ungauged streamflow (Gacu et al. 2025, Water 17(18), 2722) sets out the field’s own list of unresolved problems:

    • Inconsistent evaluation protocols and non-standardised metrics make cross-study comparison difficult.
    • Poor transferability across heterogeneous regions, with no standardised similarity metric for selecting donors.
    • Limited reproducibility — few open benchmarks, little shared code.
    • Insufficient integration of physical knowledge into AI models.
    • Underdeveloped uncertainty quantification and interpretability.
    • Geographic imbalance — about 47% of reviewed studies are from Asia and 35% from North America; Africa and Oceania together account for under 5%.
    • Robustness under non-stationarity (land-use and climate change) and real-time deployment in data-scarce settings are both underexplored.
    A caution on that source

    Resolved on 17 October 2026 by reading the full text. The paper identifies 239 records, includes 120 studies, and cites 33 more “to support specific ideas and contextual discussions” — while the Figure 3 caption says 143 reviewed studies. 120 + 33 is 153, so no reading of the text reproduces 143. Quote 120 as the number of included studies and do not quote 143 at all. It is also one of two MDPI venues in this review, the other being Gleason and Durand (2020) in Remote Sensing, and it is cited for its own stated list of gaps rather than for a finding.

    Six gaps I would add from this reading

    • The data paradox. The best methods (LSTM, differentiable) need CAMELS-scale samples from well-gauged countries, and the gauges behind them are shrinking: about two-thirds of national networks are in decline, a loss that “will gradually erode the performance and reliability of AI-based tools” (Olsson et al. 2026). Transfer learning (§09) and surrogate discharge (§08) are two answers, never benchmarked against each other.
    • Discharge is not the only ungauged variable. The literature scores discharge at a point. Depth, velocity, inundation extent and flood timing are what applications need, and a discharge-trained network predicts none of them.
    • The two halves of the surrogate family are rarely combined. River signals get hydrograph shape; ET and storage constraints get volume. Only Hulsman et al. (2020) use both (GRACE, then altimetry, one Zambian basin). An imagery proxy plus an ET or storage constraint is untested.
    • Satellites and models are loosely coupled. SWOT gets the dynamics with about 50% median bias (Andreadis et al. 2025); network-scale assimilation now exists (Larnier et al. 2025, §07) but is not yet routine.
    • No cross-family benchmark. No study compares all seven families on one dataset under one protocol; §03 had to be assembled from incompatible experiments.
    • Observation-based skill under change is untested. Families 4 and 5 observe the river rather than transfer a relation from donors or training basins, so in principle they should hold up after land-use or climate change, where Families 1, 2 and 6 assume the relation still holds. No study in this review tests that.

    The niche for a conceptual inundation model

    This card is my synthesis, not a sourced claim: a framing to test against your own results. LSTMs have largely settled point-discharge accuracy where data are rich, so competing on NSE at a gauge is weak ground. The defensible ground is where deep learning structurally cannot go:

    • Spatial output. An inundation model predicts a field (extent, depth), not a scalar. Feng et al. (2023) made the same case for ET, which differentiable models reproduced untrained and an LSTM could not.
    • A ready calibration target. §08 calibrates against satellite signals, and water extent is one of them, from passive microwave (Revilla-Romero et al. 2015) and SAR (Han et al. 2026). For an inundation model, extent is both output and observation, a loop no discharge-only method closes.
    • Extrapolation is now a measured limit. A stand-alone LSTM cannot predict above a ceiling below its own training maximum (Baste et al. 2025); under regional holdout its high-flow trend R2 fell from 0.76 to 0.27 while differentiable models held near 0.77 (Feng et al. 2023); and δHBV beat an LSTM on unseen events of 5-year return period and above, by more as events got rarer (Song et al. 2026).
    • Cost. Conceptual inundation models exist because full hydrodynamics is too expensive at scale, an argument that grows with domain size (§10).

    The strongest counter-argument. Nearing et al. (2020), WRR: deep learning extracts more from large datasets than hydrologists have turned into theory, and the preference for process models is “deeply subjective and nonevidence-based”. Answer it rather than pass over it.

    The reply. Beven (2020), Hydrological Processes 34(16), 3608, argues the uniqueness of place: catchments are not interchangeable samples, which is what a single regional network assumes. The same idea kept a community-model proposal off the 2019 UPH shortlist (§02).

    The honest position: process models often do not predict discharge better, but they predict different things (fields, internal states, untrained variables) and stay constrained beyond the training range. A framing for your introduction: PUB has moved from “can we predict discharge without a gauge?” (largely yes, given a regional sample) to “can we predict the hydraulic quantities people need where there is no regional sample?” That question is open, and it is where a conceptual inundation model sits.

    Read these first

    Start with these. Between them they cover most of what this section concludes. Key points opens a short summary of each paper and why it comes first.

    1. R9Gacu et al. 2025 Waterthe gaps the field names itself

      Main points

      • A systematic review of AI methods for streamflow in ungauged watersheds: 239 records identified, 120 studies included, 33 more cited.
      • Lists the field’s own unresolved problems: inconsistent evaluation, poor transferability, limited reproducibility, weak physics integration and uncertainty quantification.
      • Geographic imbalance: about 47% of studies from Asia and 35% from North America; Africa and Oceania together under 5%.

      Why read it first

      It is cited for its own stated list of gaps, which this review uses as a checklist. Quote 120 as the number of included studies; its Figure 3 says 143, which the text does not support.

    2. R10Olsson et al. 2026 npj Natural Hazardsthe data paradox

      Main points

      • A commentary on the paradox of AI advances built on declining in-situ networks in hydrometeorology.
      • Roughly two-thirds of national hydrological networks are in decline (citing a 2018 World Bank assessment); river-flow series available through the GRDC have trended down since the mid-1980s.
      • Warns that the decline “will gradually erode the performance and reliability of AI-based tools”, and proposes countermeasures.

      Why read it first

      It frames why prediction without gauges matters more each year, and why the most data-hungry methods face a shrinking foundation.

    3. R78Nearing et al. 2020 WRRthe case for deep learning, at its strongest

      Main points

      • Argues that deep learning reveals far more information in large hydrological datasets than hydrologists have turned into theory or models.
      • Says the community holds “deeply subjective and non-evidence-based preferences” for models built on a particular notion of process understanding.
      • Calls for a quantitative understanding of where and why process knowledge adds value.

      Why read it first

      It is the strongest form of the case against process models, and anyone defending one should answer it.

    4. R79Beven 2020 Hydrological Processesthe reply: uniqueness of place

      Main points

      • A direct reply to Nearing et al. (2020), from the author they cite.
      • Finds it “somewhat disconcerting to have something you wrote more than 30 years ago cited” as though it were still current.
      • Argues for the uniqueness of place: catchments are not interchangeable samples from one population, which is what a single regional network assumes.

      Why read it first

      Read it with Nearing et al. 2020: together they are the debate the review’s position on process models rests on.

    Section 14 · Positioning

    Where this research programme stands, and what to watch

    One research programme read against the literature above: a conceptual inundation model, geometric surrogates for reach discharge, and a gauge-free conversion of satellite water extent into a volume.

    Statements about the literature are sourced to §16. Statements about the work come from its own analysis logs, are labelled as such and have not been independently checked; open numbers are marked open.

    Where it sits

    The programme is Family 5 crossed with the geometry layer. It takes Family 5’s unitless satellite signal and supplies the scale from channel geometry (HAND, bankfull width and depth, a power-law bed), turning water area into a volume in m³, where Yoon et al. (2024) take it from climate through Budyko.

    It joins two published points: Han et al. (2026) turn SAR extent into a streamflow inference but stop at the pixel count; Zheng et al. (2018b) turn HAND geometry into a rating curve but use no satellite. Satellite extent in, terrain geometry as the transfer function, volume out: the join is the contribution.

    Geometry as the source of scale is gaining ground. Magnitude is the main weakness of Families 4 and 5 (§07, §08), and the recent fixes for it all add geometry: priors by river type (Brinkerhoff et al. 2020), bathymetry from altimetry and imagery with a width-to-depth function (Scherer et al. 2024), and bathymetry inferred along a river network (Larnier et al. 2025), and channel geometry with Manning to turn model flow into the observed water level and area (Liu et al. 2015; Hulsman et al. 2020). That supports this programme’s claim that geometry can replace climate as the source of scale. Scherer et al. 2024 is now the closest gauge-free precedent and the one to position against. For a SAR-area signal at low flow, where Han et al. 2026 report weak discrimination, note that reflectance beat width on narrow rivers (Hao et al. 2024).

    It is also a conceptual inundation model (HAND, a reach network, bankfull geometry, variable-parameter Muskingum–Cunge routing) run forwards from discharge to inundation; the surrogate analysis runs it backwards. Keep the two directions distinct in the paper, because the synthetic validation depends on it.

    • Bed shape is fitted from observations in two methods and tested in a third: Chen et al. 2026 (r 1.0–9.8) and Wu et al. 2023 (r 4.1–7.7) fit it; Legleiter and Kinzel 2026 find the symmetric single-exponent shape the least reliable of four for depth. Assuming one shape, as here, is the step a referee will question first.
    • Depth from observations instead of a regression: Chen (fitted bed level), Scherer et al. 2024 (level–area pairs plus a width-to-depth rule) and, globally where altimetry crosses, Paris et al. 2026 (mean depth from rating curves). This programme takes it from a drainage-area regression, which is why the DEPTH5–DEPTH95 band has to be carried through.
    • Everyone else who uses geometry also reports discharge skill: Chen NSE 0.84, Hulsman et al. 2020 NSE 0.60, Scherer NSE 0.56, Liu et al. 2015 NSE 0.758, and the parent method Han et al. 2026 NSE 0.47–0.53. This programme reports only correlation so far.
    • What no other row has: a scale in m³ from terrain alone, with no gauge, no altimetry track and no climate formula. That is the contribution to state, once discharge skill is reported.

    It repairs a named weakness of the parent methodSupportedA curved bed gives every in-bank image its own volume instead of the same bankfull constant. Han et al. (2026) names the weakness in words, not in a threshold: performance is weaker in “persistently low-flow” reaches, where “pixel-count variability” is higher and “discriminative power” lower, and its Daly quadratic “exhibits a locally nonphysical segment near the lower boundary of the observed range”. Your 494 in-bank images sit in that regime. Corrected 17 October 2026 from the full text. This cell previously cited “rank correlation 0.80 at high flow but 0.46 below 100 m³/s”. Neither number is in the paper, which states that its “results did not support a universal discharge cutoff”; the 100 m was an elevation cutoff for the analysis domain at Pilseung Bridge, not a discharge threshold.Report in-bank and overbank skill separately, as you already do — and argue the regime in the parent’s own terms (pixel-count discrimination at low flow), not with a cutoff it declined to set.
    The relation transfers between rivers, where a pixel count cannotUntested — and the strongest claim availableBecause the transformation is built from each reach’s own Wb, Db and HAND, it differs reach by reach, so the monotone-transformation objection does not apply across sites. Your four-catchment model result points this way but is synthetic, and the SAR validation is one river.Fit one relation across several sites for SRvol and one for SAR area. If volume pools and area needs a per-site fit, that is a genuine, publishable result.

    The ordering matters more than any single row. The claim most likely to be made in a first draft — that a volume carries more information than an area — is the one the data refute. The claim least likely to be made is the one worth the paper.

    What this contributes to the gaps the literature names

    The claims above are about whether the work holds up. This table is about whether it matters — each open gap the literature states, what this programme does about it, and how far that actually gets.

    Of the thirteen gaps below, the work addresses three directly, narrows four, opens a route into two, leaves one untested — and does not touch three. One of those three it currently makes worse, which is said plainly in the table rather than left out of it.

    The gaps come from three places: the community’s own list of unsolved problems (§02), the AI-for-PUB review’s stated gaps and the ones this review adds to them (§13), and limitations the surrogate papers write about themselves (§08). Every source the gaps rest on has now been read in full, and the cells say so.

    One experiment that would close three gaps at once

    The table keeps pointing to the same missing piece: a second site, dry, outside Asia and North America. An Australian dryland reach does four jobs in one experiment.

    1. It tests the contribution where it is strongest. Budyko is compromised in arid and semi-arid regions (Yoon et al. 2025); geometry is not. Two cautions: extent-based gauging does poorly in arid regions, “where flow pulses are few and recede rapidly” (van Dijk et al. 2016), and the worst AMHG failure (RMSE 1,083% against 26–27% elsewhere) was the semi-arid, anabranching Rio Grande (Gleason and Smith 2014). The damage comes from an unstable multi-thread planform at low flow, not aridity as such. Choose a semi-arid, single-thread, geomorphically stable reach with real flow variability, and show the planform. Added 17 October 2026 after reading both papers in full; the first version recommended an arid reach with no caveat.
    2. It turns the untested claim into a tested one. Two reaches with different Wb, Db and HAND are the minimum for asking whether one SRvol relation holds where a SAR-area relation needs refitting.
    3. It answers the one-site risk: Pilseung Bridge is Han et al.’s own test case, in the flat terrain his method favours.
    4. It shifts the geographic balance away from the over-represented 47% named by the AI review.

    No fieldwork is needed: Sentinel-1, the Copernicus DEM and the JRC water layer are free, Australian gauge records are public, and CAMELS-AUS (§12) carries rating-curve uncertainty for three-quarters of its catchments, so the NSE can be reported honestly.

    The site selection is my suggestion, not a result. The table establishes only that these four requirements overlap.

    What to watch out for

    Table scrolls sideways →

    RiskSeverityWhy it bitesWhat to do about it
    The monotone-transformation objectionHighA referee who reads your sensitivity table will see the identical Spearman and ask what the volume added. If the paper has claimed new information, the argument collapses at that point.Pre-empt it. Say plainly that at a single site the transform is monotone, and that the contribution is units, linearity and cross-site comparability.
    Correlation is not dischargeHighThe parent method has already taken the step you have not. Han et al. (2026) does not stop at correlation: it drives an SRM and reports median NSE 0.47 and 0.53. Corrected 17 October 2026: this row previously said Han reports correlation and so do you. He reports both. Chen et al. (2026) reports NSE 0.84 and KGE 0.86. A correlation study does not supersede a correlation study, and the reader who wants m³/s will notice. There is also a name for the underlying difficulty, and using it will help you. Beven (2005) calls it incommensurability: a modelled quantity and a measured one may share a name without being the same variable, because of scale and support. An inundation-derived flow signal and a gauged discharge are incommensurate in exactly that sense, which is why a correlation is the natural first result — and why converting to m³/s is the step that makes the comparison commensurate rather than merely rhetorical. Knoben et al. (2019) is the reference for why an efficiency needs a stated benchmark — and it carries a number you will need: the mean-flow benchmark is KGE = 1 − √2 ≈ −0.41, not 0, so any KGE above −0.41 already beats the mean flow, and NSE and KGE values cannot be compared with each other.You are one step away: SRvol / L is a flow area and your notebook already computes a Manning velocity. Report NSE and KGE against the gauge.
    The depth term is never observedHighBankfull depth in Andreadis et al. (2013) is a drainage-area regression, and the authors say so: width and depth are “essentially a function of drainage area”, with the regression uncertainties propagating through. It was validated — 24% mean error at two US rivers, against 8–62% for width at nine. Corrected 17 October 2026; the earlier claim that depth was never validated was wrong, and the real weakness is narrower and more defensible: two rivers, and a regression on area. Lin et al. (2020) finds reach-level schemes capture only 30–40% of global width variance. Your Vb inherits both.Propagate DEPTH5/DEPTH95 as the stated uncertainty band on every SRvol, not only in the sensitivity appendix.
    No published rule maps occurrence to bankfullMediumYour choice of a JRC occurrence threshold sets Wb, and Pekel et al. (2016) offers occurrence, not bankfull. Your own notes record that the citation usually invoked for the 70% figure could not be verified.Argue T from the bankfull exceedance frequency and show the T-scan; do not cite a threshold rule that does not exist.
    Synthetic truth is not independent of the geometry being testedHighThe four-catchment result is validated against discharge from your own v6 model — which spreads one lumped reach depth over HAND and loses ~6.5% of volume. The “truth” and the surrogate share a geometry, so agreement is partly built in.Keep the synthetic experiment as a design study and let the gauge comparison carry the validation claim.
    One real site, and it is the parent method’s ownHighPilseung Bridge is Han et al. (2026)’s test case. The paper reports its method is weaker in “levee-confined, storage-influenced, persistently low-flow, and steep reaches”, and includes no alpine or high-altitude basin. Pilseung Bridge is also roughly 50 km downstream of the Hwanggang Dam, whose operation records are not public — so the reach you share with him carries an unobserved upstream control.Add at least one contrasting site. A steep or confined reach tests the bed-shape assumption hardest, and any site without an unmonitored upstream dam removes a confound you currently inherit.
    Your headline correlations are level correlations on persistent seriesHighThe parent method ran this diagnostic on itself and published the result. Han et al. (2026) reports median Pearson 0.71 and Spearman 0.70 for levels, falling to 0.28 and 0.36 for elapsed-time-normalised changes, and concludes that “level correlation alone overstates the strength of short-term co-variation”. Your evidence for the dimensioning claim is a level Pearson rising from 0.758 to 0.902 / 0.920 — the same kind of statistic, on the same kind of series, uncorrected.Run the same diagnostic before a referee does. Report the change-correlation for SAR area and for each bed shape. If the gap between them survives in changes, that is a far stronger result than the level numbers; if it does not, you have learned something you need to know before submission rather than after.
    The polygon width result is unresolvedMediumWidening the water-mask filter from 125 m to 175 m raised SAR area at every flow and dropped Spearman from 0.615 to 0.469. That is a change in the benchmark, and it moves the headline numbers.Resolve it before submission — check the masks for stable land or paddy pixels, and report whichever polygon you keep with the reason.
    Bed shape is metric-dependentMediumThe triangle wins Pearson over all images and the parabola wins in-bank, and your own analysis shows why: Pearson over all images rewards a smaller Vbf. Dingman (2007) gives the analytical basis for a single exponent, and Dingman and Afshari (2018) verified it on 109 surveyed New Zealand sections. Both papers are more qualified, and more useful to you, than the abstracts suggest. Dingman reports that observed exponents at individual sections “commonly fall outside the theoretical ranges”, and the 2018 verification covers sections “at which boundary-grain roughness is the dominant source of resistance” — a scope restriction, not a universal result. But the exponent does not require a survey. Dingman and Afshari give four routes to it (their Table 5), one of which estimates it from paired observations of width and maximum depth, and they close by proposing exactly your programme: that global width relations of the Andreadis et al. (2013) kind “may also be helpful in predicting AHG relations from remotely-sensed data”. They also quote Park (1977) — no significant central tendency for the AHG exponents by climate or geology, and “perhaps the greatest problem remains that of accounting for observed variations in the hydraulic geometry relations” — which means the scatter you inherit is a named open problem in the field, not a defect of your implementation. One new caution falls on your velocity step: the paper finds the velocity–depth exponent “generally considerably different from conventional uniform-flow equations such as Manning/Chézy”, so a Manning velocity imposed on top of a power-law section is internally inconsistent with the geometry it sits on. Rewritten 17 October 2026 from the full text of both papers; the earlier version of this row said the exponent needed a survey, which the full text contradicts.Judge bed shape on in-bank skill only, and say so before showing the all-image numbers. Cite Table 5 for how r is set, and state the Manning inconsistency rather than leaving it to a reviewer.
    A flat DEM-resolution result is the expected resultLowAristizabal et al. (2024) found no significant effect on flood-extent quality between 3 and 20 m, while source quality mattered in ~80% of catchments — but reports significant degradation at 60 and 90 m. So your 5/10/30 m cases should come back flat and your 90 m case should not. Corrected 17 October 2026: the earlier version of this row predicted a flat result across all four, because the coarse-resolution finding is in the full text and not the abstract.Report it as two results, not one: confirmation of the published flat band, plus the degradation point. A clean break between 30 and 90 m is a stronger result than a null, and it tells a user of your method which DEMs are usable.
    The idea is not unprecedented — the execution isMediumExtent as the calibration signal is Revilla-Romero et al. (2015) and van Dijk et al. (2016). Geometry inverted for discharge is Gleason and Smith (2014) and Hagemann et al. (2017). Terrain geometry turned into a rating curve is Zheng et al. (2018b). The PUB handbook itself (Parajka et al. (2013), ch. 10) called in 2013 for “inundation patterns” to constrain models.Position the contribution as the first gauge-free combination of these with globally fixed parameters, and cite the precedents yourself rather than letting a referee supply them.
    Your benchmark carries its own errorMediumEvery skill number in your thesis is computed against gauged discharge treated as truth. Bates (2022), reporting McMillan et al. (2012), puts the error on that truth at ±10–20% for medium and high in-bank flows and up to ±40% out of bank — and notes the skill has not improved in half a century. His Table 1 does the same to your predictor: SAR captures roughly 75% of true flooded area. So your mask-threshold result (Spearman 0.615 to 0.469 between the 125 m and 175 m filters) is a change of the same order as the extent error already present in any SAR scene. That cuts both ways: it means the sensitivity is not evidence of a broken method, and it means no comparison at this precision can separate two variants of your own model. Westerberg et al. (2016) sharpen this per signature, and add the part that is easy to get wrong: rating-curve error is systematic, so it does not average out over a long record — mean flow itself carried ±30–40% at three of their 43 catchments. Added 17 October 2026 from the Bates and Westerberg full texts.State the benchmark error once, early, with the citation — then stop claiming differences smaller than it. It converts your weakest-looking result into a statement about the data, and it is the standard move in this literature rather than a concession.
    HAND has documented failure modesMediumLi et al. (2023) is narrower than this review previously claimed: it compares two HAND implementations in two Iowa watersheds, and two of its three underestimation factors are artefacts of a JavaScript web app. The part that does transfer is drainage-threshold sensitivity — raising the threshold moves nearest-drainage pixels downstream, raises HAND values and shrinks the mapped extent, stabilising only above roughly 8% of the study area. Your HAND grid has the same knob. A second, structural criticism comes from a source a referee is more likely to reach for. Bates (2022) classes HAND with the methods that conserve neither mass nor momentum: it marks a cell flooded whenever the cell sits below the channel water height, so it “does not preserve hydraulic connectivity” and assumes “infinite water mass is available to fill the floodplain”, and he reports that such methods perform significantly less well than codes that solve the shallow water equations. His warning lands close to your own result: studies showing good performance for non-conservation approaches “need to be treated with caution, as it is always possible to find test cases and evaluation metrics that appear acceptable”. That is the metric-dependence problem two rows up, stated by the field’s review of record. Corrected 17 October 2026 from the Li et al. full text; Bates added the same day.Report your drainage threshold and show the extent is stable with respect to it, exactly as they do. Then report where your HAND geometry is least trustworthy — flat floodplains and the bank-slope pixels your dig step touches. Cite Bates yourself on connectivity and mass, and say why it is acceptable here: you are after a reach-integrated flow signal, not a hazard map, and your volume term is bounded by the SAR extent rather than free to fill.

    The three things that would most strengthen it

    1. Report m³/s. Convert SRvol to a mean flow area, apply Manning, and score the result with NSE and KGE. This single change moves the work from the correlation literature into the discharge-estimation literature, where Chen et al. (2026) and the SWOT assessments live. It is the difference between a proxy study and a method. The nearest precedent there is Scherer et al. (2024), RSE: gauge-free Manning on 27 reaches, many under 100 m wide, with bathymetry from altimetry and PlanetScope water area and an empirical width-to-depth function for the part never seen. It reaches median NRMSE 12% and NSE 0.56, and its 90% band covers 91% of in-situ values, which is also the model for point 3.
    2. Pool across sites. Two or three reaches with different widths and bankfull depths would test the one claim that a single site cannot. If one global relation fits SRvol where SAR area needs a per-site fit, the transferability argument is made.
    3. Carry the depth uncertainty through. The bankfull depth is the weakest input and it is never observed. Propagating DEPTH5–DEPTH95 into the reported skill converts the review’s most obvious criticism into a stated, bounded limitation.
    One framing to avoid

    “Next generation of” is a claim about information, and a reader will test it against the rank correlations. “Gives the proxy units and a transferable form” is a claim about dimensioning, and it survives that test. The second is both more modest and more defensible, and it is the one your numbers support.

    Read these first

    Start with these. Between them they cover most of what this section concludes. Key points opens a short summary of each paper and why it comes first.

    1. R63Han et al. 2026 IEEE JSTARSthe parent method, and the bar it sets

      Main points

      • Turns Sentinel-1 SAR water extent into a surrogate discharge with adaptive thresholding and connectivity and geometry filters, for 19 rivers in 13 countries.
      • Median level correlation is about 0.7, but only 0.28–0.36 for elapsed-time-normalised changes: “level correlation alone overstates the strength of short-term co-variation”.
      • Drives an SRM to median NSE 0.47 and 0.53 in two basins; weaker in levee-confined, storage-influenced, low-flow and steep reaches.

      Why read it first

      It is the parent method of the §14 programme, and it already reports NSE and runs the persistence diagnostic, so it sets the bar.

    2. R60Yoon et al. 2024 Journal of Hydrologythe climate-based scale your geometry replaces

      Main points

      • Asks which hydrological signature can convert a unitless surrogate (SR) into discharge, and how accurate it must be.
      • Uses the Budyko mean catchment discharge, which needs only mean precipitation and PET, and tests the model’s sensitivity to it on synthetic and real data.
      • Over 384 Australian stations, analyses the 49 with SR–discharge correlation above 0.6 first; SR is noisiest at low flow.

      Why read it first

      It is the clearest statement of the unit problem in surrogate calibration and of the Budyko fix that the C/M-ratio line now relies on.

    3. R108Dingman and Afshari 2018 Journal of Hydrologywhat a bed-shape exponent can and cannot claim

      Main points

      • Field-verifies the analytical at-a-station hydraulic-geometry relations of Dingman (2007) on 109 surveyed cross-sections at 34 New Zealand reaches (bankfull width 8–234 m).
      • Fits between the quasi-analytical and empirical coefficients and exponents are highly significant.
      • But the shape exponent is fitted to a measured section, and the velocity–depth exponent is “generally considerably different from conventional uniform-flow equations such as Manning/Chezy”.

      Why read it first

      It is the verification behind using a bed-shape exponent with a bankfull width and depth, and it marks exactly what still needs a survey.

    4. R103Andreadis et al. 2013 WRRwhere the depth prior comes from, and its error

      Main points

      • Builds a near-global bankfull width and depth database by applying hydraulic-geometry equations across HydroSHEDS, with 95% confidence intervals.
      • Width checked against Landsat on nine major rivers: errors 8–62%, correlation 0.88. Depth checked on two US rivers: mean error 24%.
      • Width and depth are essentially functions of drainage area, so regression uncertainty propagates straight into them.

      Why read it first

      It is the standard source of a bankfull prior for ungauged reaches, and it ships its own uncertainty band.

    5. R118Knoben et al. 2019 HESShow to report skill without the KGE trap

      Main points

      • Shows that the mean-flow benchmark gives NSE = 0 but KGE = 1 − √2 ≈ −0.41.
      • So NSE and KGE values cannot be compared directly, and a negative KGE above −0.41 still improves on the mean flow.
      • Recommends purpose-dependent evaluation with explicit benchmarks, such as a KGE skill score.

      Why read it first

      Read it before writing any efficiency score into a results section: it prevents the most common misreading of KGE.

    Why the entries below Q1 are here

    Quartile is reported so you can weigh an entry, never used to decide whether it belongs. In this section:

    • R9 — Gacu et al. 2025 (Q2): an MDPI review cited only for its own stated list of research gaps, with its internal study-count inconsistency flagged where it appears.
    • R13 — Parajka et al. 2013 (book): a chapter of the Cambridge handbook, read in full from the PDF you supplied.
    • R16 — Blöschl et al. 2019 (Q2): the community’s own list of twenty-three unsolved problems, published by IAHS in its own journal.
    • R110 — Zheng et al. 2018b (Q2): the primary source for HAND-derived synthetic rating curves — the closest published precedent to turning terrain geometry into discharge.

    §16 sets out the same reasoning for the reference list as a whole.

    Section 15

    Start here: ten papers, in reading order

    If you read nothing else, read these.

    They are ordered by reading sequence, not by year — the full reference list in §16 is grouped by theme and sorted by year ascending.

    Table scrolls sideways →

    #Paper and yearJournalResearch question it addressesWhy read it at this point
    1Hrachowitz et al. 2013Hydrological Sciences Journal 58(6)What did the PUB decade achieve, and what remains open?The authoritative statement of the problem. Everything later is a response to it
    2Parajka et al. 2013HESS 17Under what conditions does each regionalisation method class win?The main cross-study empirical evidence (a meta-analysis of 34 studies); sets the baseline expectations you will be measured against
    3He, Bárdossy and Zehe 2011HESS 15How should the regionalisation literature be organised?The cleanest taxonomy: distance-based vs regression-based. Useful structure for your Introduction
    4Parajka, Merz and Blöschl 2005HESS 9Which scheme transfers conceptual model parameters best?The classic controlled comparison, with the efficiency numbers still quoted today
    5Zhang and Chiew 2009WRR 45(7)Which design choice actually matters: similarity measure, donor count, or extra data?The Australian large-sample study; directly relevant to a UNSW catchment context
    6Kratzert et al. 2019WRR 55(12)Can one regional network beat locally calibrated models in basins it has never seen?The result that reframed the field. Cite this one, not the HESS companion, for PUB
    7Arsenault et al. 2023HESS 27Was the LSTM advantage an artefact of unequal information?Closes the loophole by giving both sides identical data. Sets the current benchmarking standard — though its authors note that their catchment filter “probably favours the LSTM models in all cases”
    8Feng, Beck, Lawson and Shen 2023HESS 27Do differentiable process models hold up in ungauged regions and under climate extrapolation?The strongest published case for keeping process structure. Most relevant paper to your position
    9Gleason and Durand 2020Remote Sensing 12(7)What does “ungauged” mean when data exist but are not shared?Reframes the problem usefully, and orients you in the satellite literature before SWOT results
    10Andreadis et al. 2025GRL 52(9)Do synthetic-data expectations survive real SWOT observations?The newest structural change in the field. Shows what satellite discharge actually delivers

    If you have time for three more

    • Knoben, Freer and Woods (2019), HESS 23(10) — before you write a single efficiency score into your results section.
    • Nearing et al. (2024), Nature 627 — the operational scale the field is now working at.
    • Clerc-Schwarzenbach et al. (2024), HESS 28(17) — before you use Caravan forcing for anything.
    One addition for your own topic

    If the target is a conceptual inundation model rather than point discharge, add Yoon et al. (2024) as an eleventh: it is the clearest statement of the unit problem in surrogate calibration and of the Budyko fix for it, which is the mechanism §08 turns on.

    A note on verification

    Bibliographic details were checked against publisher pages or bibliographic APIs. Every quantitative result quoted was taken from the source paper itself, never from another paper’s description of it. Three tiers of evidence sit behind this review, and it is worth knowing which applies where.

    Read in full or substantially — all 163, after a sustained pass on 17 October 2026 that used the reader’s own authenticated browser and the UNSW library to reach publishers this session cannot. The tier now covers every entry whose numbers appear in the cross-family comparison of §03, the whole of the geometry chain in §11, the surrogate family of §08 end to end, and the machine-learning and differentiable papers of §09 and §10. Entry 16 (the 23 Unsolved Problems) was read at length for §02: the seven themes, the discussion of Questions 17, 19 and 20, the PUB comparison under Question 5, and the stated limitations of the consultation all come from the article text rather than its abstract.

    Abstract verified from the publisher or a bibliographic API — this tier is now empty. It held 18 entries until 17 October 2026: framing and agenda citations (the IAHS decade statements, Razavi and Coulibaly, Willard et al.), the Cambridge handbook, the 1978 ASCE paper, Smith’s 1997 review and a short list still to be attempted. All were then read from local full text. Two cases are partial, and their rows say so. The handbook was read for chapters 1 and 5–13, not cover to cover. Ponce and Yevjevich (entry 98) was read from the authors’ own online edition, because the 1978 journal is not in the UNSW subscription.

    What the last full-text pass changed, 17 October 2026. Four entries changed in substance. 54 (Dembélé et al. 2020) is not gauge-free: the satellite patterns are added to streamflow from 11 gauges, not substituted for it. 50 (Sun et al. 2011, the framework paper) used gauge records thinned to satellite-like sampling, not satellite data. 36 (the SIMFEN paper) now has its authors and pages, and covers Brittany only. 98 (Ponce and Yevjevich) now has the mass-conservation figures behind its limitation. The rest gained numbers from their bodies: Mohamoud’s held-out R2, Desai and Ouarda’s metric-dependent ranking, Sun et al.’s altimetry NSE, Guo et al.’s 33-study medians, and the handbook’s cross-signature finding that skill falls with aridity for every signature.

    Metadata only — this tier is now empty. It held two entries until 16 October 2026, when the reader supplied both as PDFs: the Cambridge handbook chapter (entry 13) and the transfR reference manual (entry 38). Both were then read in full and both entries moved to the top tier. Every source in this review now rests on at least its own abstract.

    Full text, 16 October 2026 — the §08 core. Four more entries moved into the top tier when the reader supplied them: 59 (Yu et al. 2023), 60 (Yoon et al. 2024), 61 (Filippucci et al. 2025) and 62 (Yoon et al. 2025). Most of what their tables already said survived the check unchanged, which is the point of doing it. Four things did not: the SRM paper reports NSE 0.62–0.79 and KGE 0.66–0.84 in its text where its abstract says only “> 0.6”; it states that its discharge underestimates high flows and that the Budyko mean flow is compromised in arid and semi-arid regions; Yoon et al. 2024 explains that SR is referenced in time rather than against a neighbouring dry pixel, and that SR is noisiest at low flow. The same reading turned up the naming disagreement over the C/M, MC and CM ratio, which now has its own warning in §08.

    Full text, 17 October 2026 — a second pass, and the one that found errors. Seventeen more entries were read in full after the reader asked whether anything useful was hidden behind the abstracts. It was. Three statements in this review were wrong, not merely thin:

    Full text, 17 October 2026 — ten references added. Entries 124–133 were added after a count of the review’s own sources showed which works they lean on most that the review did not cite: the PUB science plan, the original CAMELS (two papers), the first MPR paper, Oudin et al. 2010 on physical versus hydrological similarity, regional calibration, Smith and Pavelsky’s Lena width rating, Yadav et al.’s regionalised signatures, Merz and Blöschl 2004 and the decomposition behind KGE. All ten were read in full before anything was written about them.

    Full text, 17 October 2026 — nine Family 4 and 5 references added. Entries 134–142 come from a deep review of the two satellite families with a search from 2015 onwards: the SWOT discharge framework (Durand et al. 2023), surrogate calibration from remote sensing alone (Yoon et al. 2023), gauge-free discharge for narrow rivers (Scherer et al. 2024), the first large-sample test of flow-law inversion (Lin et al. 2023), geomorphic priors (Brinkerhoff et al. 2020), deep learning on reflectance (Hao et al. 2024), network-scale SWOT assimilation (Larnier et al. 2025), the 40 m width floor (Feng et al. 2019) and global satellite gauging reaches (Hou et al. 2020). All nine were read in full before anything was written about them. Reading Yoon et al. 2023 moved one date in §08: the Budyko mean flow entered the surrogate line in 2023, not 2024.

    Full text, 19 October 2026 — fourteen more Family 4 references. Entries 150–163 came from a search of Family 4 approaches from 2015 onwards and from Chen et al. 2026’s own references: bathymetry from water height and width (Schaperow et al. 2019; Wu et al. 2023), entropy-based bathymetry with satellite velocity (Moramarco et al. 2019), ICESat-2 hydraulic models (Coppo Frias et al. 2023; Musaeus et al. 2024), channel-shape approximations tested on 46,971 surveyed sections (Legleiter and Kinzel 2026), SWOT bank shapes (Cerbelaud et al. 2026), altimetry rating curves (Paris et al. 2016, 2026), the Manning roughness route Chen et al. use (Bjerklie et al. 2018), surface velocity from satellite video (Masafu et al. 2023), the first swath-altimetry test (Tuozzolo et al. 2019), global width relations (Frasson et al. 2019) and width rating curves at 2,168 gauges (Riggs et al. 2023). All fourteen were read in full before anything was written about them. Two corrections came with them: Coppo Frias et al. 2023 and Musaeus et al. 2024 are not gauge-free (both drive the hydraulic model with gauged or modelled discharge), and Wu et al. 2023 report bed-elevation errors as a percentage of absolute elevation, so its 1.25–6.18% means 3–11 m. Nature Communications’ quartile and impact factor come from journalmetrics.org.

    Full text, 18 October 2026 — seven width and water-extent references added. Entries 143–149 come from a search for papers that use river width or surface-water extent in place of discharge, Q1 journals first: width-based calibration in a real ungauged basin (Sun et al. 2015), with high-resolution images on a regional river (Sun et al. 2018) and on narrow headwaters (Huang et al. 2022); altimetric level and Landsat water area together (Liu et al. 2015); Landsat water extent at 671 catchments (Meyer Oliveira et al. 2023); Sentinel-1 water area against flow at 15 stations (Ahmad and Kim 2019); and assimilation of water extent at continental scale (Revilla-Romero et al. 2016). All seven were read in full before anything was written about them.

    • Entry 44 (GRUN). Global long-term mean runoff was given as 37,419 km3 yr−1. The paper says 38,452. Corrected in §06.
    • Entry 82 (Höge et al. 2022). §10 said the method “matches state-of-the-art deep learning” — which is the abstract’s claim. The body reports that the LSTM is “considerably better regarding NSE and mNSE”, with the hybrid ahead only on FHV and mNSE. The row now says both.
    • Entry 116 (Aristizabal et al. 2024). The flat DEM-resolution result holds between 3 and 20 m, but the full text reports significant degradation at 60 and 90 m. §11 had only the first half, and on the strength of it §14 advised the reader to expect a flat result across a 5/10/30/90 m comparison. That advice was wrong and is now reversed.

    Five further statements were true but materially incomplete, and the omission flattered the source each time: entry 46 (World-Wide HYPE beats gridded global models, but at a median monthly KGE of 0.4 that its own authors say most modellers would judge poor); entry 41 (the best gauge-corrected precipitation product is one the paper says is unlikely to translate to sparsely or ungauged regions); entry 84 (the authors state their catchment filter “probably favours the LSTM models in all cases”); entry 120 (CAMELS-GB’s abstraction data cover England only); and entry 88 (numerical compensation obscures the physical meaning of the calibrated parameters — which cuts against the interpretability case that family rests on).

    Four numbers were sharpened rather than corrected: entry 123 gives the Caravan precipitation discrepancy as −53% to +101% and attributes the calibration loss mainly to precipitation; entry 91 puts the deep-learning ceiling at 73 mm d−1 against a 183 mm d−1 training maximum, and reports that the hybrid has no such limit at all; entry 118 supplies the figure anyone reporting KGE needs — the mean-flow benchmark is KGE = 1 − √2 ≈ −0.41, not 0; and entry 9’s study-count discrepancy is now resolved exactly (239 identified, 120 included, 33 more cited, against a figure caption saying 143 — no reading reproduces 143).

    Everything else checked out. Entries 85, 72, 22, 15 and 121 were confirmed against their full texts with no change, including every figure in the §03 comparison table that came from them. Three papers could not be promoted because their pages serve only an abstract (Skøien et al. 2006, Samaniego et al. 2017, Sun et al. 2010), and Wiley, Elsevier and IEEE pages do not return text to this session at all — which was why entry 63 (Han et al. 2026) stayed abstract-level until the reader supplied it as a PDF the same day.

    Full text, 17 October 2026 — entry 63, supplied by the reader. Han et al. (2026) is the paper §14 argues against most directly, and reading it overturned what this review said about it. The review had attributed to it a “rank correlation 0.80 at high flow but 0.46 below 100 m³/s”. Neither figure appears in the paper. There is no correlation split by flow regime, and the paper states that its “results did not support a universal discharge cutoff”; the 100 m was an elevation cutoff for the analysis domain at Pilseung Bridge, carried across as if it were a discharge threshold. What the paper reports is a median level Pearson of 0.71 across 19 rivers in 13 countries, ranging from 0.87 down to 0.20 by site.

    Two further things it changed. First, the paper does not stop at correlation: it drives an SRM and reports median NSE of 0.47 and 0.53 for SAR-derived surrogates against 0.40 and 0.48 for SMOS — so §14’s advice to report an efficiency is not a step ahead of the parent method but a step behind it, and now says so. Second, and most consequentially for the reader’s own work, the paper deliberately tests whether its correlations are inflated by shared temporal persistence: level correlations of 0.71 and 0.70 fall to 0.28 and 0.36 for elapsed-time-normalised changes, which it describes as showing that “level correlation alone overstates the strength of short-term co-variation”. That diagnostic has been added to §14 as a risk in its own right.

    Full text, 17 October 2026 — the geometry chain, read through the reader’s own browser. Publisher paywalls that refuse this session were opened from the reader’s authenticated Chrome session. Two more rows were wrong.

    • Entry 110 (Zheng et al. 2018b). §11 said it produced synthetic rating curves “from terrain alone”. It does not. The abstract’s phrase “after some adjustment” covers a bottom shift — 0.64 m of depth and 22 m³/s of discharge for the demonstration reach — read off a calibrated HEC-RAS model, plus per-site tuning of Manning’s n whose best-fit values reach 0.15, far outside the physical range. The row now says so, and the correction strengthens the gauge-free claim §14 makes for the reader’s own method.
    • Entry 115 (Li et al. 2023). §11 described it as setting out the conditions under which HAND fails. It is narrower: a comparison of two HAND implementations across two Iowa watersheds. Two of its three underestimation factors are artefacts of a JavaScript web application — elevation precision lost in a GeoTIFF-to-PNG conversion, and HAND values stored as integers. §14 had cited it as though its failure modes transferred to any HAND workflow; they do not, and that row would have been a mis-citation. What does transfer is its drainage-threshold sensitivity, which is now what both sections cite.

    A correction to this note itself, 17 October 2026. An earlier version said that entries 100, 107 and 108 (Dingman 2007; Allen and Pavelsky 2018; Dingman and Afshari 2018) could not be read because the publishers “refuse to serve to any scripted reader”. That was wrong, and the reader was right to push back on it. Two retrieval methods had never been tried on those domains: a plain page-text read, which worked immediately on Science, and scrolling the page before reading, which triggers ScienceDirect’s lazy loading and returned the full body of Dingman and Afshari. The stopping point had been rationalised as a publisher restriction when it was an untried method. All three entries are now in the top tier.

    • Entry 108 (Dingman and Afshari 2018). The full text reverses the direction of the §14 caution. Their Table 5 gives four routes to the section-shape exponent, one of them from paired observations of width and maximum depth rather than a survey, and the paper closes by proposing that global bankfull-width relations of the Andreadis kind “may also be helpful in predicting AHG relations from remotely-sensed data” — which is this review’s §14 programme, named by the authors. The verification is also scoped to sections where boundary-grain roughness dominates resistance, and it reports the velocity–depth exponent as “generally considerably different from” Manning or Chézy. The §14 row has been rewritten on all three points.
    • Entry 107 (Allen and Pavelsky 2018). The headline figures were right, but the §11 row omitted the part that decides whether the mask is usable on a small catchment: the database is “most accurate and complete at widths wider than 90 m”, only rivers above that threshold entered the statistics, directly observed area is 468,000 km2 of the 773,000, and the remainder is a Pareto extrapolation down to a median first-order width of 32 cm. Added to the row.
    • Entry 100 (Dingman 2007). The summary and conclusions confirm the abstract and the §11 row as written; no change was needed, which is worth recording too.
    • Entry 49 (Sun et al. 2010) — the closest precedent in the whole list. HESS serves this one only as a PDF, which the earlier passes treated as unreachable; it was read by extracting the PDF’s text layer inside the browser. The §08 row had the design and none of the numbers, and the numbers are the point: calibrating a rainfall-runoff model on satellite width alone identifies the hydraulic-geometry parameters sharply while leaving four of five rainfall-runoff parameters unconstrained, and the discharge intervals cover 39.8–70.3% of daily observations depending on the rejection threshold. The paper also states the assumption that a good width simulation implies a good discharge simulation, calls it doubtful, and tests it. All added.
    • Entry 68 (Biancamaria et al. 2015). Springer, through the reader’s authenticated session. The §07 card had the abstract’s motivation and none of the specifications. The body gives the swath geometry, the 20.86-day repeat, the 10 cm accuracy over 1 km2 rather than per pixel, the layover and rain-rate limits, and the 8.1% mean temporal-sampling error on monthly means. Two statements in it are load-bearing for §14: SWOT will not measure water depth, and it is designed for rivers wider than 100 m with a goal of 50 m — so small and medium catchments are outside the mission by design. Added to §07.
    • Entry 64 (Smith 1997) — and an honest limit. Like entry 66, an early review of the area–discharge approach had no row in this review at all. It now has one, built from the abstract, which is unusually substantive: it names area–discharge curves as the route to discharge from space, restricts their extrapolation to ungauged sites to “the special case of braided rivers”, and warns that single-polarisation fixed-frequency SAR is not sufficient in all riverine environments. The body could not be read: Wiley serves the 1997 article as a typeset PDF with no text layer, and three routes were tried (article page, the ePDF viewer, the direct PDF). The row says so, and claims nothing the abstract does not support. This entry therefore stays in the abstract tier. Update, later the same day: a copy with a text layer arrived through the UNSW library. The body confirms every statement in the row and adds two, on per-site curves and on Kruus et al. (1981); entry 64 is now read in full.
    • Entry 31 (Smakhtin 2001). ScienceDirect again, same method. The §05 card summarised the parts on low-flow indices and ungauged estimation. The part this review should have had is the account of transmission losses — bed losses through alluvium, riparian evapotranspiration, recharge where the water table sits below the bed — which Smakhtin says can be substantial during the early stages of flood events and whose regional importance is “largely unknown”. In a dryland reach these losses sit between the inferred flow and the gauge, so they belong in §05 and in the site-selection argument. Added to §05.
    • Entry 20 (Beven 2005). Reached through ScienceDirect with the scroll-then-read method. It had been in the “framing citations that carry no quantitative claim” group, which was a misjudgement: the manifesto contains incommensurability — the argument that a modelled and a measured variable may share a name without being the same quantity — which is the concept this review needed for the gap between an inundation signal and a gauged discharge, and did not have. Added to §13 with the effective-observation-error construction that follows from it, and to the §14 row on correlation.
    • Entry 28 (Prieto et al. 2019). Free access at WRR. The §04 entry described the method and the adequacy tests; the full text supplies the result that makes the tests worth having. The regionalisation was adequate in 12 of 16 held-out catchments and the hydrological model in 1 of 16, from which they conclude that a better conditioning signal does not help while the model itself is inadequate. Added, because it is a direct caution on the shape of this review’s §14 argument.
    • Entry 26 (Arsenault and Brissette 2014) — a seventh correction. Free access at WRR. §13 cited it as the standard reference for why transferring a single best parameter set is fragile, and named equifinality as the reason. The paper concludes the opposite: parameter-set selection matters, but “equifinality does not contribute significantly to the overall uncertainty”. The paragraph has been rewritten, and the findings it does support — output averaging over parameter averaging, four to seven donors, four descriptors rather than all of them, and a 75% ceiling on success rate — added in place of the framing.
    • Entry 40 (Westerberg et al. 2016). Open access at WRR. The review had been citing it for the general point that signature uncertainty is not negligible; the full text supplies per-signature magnitudes and, more usefully, the finding that rating-curve error is systematic and so does not average out — mean flow itself carried ±30–40% at three of 43 UK catchments. Added to §13 and to the new §14 benchmark row.
    • Entry 25 (Winsemius et al. 2009). Free access at WRR all along. The §04 card had the idea but none of the mechanism: how the limits of acceptability are derived from interannual variability rather than chosen, that 99.94% of three million parameter sets were rejected, that only the routing parameters were constrained while evaporation stayed insensitive to every target, and that there is no split-sample validation because concurrent rainfall and runoff do not exist for the basin. All now in the card, because the derivation method is the part a satellite signal can borrow.
    • Entry 66 (Gleason and Smith 2014). Open access at PNAS, and until 17 October this review had no evidence row for it at all — the founding paper of Family 4’s gauge-free line appeared only in the reference list. Two things in the full text change how it should be cited. The AMHG fit is strong for depth and velocity but spans r2 = 0.13–0.97 for width, which is the only one of the three a satellite can measure. And the method’s one catastrophic case, 1,083% RMSE, is a semi-arid intermittently anabranching river — which bears on the site recommendation in §14, now qualified again.
    • Entries 1, 6 and 32 (Seibert and Beven 2009; Parajka et al. 2013; Skøien et al. 2006). A fourth untried method: the Copernicus landing pages serve only abstracts, but the PDF at the sibling URL serves the whole article. All three had been summarised from abstracts, and all three gained numbers that change how firmly the review can lean on them. Seibert and Beven’s “surprisingly little data” is eight to thirty-two measurements reaching about 0.59 against about 0.8 for full calibration. Parajka et al. supply the median efficiencies by method, climate and catchment size that §01 and §04 had only described in words — and a caution, now quoted in §04, that NSE should not be compared across basins of differing seasonality. Skøien et al.’s “more accurate than ordinary kriging” rests on sixteen leave-one-out gauges and bar plots with no error metric reported, which §05 now says.
    • Entry 97 (Leopold and Maddock 1953). Listed here for years as having no electronic full text. The USGS serves the whole 1953 Professional Paper as a public PDF. It supplies the exponent values the §11 row only gestured at, the b + f + m = 1 identity, and one thing worth carrying into §14: the authors themselves write that averaging the exponents “does not imply any expectation that the values should be closely similar”. Their station averages are also drawn mostly from semi-arid western rivers, with humid-region data described as scarce — a caveat on the oldest layer of the geometry chain.
    • Entry 113 (Bates 2022). The same untried method — scroll, then read the page text — opened the Annual Review of Fluid Mechanics, and this was the most valuable retrieval of the day. The §11 row had summarised the abstract and nothing more. The body supplies the measurement-error figures that bound every skill number in this field (±10–20% in bank, ±40% out of bank, from McMillan et al. 2012, with no improvement in half a century), a table of validation-data errors including SAR extent at about 75% of truth, a flat statement that a global bathymetric dataset “is unlikely to exist anytime soon”, and a structural criticism of HAND as a method that conserves neither mass nor momentum. A new §14 row and two rewritten ones come from it.

    What reading entry 13 changed. Four statements in its §05 row had been marked † as general method knowledge because only the title was available. The chapter states them directly, so the marks are gone and the row now carries the chapter’s own numbers: 33 studies in the Level 1 assessment, 3–913 catchments each, median daily NSE 0.54 in arid, 0.64 in cold and 0.66 in humid regions, with overall quartiles 0.53–0.68. It also supplies the attribution for the drainage-area ratio method (Stedinger et al. 1993) and an explicit statement that network-aware geostatistical methods work much better than process-based ones in data-rich regions — which is the handbook agreeing, in its own words, with what §05 concludes from Viglione et al. (2013). Reading it also turned up a passage worth quoting in any inundation paper: the chapter calls for using “inundation patterns” among the proxy data that should constrain model predictions.

    What the 16 October retrieval pass changed. A reader asked whether insights drawn from metadata-only entries could be trusted. Re-deriving the tier list from the records rather than editing it in place moved sixteen entries up into the abstract-verified tier: 17, 20, 26, 36, 37, 48, 64, 65, 68, 86, 97, 98, 99, 100, 101, 102, 105, 106 and 108. Where a claim had been written from a title alone it was rewritten from the abstract — so the §11 evidence table now reports that Dingman’s exponents depend only on the hydraulic depth exponent p and the cross-section form exponent r, that Pekel et al. used three million Landsat images over 32 years at 30 m, and that Ponce and Yevjevich found the three-point and iterative four-point schemes accurate while the two-point scheme is not. §08’s account of the C/M ratio is now sourced to Brakenridge’s own abstract instead of to the later papers that cite it.

    Four sources were reached only because the usual two indexes do not hold everything: OpenAIRE supplies the Elsevier and Wiley abstracts that OpenAlex, Crossref and Semantic Scholar all return empty (Dingman 2007, Rennó 2008, Nobre 2011, Teng 2017, Bates and De Roo 2000, Bjerklie 2003, Beven 2005, Smith 1997, Ponce and Yevjevich 1978), the USGS Publications Warehouse supplies Leopold and Maddock’s, and the publishers’ own pages supply Pekel’s and Biancamaria’s. ScienceDirect remains behind a bot challenge that this review did not attempt to defeat, and did not need to.

    Two corrections found by the same pass. Entry 26 was carrying a shortened title; the full one is “Continuous streamflow prediction in ungauged basins: The effects of equifinality and parameter set selection on uncertainty in regionalization approaches”. And an earlier version of this note described entries 13 and 17 as “the Panta Rhei and HELPING decade papers”; those are entries 14 and 18, and the label had been left behind by a renumbering.

    Two further works — Archfield et al. (2013) and Laaha et al. (2014), in §05 — appear only as findings reported inside de Lavenne et al. (2016) and were not independently verified. They are marked as such where they appear.

    On venue quality

    On the quartiles and impact factors. Every Q·, IF tag on this page comes from Journal Citation Reports 2025 (Clarivate; dataset updated 14 October 2026), read journal by journal through UNSW access. Where a journal sits in several JCR categories its quartile differs between them, and the tag shows the best quartile — Environmental Modelling & Software is Q1 in Water Resources but Q2 in three other categories, Remote Sensing is Q1 in Geosciences and Q2 elsewhere, and JAWRA is Q2 in Water Resources and Q3 in two others. Two venues carry no figure: npj Natural Hazards is too new to have a JIF, and the Cambridge handbook and the transfR package are not journals at all.

    One hundred and thirty-one of the 163 entries are Q1, concentrated in Water Resources Research, HESS, Journal of Hydrology, Remote Sensing of Environment, Nature, Nature Reviews Earth & Environment, Geophysical Research Letters, Science, PNAS, Scientific Data, Earth System Science Data and Environmental Modelling & Software. The remaining 32 are not, and the rest of this card says why each is here.

    Why a sub-Q1 paper is still in the list

    The quartile is reported, never used as a filter. An entry earns its place by being the best available evidence for the claim it supports; the JCR tag is there so you can weigh it, not to decide it. An impact factor describes a journal’s citation rate in 2025 — it says nothing about whether a particular paper is correct, and nothing at all about a paper published before the metric existed. Applied as an inclusion rule it would delete the origin of hydraulic geometry, the founding paper of this review’s own Family 5, and the entire PUB decade.

    The 32 entries below Q1 fall into five groups.

    1. Not a journal, so no quartile exists (6). Entries 4, 11, 12, 13 — the Cambridge handbook and three of its chapters; 38 — the transfR R package on CRAN; 97 — Leopold and Maddock’s 1953 USGS Professional Paper. The last is the most-cited item in its column of §11’s map and predates the Journal Impact Factor by two decades.

    2. The journal carries no JCR figure (2). Entry 10 is in npj Natural Hazards, too new to have been assigned one; entry 98 is in the ASCE Journal of the Hydraulics Division, which ceased publication in 1983. Variable-parameter Muskingum–Cunge was published there and nowhere else.

    3. Q2 or Q3, but the primary source (16). Citing a higher-quartile paper that describes the method second-hand would be worse scholarship, not better. Entries 64 (Smith’s 1997 review, the origin of satellite river-discharge estimation), 50 and 51 (Sun et al. 2011 — the two papers that founded surrogate calibration, which §08 is built on), 33 (Mohamoud 2008, the source for regional flow-duration curves and QPPQ), 104 (Nobre et al. 2016, HAND contour), 110 (Zheng et al. 2018b, HAND synthetic rating curves — the closest precedent in the literature to converting terrain geometry into discharge), 114 (Hawker et al. 2022, the FABDEM dataset paper), 45 (Beck et al. 2020, global distributed parameter regionalisation), 47 (Skoulikaris and Piliouras 2023), 79 (Beven 2020 — the deep-learning counter-argument, made by the person who made it), 80 (Frame et al. 2021, the National Water Model post-processing benchmark), 131 (Yadav et al. 2007, the source of regionalised signature constraints that §04’s signature-conditioning papers build on), 163 (Riggs et al. 2023, satellite width rating curves at 2,168 gauges), 135 (Yoon et al. 2023, surrogate calibration driven by remote sensing alone, tested across 130 catchments), 3 (Razavi and Coulibaly 2012, Q3 — the standard two-decade review of regionalisation methods) and 8 (Willard et al. 2025, Q3 — the survey that names the “predictions in unmonitored sites” framing this review borrows).

    4. The field’s own statements about itself (7). Entries 5, 14, 16, 18, 19, 36 and 124 are in Hydrological Sciences Journal (Q2, IF 2.9) because IAHS publishes its decade reviews and community agendas there. The PUB science plan and decade review, Panta Rhei, the twenty-three unsolved problems and HELPING have no higher-quartile venue — they are the field speaking in its own journal, and a quartile is the wrong instrument for reading them.

    5. Cited for a named, checkable thing rather than for authority (1). Entry 9 (Water, MDPI, Q2) is used only for its own stated list of research gaps, and its internal inconsistency — 120 studies in the methods, 143 in a figure caption — is flagged in §13 where it is cited. The other MDPI venue here, Remote Sensing (entry 72), is Q1 and is the field’s standard orienting review of remote sensing of discharge.

    Two further cautions on reading the tags. A journal in several JCR categories has a different quartile in each, and these tags show the best one — Environmental Modelling & Software is Q1 in Water Resources and Q2 in three other categories; JAWRA is Q2 in Water Resources and Q3 in two others. And the tag describes the journal as it stands in 2025, not as it stood when the paper appeared.
